  434: Broughan's related full-adic result counts prime factors with
  435: multiplicity and identifies closures of the corresponding strata
  436: \cite[Theorem~4.3]{Broughan2003}. The preceding proposition instead
  437: uses distinct prime support, deletes the finite set \(S\), imposes
  438: bounded \(S\)-adic valuations, and computes the intrinsic derivative
  439: rank.
  440: 
  441: \begin{theorem}[Nonunit escape dichotomy and MCF-immunity]
  442:   \label{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}
  443:   Let \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) be an infinite MCFL. Then either
  444:   \[
  445:     \sup_{w\in L}\omega_{S^c}(\val_U(w))=\infty,
  446:   \]
  447:   or there is a prime \(p\mid a_0\) such that
  448:   \[
  449:     \sup_{w\in L}v_p(\val_U(w))=\infty.
  450:   \]
  451:   Consequently the following languages are MCF-immune whenever they are
  452:   infinite:
  453:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
  454:     \item the prime representation language \(\mathcal P_U\);
  455:     \item every language on which \(\Omega(\val_U(w))\) is bounded;
  456:     \item every finite-prime-support language on which all
  457:     \(v_p(\val_U(w))\), \(p\mid a_0\), are bounded.
  458:   \end{enumerate}
  459:   In a unit system, every bounded-\(\omega(\val_U(w))\) language is
  460:   MCF-immune.
  461: \end{theorem}
  462: 
  463: \begin{proof}
  464:   If neither alternative held, finiteness of \(S\) would give
  465:   \(K\ge0\) and \(E\in\NN_0^S\) such that
  466:   \[
  467:     \{\val_U(w):w\in L\}\subseteq X_{K,E}.
  468:   \]
  469:   By \Cref{prop:local-prime-factor-cb-rank}, \(X_{K,E}\) is scattered.
  470:   This contradicts
  471:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-local-adic-fingerprint}. Prime values satisfy
  472:   \(\omega_{S^c}\le1\) and \(v_p\le1\); bounded \(\Omega\) bounds both
  473:   alternatives; and finite prime support bounds \(\omega_{S^c}\), with
  474:   the remaining valuations bounded by hypothesis. If \(S=\varnothing\),
  475:   the second alternative is absent, giving the unit-system assertion.
  476: \end{proof}
  477: 
  478: The second alternative is necessary. In ordinary base \(b\), where
  479: \(a_0=b\), the regular LSD-first language
  480: \(\{0^n1:n\ge0\}\) represents \(b^n\). Its distinct prime support is
  481: fixed, while \(v_p(b^n)\) is unbounded for every \(p\mid b\).
  482: 
  483: \begin{proposition}[Recurrence-witness inflation and strict separation]
  484:   \label{prop:recurrence-witness-separation}
  485:   If a tail has minimal recurrence polynomial \(\mu_U\), then for every
  486:   prime \(p\) it also has a recurrence witness with characteristic
  487:   polynomial \((X-p)\mu_U(X)\).  When \(\abs{\mu_U(0)}=1\), the trailing
  488:   coefficient of this witness has absolute value \(p\).
  489: 
  490:   Moreover, there are two canonical eventually recurrent
  491:   numeration systems with regular representation languages and recurrence
  492:   witnesses whose trailing-coefficient prime set is \(\{p\}\), but with
  493:   opposite bounded-outside-prime escape behavior:
  494:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
  495:     \item ordinary base \(p\) contains the infinite regular language
  496:     \(\{0^n1:n\ge0\}\), whose values are \(p^n\);
  497:     \item the Zeckendorf system, with \(F_0=0,F_1=1\) and
  498:     \(F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_n\), equipped with the order-three recurrence
  499:     witness
  500:     \[
  501:       F_{n+3}=-pF_n+(1-p)F_{n+1}+(p+1)F_{n+2},
  502:     \]
  503:     contains no infinite MCFL \(L\) for which
  504:     \[
  505:       \sup_{w\in L}\omega_{\{p\}^c}(\val(w))<\infty.
  506:     \]
  507:   \end{enumerate}
  508:   Thus the prime divisors of an arbitrarily selected trailing coefficient
  509:   do not determine the escape behavior of the numeration system.
  510: \end{proposition}
  511: 
  512: \begin{proof}
  513:   The polynomial identity \(\mu_U(C)z_J=0\) remains valid after
  514:   multiplication by \(X-p\).  In the companion convention, the trailing
  515:   recurrence coefficient is the negative of the constant term of the
  516:   characteristic polynomial, proving the first assertion.
  517: 
  518:   The base-\(p\) assertion is the preceding example.  For the Zeckendorf
  519:   sequence, multiplication of its minimal polynomial by \(X-p\) gives
  520:   \[
  521:     (X-p)(X^2-X-1)
  522:       =X^3-(p+1)X^2+(p-1)X+p,
  523:   \]
  524:   which is exactly the displayed recurrence and has trailing coefficient
  525:   \(-p\).  This changes neither the sequence nor its regular canonical
  526:   representation language.  On the other hand, its minimal recurrence
  527:   has unit trailing coefficient.  If the displayed supremum were bounded
  528:   by \(K\), then
  529:   \(\omega(\val(w))\le K+1\) on \(L\), contrary to the unit-recurrence
  530:   conclusion of
  531:   \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}.  This proves the separation.
  532: \end{proof}
  533: 
  534: Let
  535: \[
  536:   \mu_U(X)=X^{d_{\mathrm r}}-c_{d_{\mathrm r}-1}X^{d_{\mathrm r}-1}
  537:     -\cdots-c_1X-c_0
  538: \]
  539: be the minimal recurrence polynomial of a tail of \(U\). Since it
  540: divides the characteristic polynomial of a recurrence allowed in
  541: \textup{(U4)}, its constant term is nonzero. Enlarge the recurrence
  542: threshold to \(J_{\mathrm r}\) so that this minimal recurrence holds for
  543: every \(n\ge J_{\mathrm r}\), and put
  544: \[
  545:   S_{\mathrm r}=\{p:p\text{ is prime and }p\mid c_0\}.
  546: \]
  547: 
  548: \begin{definition}[Geometric synchronized scheme]
  549:   \label{def:geometric-synchronized-scheme}
  550:   A geometric synchronized scheme for \(U\) consists of
  551:   \(a\in A^{J_{\mathrm r}}\), an integer \(k\ge1\), integers
  552:   \(c\ge1,b\ge2\), and words
  553:   \[
  554:     u_1,\ldots,u_{k+1},\quad
  555:     v_1,\ldots,v_k,\quad w_1,\ldots,w_k,\quad
  556:     s_1,\ldots,s_k\in A^\ast,
  557:   \]
  558:   such that
  559:   \[
  560:     W(t)=a u_1v_1^tw_1s_1^tu_2\cdots
  561:       u_kv_k^tw_ks_k^tu_{k+1}\in\mathcal R_U
  562:       \qquad(t\ge0),
  563:   \]
  564:   \[
  565:     \sum_{j=1}^k(\abs{v_j}+\abs{s_j})>0,
  566:     \qquad \val_U(W(t))=cb^t\quad(t\ge0).
  567:   \]
  568: \end{definition}
  569: 
  570: \begin{lemma}[Arithmetic input of Evertse]
  571:   \label{lem:evertse-quotient-support-input}
  572:   Let \(K\) be a number field. For \(x\in K^\times\), let \(P_K(x)\)
  573:   be the largest norm of a finite prime ideal \(\mathfrak p\) for which
  574:   \(\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak p}(x)\ne0\), with \(P_K(x)=1\) when
  575:   \(x\) is a unit. If \(Z=(Z(n))_{n\ge0}\) is a nondegenerate linear
  576:   recurrence over \(K\) with at least two characteristic roots, then
  577:   \[
  578:     \lim_{\substack{r\to\infty\\ r>s\ge0,\ Z(s)\ne0}}
  579:       P_K\!\left(\frac{Z(r)}{Z(s)}\right)=\infty.
  580:   \]
  581:   In particular, a rational-integer recurrence with no zero terms, all
  582:   supported on one finite set of rational primes, cannot be both
  583:   nondegenerate and have at least two characteristic roots.
  584: \end{lemma}
  585: 
  586: \begin{proof}
  587:   The displayed uniform limit is exactly
  588:   \cite[Theorem~3]{Evertse1984}. For the consequence, let \(S\) be the
  589:   finite rational-prime support and choose a number field \(K\) containing
  590:   the characteristic roots and coefficients. If \(Z(r),Z(s)\ne0\), the
  591:   principal fractional ideal generated by \(Z(r)/Z(s)\) is supported
  592:   only at prime ideals above primes in \(S\). Every prime ideal
  593:   \(\mathfrak p\) above \(p\in S\) has
  594:   \[
  595:     \operatorname N\mathfrak p=p^{f(\mathfrak p/p)}
  596:       \le p^{[K:\mathbb Q]}.
  597:   \]
  598:   Consequently
  599:   \[
  600:     P_K\!\left(\frac{Z(r)}{Z(s)}\right)
  601:       \le \max\bigl(\{p^{[K:\mathbb Q]}:p\in S\}\cup\{1\}\bigr)
  602:   \]
  603:   for every \(r,s\) with nonzero denominator. This fixed bound
  604:   contradicts Evertse's limit when there are at least two characteristic
  605:   roots.
  606: \end{proof}
  607: 
  608: \begin{lemma}[Increasing \(S\)-unit recurrences]
  609:   \label{lem:s-unit-increasing-recurrence-rigidity}
  610:   Let \(Y=(Y(n))_{n\ge0}\) be a strictly increasing sequence of positive
  611:   rational integers satisfying a linear recurrence. If all prime
  612:   divisors of all \(Y(n)\) belong to one finite set, then there are
  613:   integers \(r\ge0,h\ge1,c\ge1\), and \(b\ge2\) such that
  614:   \[
  615:     Y(r+hn)=cb^n\qquad(n\ge0).
  616:   \]
  617: \end{lemma}
  618: 
  619: \begin{proof}
  620:   Write the standard exponential-polynomial expansion, after discarding
  621:   the contribution of the zero characteristic root and a finite initial
  622:   segment, as
  623:   \[
  624:     Y(n)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(n)\alpha_i^n,
  625:   \]
  626:   where the \(\alpha_i\) are distinct nonzero algebraic numbers and the
  627:   nonzero \(f_i\) are algebraic polynomials. Partition the roots by
  628:   \(\alpha_i\sim\alpha_j\) when \(\alpha_i/\alpha_j\) is a root of
  629:   unity. Choose \(h_0\ge1\) divisible by the orders of all such
  630:   quotients. For each \(j\in\{0,\ldots,h_0-1\}\), substitution of
  631:   \(n=j+h_0t\) and collection within the equivalence classes gives
  632:   \[
  633:     Y(j+h_0t)=\sum_C g_{C,j}(t)\beta_C^t,
  634:     \qquad \beta_C=\alpha_i^{h_0}\quad(i\in C).
  635:   \]
  636:   Delete the identically zero summands. Distinct remaining \(\beta_C\)
  637:   have quotient that is not a root of unity. Thus every residue
  638:   subsequence is a nonzero nondegenerate recurrence; it is nonzero
  639:   because all of its terms are positive.
  640: 
  641:   Every term of every residue subsequence is a nonzero rational integer
  642:   supported on the prescribed finite set. If a residue subsequence had
  643:   at least two characteristic roots, the consequence in
  644:   \Cref{lem:evertse-quotient-support-input} would contradict the fixed
  645:   support of all its term quotients. Hence every residue subsequence has
  646:   exactly one characteristic root and therefore has the form
  647:   \[
  648:     Z(n)=f(n)\lambda^n
  649:   \]
  650:   with one characteristic root.
  651: 
  652:   Choose one residue subsequence and shift its index if necessary so
  653:   that the displayed expansion holds from \(n=0\). The Hankel matrix of
  654:   \(Z\) has rational entries and finite rank, so a minimal linear
  655:   dependence among its shift columns has coefficients in
  656:   \(\mathbb Q\). Thus the minimal annihilating polynomial of \(Z\) lies
  657:   in \(\mathbb Q[X]\). Over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\) it is a power of
  658:   \(X-\lambda\). Galois invariance therefore gives
  659:   \(\lambda\in\mathbb Q\). Now \(f(n)=Z(n)/\lambda^n\in\mathbb Q\)
  660:   for every \(n\), and interpolation from \(\deg(f)+1\) integer
  661:   arguments gives \(f\in\mathbb Q[X]\). If \(f\) were nonconstant, clear its
  662:   denominators to obtain a nonconstant \(g\in\mathbb Z[X]\). The
  663:   identity \(Z(n)=f(n)\lambda^n\) would confine every prime divisor of
  664:   every nonzero \(g(n)\) to a fixed finite set. Indeed, if
  665:   \(\lambda=a/b\) is in lowest terms and \(g=Df\), then
  666:   \[
  667:     g(n)a^n=Db^nZ(n).
  668:   \]
  669:   Thus that fixed set is the union of the prescribed prime set and the
  670:   prime divisors of \(Dab\). This contradicts Schur's theorem that a
  671:   nonconstant integer polynomial has values divisible by infinitely
  672:   many primes; see, for example, \cite{HardyWright2008}. Hence \(f\) is
  673:   constant.
  674: 
  675:   We have therefore \(Z(n)=c\lambda^n\), where
  676:   \(c=Z(0)\) is a positive integer. If \(\lambda=a/b\) in lowest terms,
  677:   integrality for every \(n\) forces \(b^n\mid c\) for every \(n\), so
  678:   \(b=1\). Positivity and strict increase then force
  679:   \(\lambda\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\). Translating the chosen residue and
  680:   index shift back to \(Y\) supplies the asserted \(r\) and \(h\).
  681: \end{proof}
  682: 
  683: \begin{theorem}[Geometric-ray characterization]
  684:   \label{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}
  685:   For a canonical eventually recurrent numeration system satisfying
  686:   \textup{(U1)--(U4)}, the following are equivalent.
  687:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
  688:     \item There are a finite \(k\) and an infinite \(k\)-MCFL
  689:     \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) such that
  690:     \[
  691:       \sup_{w\in L}\omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(\val_U(w))<\infty.
  692:     \]
  693:     \item The system admits a geometric synchronized scheme in the
  694:     sense of \Cref{def:geometric-synchronized-scheme}.
  695:     \item The language \(\mathcal R_U\) contains an infinite linear MCFL
  696:     \(L_0=\{W(t):t\ge0\}\) of finite fan-out for which there are
  697:     \(c\ge1,b\ge2\) satisfying
  698:     \[
  699:       \val_U(W(t))=cb^t\qquad(t\ge0).
  700:     \]
  701:   \end{enumerate}
  702: \end{theorem}
  703: 
  704: \begin{proof}
  705:   Suppose first that \textup{(i)} holds. Use the minimal tail recurrence
  706:   as the witness in
  707:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}, and write its resulting
  708:   ray and strictly increasing value sequence as \(W(t)\) and \(N(t)\).
  709:   Let
  710:   \[
  711:     K_0=\max_{t\ge0}\omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(N(t)),
  712:   \]
  713:   and choose \(t_0\) attaining the maximum. Let \(T\) be the set of
  714:   primes outside \(S_{\mathrm r}\) that divide \(N(t_0)\), and put
  715:   \(q=\prod_{\ell\in T}\ell\). If \(T\ne\varnothing\), take the return
  716:   time \(H=H(q)\) from
  717:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}; if \(T=\varnothing\),
  718:   put \(H=1\). Every prime in \(T\) divides every \(N(t_0+nH)\). A prime
  719:   divisor outside \(S_{\mathrm r}\cup T\) would therefore give at least
  720:   \(K_0+1\) distinct prime divisors outside \(S_{\mathrm r}\), contrary
  721:   to the definition of \(K_0\). Thus all terms of
  722:   \[
  723:     Y(n)=N(t_0+nH)
  724:   \]
  725:   are supported on the fixed finite set \(S_{\mathrm r}\cup T\).
  726: 
  727:   The entries of every matrix power \(M^n\) satisfy a linear recurrence
  728:   by Cayley--Hamilton. The expression for \(N(t)\) is a finite sum of
  729:   finite products of such entries, and linear recurrence sequences are
  730:   closed under sums and termwise products. Hence \(Y\) is a strictly
  731:   increasing positive integer recurrence. By
  732:   \Cref{lem:s-unit-increasing-recurrence-rigidity}, there are
  733:   \(r\ge0,h\ge1,c\ge1,b\ge2\) such that
  734:   \(N(t_\ast+h_\ast n)=cb^n\), where
  735:   \(t_\ast=t_0+Hr\) and \(h_\ast=Hh\).
  736: 
  737:   In the synchronized factorization, replace
  738:   \[
  739:     u_j\ \text{by}\ u_jv_j^{t_\ast},\qquad
  740:     v_j\ \text{by}\ v_j^{h_\ast},\qquad
  741:     w_j\ \text{by}\ w_js_j^{t_\ast},\qquad
  742:     s_j\ \text{by}\ s_j^{h_\ast}.
  743:   \]
  744:   This absorbs the fixed powers and parametrizes exactly the subray
  745:   \(W(t_\ast+h_\ast n)\). Its total pumped length remains positive, so
  746:   it is a geometric synchronized scheme. This proves
  747:   \textup{(i)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(ii)}.
  748: 
  749:   The implication \textup{(ii)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(iii)} is
  750:   \Cref{lem:synchronized-ray-linear-mcfg}. Finally, under
  751:   \textup{(iii)}, the language \(L_0\) is an infinite MCFL and
  752:   \[
  753:     \omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(cb^t)\le\omega(cb)
  754:     \qquad(t\ge0),
  755:   \]
  756:   proving \textup{(i)}.
  757: \end{proof}
  758: 
  759: \begin{lemma}[Prime support of the geometric ratio]
  760:   \label{lem:geometric-ratio-tail-support}
  761:   In every geometric synchronized scheme
  762:   \(\val_U(W(t))=cb^t\), each prime divisor of \(b\) divides the
  763:   constant coefficient \(c_0\) of the minimal tail recurrence.  Equivalently,
  764:   \[
  765:     \operatorname{rad}(b)\mid\operatorname{rad}(\abs{c_0}).
  766:   \]
  767: \end{lemma}
  768: 
  769: \begin{proof}
  770:   Suppose that a prime \(p\mid b\) does not divide \(c_0\), put
  771:   \(e=v_p(c)\), and take the allowed modulus \(q=p^{e+1}\).  Every
  772:   nonempty block matrix among the \(M_{v_j}\) and \(M_{s_j}\) is invertible
  773:   modulo \(q\) by \Cref{lem:affine-recurrence-block-action}.  A common
  774:   multiple \(H\ge1\) of their orders gives, by the matrix product defining
  775:   the scheme exactly as in the proof of
  776:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit},
  777:   \[
  778:     \val_U(W(t+H))\equiv\val_U(W(t))\pmod q
  779:     \qquad(t\ge0).
  780:   \]
  781:   At \(t=0\) this says
  782:   \[
  783:     cb^H\equiv c\pmod {p^{e+1}}.
  784:   \]
  785:   But \(p\mid b\) implies \(p\nmid b^H-1\), so
  786:   \(v_p(c(b^H-1))=e\), contradicting the displayed congruence.
  787: \end{proof}
  788: 
  789: \begin{corollary}[Positive semidecidability]
  790:   \label{cor:bounded-outside-support-semidecidable}
  791:   Suppose the numeration system is given effectively by its finite
  792:   digit alphabet, recurrence and initial data, and a DFA recognizing
  793:   \(\mathcal R_U\), with the minimal tail recurrence and a valid
  794:   threshold \(J_{\mathrm r}\) effectively computable from these data.
  795:   Then the property in
  796:   \Cref{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}\textup{(i)} is
  797:   recursively enumerable, equivalently it has a \(\Sigma^0_1\) upper
  798:   bound.
  799: \end{corollary}

  483: \begin{proposition}[Recurrence-witness inflation and strict separation]
  484:   \label{prop:recurrence-witness-separation}
  485:   If a tail has minimal recurrence polynomial \(\mu_U\), then for every
  486:   prime \(p\) it also has a recurrence witness with characteristic
  487:   polynomial \((X-p)\mu_U(X)\).  When \(\abs{\mu_U(0)}=1\), the trailing
  488:   coefficient of this witness has absolute value \(p\).
  489: 
  490:   Moreover, there are two canonical eventually recurrent
  491:   numeration systems with regular representation languages and recurrence
  492:   witnesses whose trailing-coefficient prime set is \(\{p\}\), but with
  493:   opposite bounded-outside-prime escape behavior:
  494:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
  495:     \item ordinary base \(p\) contains the infinite regular language
  496:     \(\{0^n1:n\ge0\}\), whose values are \(p^n\);
  497:     \item the Zeckendorf system, with \(F_0=0,F_1=1\) and
  498:     \(F_{n+2}=F_{n+1}+F_n\), equipped with the order-three recurrence
  499:     witness
  500:     \[
  501:       F_{n+3}=-pF_n+(1-p)F_{n+1}+(p+1)F_{n+2},
  502:     \]
  503:     contains no infinite MCFL \(L\) for which
  504:     \[
  505:       \sup_{w\in L}\omega_{\{p\}^c}(\val(w))<\infty.
  506:     \]
  507:   \end{enumerate}
  508:   Thus the prime divisors of an arbitrarily selected trailing coefficient
  509:   do not determine the escape behavior of the numeration system.
  510: \end{proposition}
  511: 
  512: \begin{proof}
  513:   The polynomial identity \(\mu_U(C)z_J=0\) remains valid after
  514:   multiplication by \(X-p\).  In the companion convention, the trailing
  515:   recurrence coefficient is the negative of the constant term of the
  516:   characteristic polynomial, proving the first assertion.
  517: 
  518:   The base-\(p\) assertion is the preceding example.  For the Zeckendorf
  519:   sequence, multiplication of its minimal polynomial by \(X-p\) gives
  520:   \[
  521:     (X-p)(X^2-X-1)
  522:       =X^3-(p+1)X^2+(p-1)X+p,
  523:   \]
  524:   which is exactly the displayed recurrence and has trailing coefficient
  525:   \(-p\).  This changes neither the sequence nor its regular canonical
  526:   representation language.  On the other hand, its minimal recurrence
  527:   has unit trailing coefficient.  If the displayed supremum were bounded
  528:   by \(K\), then
  529:   \(\omega(\val(w))\le K+1\) on \(L\), contrary to the unit-recurrence
  530:   conclusion of
  531:   \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}.  This proves the separation.
  532: \end{proof}

  570: \begin{lemma}[Arithmetic input of Evertse]
  571:   \label{lem:evertse-quotient-support-input}
  572:   Let \(K\) be a number field. For \(x\in K^\times\), let \(P_K(x)\)
  573:   be the largest norm of a finite prime ideal \(\mathfrak p\) for which
  574:   \(\operatorname{ord}_{\mathfrak p}(x)\ne0\), with \(P_K(x)=1\) when
  575:   \(x\) is a unit. If \(Z=(Z(n))_{n\ge0}\) is a nondegenerate linear
  576:   recurrence over \(K\) with at least two characteristic roots, then
  577:   \[
  578:     \lim_{\substack{r\to\infty\\ r>s\ge0,\ Z(s)\ne0}}
  579:       P_K\!\left(\frac{Z(r)}{Z(s)}\right)=\infty.
  580:   \]
  581:   In particular, a rational-integer recurrence with no zero terms, all
  582:   supported on one finite set of rational primes, cannot be both
  583:   nondegenerate and have at least two characteristic roots.
  584: \end{lemma}
  585: 
  586: \begin{proof}
  587:   The displayed uniform limit is exactly
  588:   \cite[Theorem~3]{Evertse1984}. For the consequence, let \(S\) be the
  589:   finite rational-prime support and choose a number field \(K\) containing
  590:   the characteristic roots and coefficients. If \(Z(r),Z(s)\ne0\), the
  591:   principal fractional ideal generated by \(Z(r)/Z(s)\) is supported
  592:   only at prime ideals above primes in \(S\). Every prime ideal
  593:   \(\mathfrak p\) above \(p\in S\) has
  594:   \[
  595:     \operatorname N\mathfrak p=p^{f(\mathfrak p/p)}
  596:       \le p^{[K:\mathbb Q]}.
  597:   \]
  598:   Consequently
  599:   \[
  600:     P_K\!\left(\frac{Z(r)}{Z(s)}\right)
  601:       \le \max\bigl(\{p^{[K:\mathbb Q]}:p\in S\}\cup\{1\}\bigr)
  602:   \]
  603:   for every \(r,s\) with nonzero denominator. This fixed bound
  604:   contradicts Evertse's limit when there are at least two characteristic
  605:   roots.
  606: \end{proof}
  607: 
  608: \begin{lemma}[Increasing \(S\)-unit recurrences]
  609:   \label{lem:s-unit-increasing-recurrence-rigidity}
  610:   Let \(Y=(Y(n))_{n\ge0}\) be a strictly increasing sequence of positive
  611:   rational integers satisfying a linear recurrence. If all prime
  612:   divisors of all \(Y(n)\) belong to one finite set, then there are
  613:   integers \(r\ge0,h\ge1,c\ge1\), and \(b\ge2\) such that
  614:   \[
  615:     Y(r+hn)=cb^n\qquad(n\ge0).
  616:   \]
  617: \end{lemma}
  618: 
  619: \begin{proof}
  620:   Write the standard exponential-polynomial expansion, after discarding
  621:   the contribution of the zero characteristic root and a finite initial
  622:   segment, as
  623:   \[
  624:     Y(n)=\sum_{i=1}^m f_i(n)\alpha_i^n,
  625:   \]
  626:   where the \(\alpha_i\) are distinct nonzero algebraic numbers and the
  627:   nonzero \(f_i\) are algebraic polynomials. Partition the roots by
  628:   \(\alpha_i\sim\alpha_j\) when \(\alpha_i/\alpha_j\) is a root of
  629:   unity. Choose \(h_0\ge1\) divisible by the orders of all such
  630:   quotients. For each \(j\in\{0,\ldots,h_0-1\}\), substitution of
  631:   \(n=j+h_0t\) and collection within the equivalence classes gives
  632:   \[
  633:     Y(j+h_0t)=\sum_C g_{C,j}(t)\beta_C^t,
  634:     \qquad \beta_C=\alpha_i^{h_0}\quad(i\in C).
  635:   \]
  636:   Delete the identically zero summands. Distinct remaining \(\beta_C\)
  637:   have quotient that is not a root of unity. Thus every residue
  638:   subsequence is a nonzero nondegenerate recurrence; it is nonzero
  639:   because all of its terms are positive.
  640: 
  641:   Every term of every residue subsequence is a nonzero rational integer
  642:   supported on the prescribed finite set. If a residue subsequence had
  643:   at least two characteristic roots, the consequence in
  644:   \Cref{lem:evertse-quotient-support-input} would contradict the fixed
  645:   support of all its term quotients. Hence every residue subsequence has
  646:   exactly one characteristic root and therefore has the form
  647:   \[
  648:     Z(n)=f(n)\lambda^n
  649:   \]
  650:   with one characteristic root.
  651: 
  652:   Choose one residue subsequence and shift its index if necessary so
  653:   that the displayed expansion holds from \(n=0\). The Hankel matrix of
  654:   \(Z\) has rational entries and finite rank, so a minimal linear
  655:   dependence among its shift columns has coefficients in
  656:   \(\mathbb Q\). Thus the minimal annihilating polynomial of \(Z\) lies
  657:   in \(\mathbb Q[X]\). Over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\) it is a power of
  658:   \(X-\lambda\). Galois invariance therefore gives
  659:   \(\lambda\in\mathbb Q\). Now \(f(n)=Z(n)/\lambda^n\in\mathbb Q\)
  660:   for every \(n\), and interpolation from \(\deg(f)+1\) integer
  661:   arguments gives \(f\in\mathbb Q[X]\). If \(f\) were nonconstant, clear its
  662:   denominators to obtain a nonconstant \(g\in\mathbb Z[X]\). The
  663:   identity \(Z(n)=f(n)\lambda^n\) would confine every prime divisor of
  664:   every nonzero \(g(n)\) to a fixed finite set. Indeed, if
  665:   \(\lambda=a/b\) is in lowest terms and \(g=Df\), then
  666:   \[
  667:     g(n)a^n=Db^nZ(n).
  668:   \]
  669:   Thus that fixed set is the union of the prescribed prime set and the
  670:   prime divisors of \(Dab\). This contradicts Schur's theorem that a
  671:   nonconstant integer polynomial has values divisible by infinitely
  672:   many primes; see, for example, \cite{HardyWright2008}. Hence \(f\) is
  673:   constant.
  674: 
  675:   We have therefore \(Z(n)=c\lambda^n\), where
  676:   \(c=Z(0)\) is a positive integer. If \(\lambda=a/b\) in lowest terms,
  677:   integrality for every \(n\) forces \(b^n\mid c\) for every \(n\), so
  678:   \(b=1\). Positivity and strict increase then force
  679:   \(\lambda\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\). Translating the chosen residue and
  680:   index shift back to \(Y\) supplies the asserted \(r\) and \(h\).
  681: \end{proof}
  682: 
  683: \begin{theorem}[Geometric-ray characterization]
  684:   \label{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}
  685:   For a canonical eventually recurrent numeration system satisfying
  686:   \textup{(U1)--(U4)}, the following are equivalent.
  687:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
  688:     \item There are a finite \(k\) and an infinite \(k\)-MCFL
  689:     \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) such that
  690:     \[
  691:       \sup_{w\in L}\omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(\val_U(w))<\infty.
  692:     \]
  693:     \item The system admits a geometric synchronized scheme in the
  694:     sense of \Cref{def:geometric-synchronized-scheme}.
  695:     \item The language \(\mathcal R_U\) contains an infinite linear MCFL
  696:     \(L_0=\{W(t):t\ge0\}\) of finite fan-out for which there are
  697:     \(c\ge1,b\ge2\) satisfying
  698:     \[
  699:       \val_U(W(t))=cb^t\qquad(t\ge0).
  700:     \]
  701:   \end{enumerate}
  702: \end{theorem}
  703: 
  704: \begin{proof}
  705:   Suppose first that \textup{(i)} holds. Use the minimal tail recurrence
  706:   as the witness in
  707:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}, and write its resulting
  708:   ray and strictly increasing value sequence as \(W(t)\) and \(N(t)\).
  709:   Let
  710:   \[
  711:     K_0=\max_{t\ge0}\omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(N(t)),
  712:   \]
  713:   and choose \(t_0\) attaining the maximum. Let \(T\) be the set of
  714:   primes outside \(S_{\mathrm r}\) that divide \(N(t_0)\), and put
  715:   \(q=\prod_{\ell\in T}\ell\). If \(T\ne\varnothing\), take the return
  716:   time \(H=H(q)\) from
  717:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}; if \(T=\varnothing\),
  718:   put \(H=1\). Every prime in \(T\) divides every \(N(t_0+nH)\). A prime
  719:   divisor outside \(S_{\mathrm r}\cup T\) would therefore give at least
  720:   \(K_0+1\) distinct prime divisors outside \(S_{\mathrm r}\), contrary

 succeeded in 205ms:
  720:   \(K_0+1\) distinct prime divisors outside \(S_{\mathrm r}\), contrary
  721:   to the definition of \(K_0\). Thus all terms of
  722:   \[
  723:     Y(n)=N(t_0+nH)
  724:   \]
  725:   are supported on the fixed finite set \(S_{\mathrm r}\cup T\).
  726: 
  727:   The entries of every matrix power \(M^n\) satisfy a linear recurrence
  728:   by Cayley--Hamilton. The expression for \(N(t)\) is a finite sum of
  729:   finite products of such entries, and linear recurrence sequences are
  730:   closed under sums and termwise products. Hence \(Y\) is a strictly
  731:   increasing positive integer recurrence. By
  732:   \Cref{lem:s-unit-increasing-recurrence-rigidity}, there are
  733:   \(r\ge0,h\ge1,c\ge1,b\ge2\) such that
  734:   \(N(t_\ast+h_\ast n)=cb^n\), where
  735:   \(t_\ast=t_0+Hr\) and \(h_\ast=Hh\).
  736: 
  737:   In the synchronized factorization, replace
  738:   \[
  739:     u_j\ \text{by}\ u_jv_j^{t_\ast},\qquad
  740:     v_j\ \text{by}\ v_j^{h_\ast},\qquad
  741:     w_j\ \text{by}\ w_js_j^{t_\ast},\qquad
  742:     s_j\ \text{by}\ s_j^{h_\ast}.
  743:   \]
  744:   This absorbs the fixed powers and parametrizes exactly the subray
  745:   \(W(t_\ast+h_\ast n)\). Its total pumped length remains positive, so
  746:   it is a geometric synchronized scheme. This proves
  747:   \textup{(i)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(ii)}.
  748: 
  749:   The implication \textup{(ii)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(iii)} is
  750:   \Cref{lem:synchronized-ray-linear-mcfg}. Finally, under
  751:   \textup{(iii)}, the language \(L_0\) is an infinite MCFL and
  752:   \[
  753:     \omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(cb^t)\le\omega(cb)
  754:     \qquad(t\ge0),
  755:   \]
  756:   proving \textup{(i)}.
  757: \end{proof}
  758: 
  759: \begin{lemma}[Prime support of the geometric ratio]
  760:   \label{lem:geometric-ratio-tail-support}
  761:   In every geometric synchronized scheme
  762:   \(\val_U(W(t))=cb^t\), each prime divisor of \(b\) divides the
  763:   constant coefficient \(c_0\) of the minimal tail recurrence.  Equivalently,
  764:   \[
  765:     \operatorname{rad}(b)\mid\operatorname{rad}(\abs{c_0}).
  766:   \]
  767: \end{lemma}
  768: 
  769: \begin{proof}
  770:   Suppose that a prime \(p\mid b\) does not divide \(c_0\), put
  771:   \(e=v_p(c)\), and take the allowed modulus \(q=p^{e+1}\).  Every
  772:   nonempty block matrix among the \(M_{v_j}\) and \(M_{s_j}\) is invertible
  773:   modulo \(q\) by \Cref{lem:affine-recurrence-block-action}.  A common
  774:   multiple \(H\ge1\) of their orders gives, by the matrix product defining
  775:   the scheme exactly as in the proof of
  776:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit},
  777:   \[
  778:     \val_U(W(t+H))\equiv\val_U(W(t))\pmod q
  779:     \qquad(t\ge0).
  780:   \]
  781:   At \(t=0\) this says
  782:   \[
  783:     cb^H\equiv c\pmod {p^{e+1}}.
  784:   \]
  785:   But \(p\mid b\) implies \(p\nmid b^H-1\), so
  786:   \(v_p(c(b^H-1))=e\), contradicting the displayed congruence.
  787: \end{proof}
  788: 
  789: \begin{corollary}[Positive semidecidability]
  790:   \label{cor:bounded-outside-support-semidecidable}
  791:   Suppose the numeration system is given effectively by its finite
  792:   digit alphabet, recurrence and initial data, and a DFA recognizing
  793:   \(\mathcal R_U\), with the minimal tail recurrence and a valid
  794:   threshold \(J_{\mathrm r}\) effectively computable from these data.
  795:   Then the property in
  796:   \Cref{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}\textup{(i)} is
  797:   recursively enumerable, equivalently it has a \(\Sigma^0_1\) upper
  798:   bound.
  799: \end{corollary}
  800: 
  801: \begin{proof}
  802:   Enumerate \(k\ge1\), \(a\in A^{J_{\mathrm r}}\), and all finite tuples
  803:   of words occurring in
  804:   \Cref{def:geometric-synchronized-scheme}, rejecting tuples of zero
  805:   total pumped length. For a fixed tuple, whether the DFA accepts
  806:   \(W(t)\) for every \(t\ge0\) is decidable: the tuple of powers of the
  807:   finitely many pumped-block transformations is eventually periodic in
  808:   the finite transition monoid, and its preperiod and period are found
  809:   by exhaustive iteration.
  810: 
  811:   The affine matrices construct an exact linear recurrence for
  812:   \[
  813:     N(t)=\val_U(W(t)).
  814:   \]
  815:   Kronecker products implement the termwise
  816:   products arising from the several synchronized block powers. For a
  817:   tuple accepted at every parameter, compute \(c=N(0)\). The only
  818:   possible integer ratio is \(b=N(1)/N(0)\). Check that
  819:   \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\), and then decide whether the recurrence
  820:   \(N(t+1)-bN(t)\) is identically zero by checking an initial segment of
  821:   length equal to an explicitly constructed recurrence order. Thus each
  822:   candidate scheme is decidable, and the enumeration halts exactly on
  823:   positive instances by
  824:   \Cref{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}. No claim of a
  825:   decision procedure for negative instances is made.
  826: \end{proof}
  827: 
  828: \begin{remark}[Exact algorithmic boundary]
  829:   \label{rem:general-decision-interface}
  830:   The preceding corollary does not yield a decision procedure. To turn
  831:   its enumeration into one, it would suffice to compute from the input
  832:   DFA and minimal tail recurrence a bound \(B\) such that every positive
  833:   instance has a geometric synchronized scheme with fan-out and total
  834:   constant and pumped-block length at most \(B\). No such compression
  835:   follows from DFA pumping: replacing a long loop by a shorter word with
  836:   the same DFA endpoints need not preserve its affine recurrence matrix,
  837:   and can therefore destroy the identity
  838:   \(\val_U(W(t+1))=b\val_U(W(t))\).
  839: 
  840:   The neighboring decision theory does not close this step. Orbit and
  841:   zero problems for linear recurrences already contain the open Skolem
  842:   problem \cite{OuaknineWorrell2012,TarasovVyalyi2011}, while unrestricted
  843:   multiplicative matrix equations include undecidable families
  844:   \cite{BellEtAl2008MatrixEquations}. Neither observation is a reduction
  845:   for the companion-form digit matrices here, and conditions
  846:   \textup{(U1)--(U3)} must also be preserved. Thus general decidability,
  847:   undecidability, and any hardness classification remain open; the proved
  848:   effective statement is exactly the positive semidecision above. The
  849:   linear Pisot subclass is resolved separately below.
  850: \end{remark}
  851: 
  852: \begin{theorem}[Arbitrarily deep quotient congruences]
  853:   \label{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain}
  854:   Suppose \(\abs{a_0}=1\), and let \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) be an
  855:   infinite MCFL. For arbitrary sequences \(M_i\ge1\) and \(r_i\ge1\),
  856:   \(L\) contains a strictly increasing sequence \(N_i\) such that
  857:   \[
  858:     N_{i+1}=N_iQ_i,\qquad Q_i>1,\qquad
  859:     Q_i\equiv1\pmod {M_iN_i^{r_i}}.
  860:   \]
  861:   If \(M_i\) is divisible by every prime at most \(B_i\), then every
  862:   prime divisor of \(Q_i\) exceeds \(B_i\).
  863: \end{theorem}
  864: 
  865: \begin{proof}
  866:   Take the fixed orbit \(N(t)\) from
  867:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}, discarding finitely many
  868:   initial parameters so that \(N(t)\ge2\). Having selected
  869:   \(N_i=N(t_i)\), apply the synchronized congruence with
  870:   \[
  871:     q_i=M_iN_i^{r_i+1}.
  872:   \]
  873:   Set \(t_{i+1}=t_i+H(q_i)\). Strict increase and the congruence give
  874:   \[
  875:     N_{i+1}=N_i+c_iM_iN_i^{r_i+1}
  876:            =N_i(1+c_iM_iN_i^{r_i})
  877:   \]
  878:   for an integer \(c_i\ge1\). This proves the first assertion. Under
  879:   the last hypothesis, \(Q_i\equiv1\pmod p\) for every prime
  880:   \(p\le B_i\), so none of those primes divides \(Q_i\).
  881: \end{proof}
  882: 
  883: \begin{theorem}[Induced full divisibility tree]
  884:   \label{thm:unit-mcfl-divisibility-tree}
  885:   Under the hypotheses of
  886:   \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain}, there is an injection
  887:   \[
  888:     \Phi:\NN^{<\omega}\longrightarrow L
  889:   \]
  890:   such that
  891:   \[
  892:     \val_U(\Phi(\sigma))\mid\val_U(\Phi(\tau))
  893:       \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad \sigma\preceq\tau,
  894:   \]
  895:   where \(\preceq\) denotes the prefix order. The quotients attached to
  896:   distinct edges can be chosen pairwise coprime. Moreover, given an
  897:   arbitrary prescribed threshold for each edge, every prime divisor of
  898:   its quotient can be required to exceed that threshold.
  899: \end{theorem}
  900: 
  901: \begin{proof}
  902:   Use the fixed strictly increasing orbit from
  903:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}. Enumerate the edges of
  904:   \(\NN^{<\omega}\) so that each parent occurs before its children. Map
  905:   the root to any orbit word of value \(R_0\ge2\). Suppose finitely many
  906:   edges have been assigned, and consider a new edge from a parent of
  907:   value \(P\). Let \(R\) be divisible by \(R_0\), by every previously
  908:   assigned edge quotient, and by every prime not exceeding the prescribed
  909:   threshold for the new edge. Apply the synchronized orbit congruence
  910:   modulo \(P^2R\) at the parameter of the parent. A sufficiently large
  911:   positive multiple of the return time gives an unused orbit word of
  912:   value \(P'>P\) with
  913:   \[
  914:     P'\equiv P\pmod {P^2R}.
  915:   \]
  916:   Hence \(P'=PQ\), where \(Q>1\) and \(Q\equiv1\pmod {PR}\). In
  917:   particular, \(Q\) is coprime to the root and to every earlier edge
  918:   quotient, and no prime up to the prescribed threshold divides \(Q\).
  919: 
  920:   Recursion defines \(\Phi\) on every node. The value at a node is the
  921:   root value times the product of the edge quotients along its path.
  922:   Since the root and all distinct edge quotients are pairwise coprime,
  923:   a node value divides another exactly when its path-edge set is an
  924:   initial segment of the other path. This is precisely the prefix
  925:   relation and also proves injectivity.
  926: \end{proof}
  927: 
  928: \begin{theorem}[Prime immunity for recurrent numeration systems]
  929:   \label{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity}
  930:   Let \((U,A,\mathcal R_U)\) satisfy \textup{(U1)--(U4)}, and put
  931:   \[
  932:     \mathcal P_U
  933:       :=\{w\in\mathcal R_U:\val_U(w)\text{ is prime}\}.
  934:   \]
  935:   Then \(\mathcal P_U\) is MCF-immune, and therefore CF-immune,
  936:   REG-immune, and not recognizable by a finite automaton over \(A\).
  937: 
  938:   If, in addition, \(\abs{a_0}=1\), then every infinite multiple
  939:   context-free
  940:   \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) has unbounded

 succeeded in 195ms:
  940:   \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) has unbounded
  941:   \(\omega(\val_U(w))\). More precisely, \(L\) contains a
  942:   coprime-quotient chain \(N_{i+1}=N_iQ_i\) with
  943:   \(Q_i>1\) and \(Q_i\equiv1\pmod {N_i}\). Thus the bounded-\(\omega\),
  944:   bounded-\(\Omega\), and finite-prime-support languages of a unit
  945:   system are MCF-immune whenever they are infinite. Without the unit
  946:   hypothesis, every bounded-\(\Omega\) language is still MCF-immune.
  947: \end{theorem}
  948: 
  949: \begin{proof}
  950:   The MCF-immunity assertions follow from
  951:   \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}, including its
  952:   bounded-\(\Omega\) conclusion. In a unit system \(S\) is empty, so
  953:   that theorem gives unbounded \(\omega\). Taking
  954:   \(M_i=r_i=1\) in
  955:   \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain} gives the stated chain.
  956:   Regular languages are context-free and context-free languages are
  957:   MCFLs. Finally, \textup{(U2)} and Euclid's theorem make
  958:   \(\mathcal P_U\) infinite.
  959: \end{proof}
  960: 
  961: \begin{corollary}[Linear Pisot \(U\)-systems]
  962:   \label{cor:linear-pisot-prime-cf-immunity}
  963:   Let \(U=(U_n)_{n\ge0}\) be a linear Pisot \(U\)-system in the
  964:   following precise sense: \(U_0=1\), the \(U_n\) are strictly increasing
  965:   integers with bounded quotients, \(\mathcal R_U\) is the LSD-first
  966:   reversal of the usual greedy representation language, and \(U\)
  967:   eventually satisfies an integral recurrence whose characteristic
  968:   polynomial is the minimal polynomial of a Pisot number. Then its prime
  969:   representation language is MCF-immune, hence CF-immune, REG-immune and
  970:   nonrecognizable. The same statements hold in the usual MSD-first
  971:   convention.
  972: 
  973:   If the dominant Pisot number is a unit and the chosen recurrence has
  974:   trailing coefficient \(a_0=\pm1\), then the full coprime-quotient and
  975:   bounded-prime-support MCF-immunity conclusions of
  976:   \Cref{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity} hold.
  977: \end{corollary}
  978: 
  979: \begin{proof}
  980:   Greedy expansion gives a unique representation of every positive
  981:   integer, and its length-\(m\) words represent values between successive
  982:   place-value thresholds; thus \textup{(U1)--(U3)} hold. The defining
  983:   Pisot recurrence gives \textup{(U4)}. Apply
  984:   \Cref{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity}. Frougny's finite
  985:   normalization theorem supplies a finite transducer for normalization
  986:   in this Pisot setting, and the associated canonical syntax and
  987:   Bertrand/substitution descriptions are standard
  988:   \cite{Frougny1992,BruyereHansel1997,Fabre1995,FrougnySolomyak1992}.
  989:   Those finite-state results identify this corollary with the usual
  990:   recognizability convention; the immunity proof itself uses only
  991:   \textup{(U1)--(U4)}. Finally, multiple context-free, context-free, and
  992:   regular languages are closed under reversal, so changing between the LSD-first proof
  993:   convention and the usual MSD-first convention preserves every
  994:   conclusion.
  995: \end{proof}
  996: 
  997: \begin{example}[Unit and nonunit Pisot systems]
  998:   \label{ex:pisot-unit-nonunit}
  999:   The Fibonacci recurrence has characteristic polynomial
 1000:   \(X^2-X-1\), the Pell recurrence has \(X^2-2X-1\), and the
 1001:   Tribonacci recurrence has \(X^3-X^2-X-1\). Their trailing recurrence
 1002:   coefficient is \(a_0=1\), so the iterated conclusion applies. In
 1003:   ordinary base \(b\), \(U_n=b^n\) and \(a_0=b\); prime MCF-immunity
 1004:   follows, recovering the classical conclusion, but the unit iteration
 1005:   is not being asserted. A genuinely nonintegral, nonunit Pisot example
 1006:   is the dominant root \(1+\sqrt3\) of \(X^2-2X-2\): the recurrence
 1007:   \(U_{n+2}=2U_{n+1}+2U_n\) has \(a_0=2\), and the action is singular
 1008:   modulo \(2\).  Nevertheless,
 1009:   \Cref{cor:linear-pisot-bounded-support-classification} shows that every
 1010:   infinite MCFL in this nonintegral system acquires unbounded prime support
 1011:   away from \(2\); singularity of the ambient action does not produce a
 1012:   valuation-only escape language.
 1013: \end{example}
 1014: 
 1015: \begin{corollary}[Bounded-support classification for linear Pisot systems]
 1016:   \label{cor:linear-pisot-bounded-support-classification}
 1017:   Let \(U\) be a linear Pisot \(U\)-system in the precise sense of
 1018:   \Cref{cor:linear-pisot-prime-cf-immunity}, let \(\beta\) be its dominant
 1019:   Pisot number, and let \(S_{\mathrm r}\) be the prime divisors of the
 1020:   constant coefficient of its minimal tail recurrence.  The following are
 1021:   equivalent:
 1022:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 1023:     \item there is an infinite MCFL \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) such that
 1024:     \[
 1025:       \sup_{w\in L}\omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(\val_U(w))<\infty;
 1026:     \]
 1027:     \item \(U\) admits a geometric synchronized scheme;
 1028:     \item \(\beta\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\).
 1029:   \end{enumerate}
 1030:   Consequently, if \(\beta\) is nonintegral, every infinite MCFL
 1031:   \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) has unbounded prime support outside
 1032:   \(S_{\mathrm r}\).  For effective input as in
 1033:   \Cref{cor:bounded-outside-support-semidecidable}, the three equivalent
 1034:   properties are decidable in this linear Pisot class: the answer is positive
 1035:   exactly when the supplied minimal polynomial has degree one.
 1036: \end{corollary}
 1037: 
 1038: \begin{proof}
 1039:   The equivalence of \textup{(i)} and \textup{(ii)} is
 1040:   \Cref{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}.  Suppose that
 1041:   \textup{(ii)} holds, write
 1042:   \[
 1043:     \val_U(W(t))=cb^t,
 1044:     \qquad \abs{W(t)}=L+Dt,
 1045:   \]
 1046:   where \(D>0\) is the total pumped length.  In a greedy \(U\)-system, a
 1047:   canonical word of length \(m\) represents a value in the half-open interval
 1048:   \([U_{m-1},U_m)\).  Hence
 1049:   \[
 1050:     U_{L+Dt-1}\le cb^t<U_{L+Dt}.
 1051:   \]
 1052:   The standard solution of the recurrence defined by the minimal polynomial
 1053:   of the Pisot number gives
 1054:   \[
 1055:     \lim_{n\to\infty}U_n^{1/n}=\beta.
 1056:   \]
 1057:   Indeed, the coefficient of the dominant root is nonzero because \(U\) is
 1058:   unbounded, while every other conjugate has modulus less than one.  Taking
 1059:   \(t\)-th roots in the preceding inequalities therefore yields
 1060:   \(b=\beta^D\).
 1061: 
 1062:   If \(\beta\) had degree greater than one, any other conjugate
 1063:   \(\beta'\) would satisfy \((\beta')^D=b\), and hence
 1064:   \(\abs{\beta'}=b^{1/D}=\beta>1\), contrary to the defining Pisot
 1065:   inequality.  Thus \(\beta\) has degree one; being an algebraic integer
 1066:   greater than one, it belongs to \(\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\).  This proves
 1067:   \textup{(ii)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(iii)}.
 1068: 
 1069:   Conversely, suppose \(\beta=B\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\).  Its minimal
 1070:   polynomial is \(X-B\), so, after the minimal recurrence threshold
 1071:   \(J_{\mathrm r}\), one has \(U_{n+1}=BU_n\).  The greedy representation
 1072:   of \(U_n\), in the LSD-first convention, is \(0^n1\).  Taking
 1073:   \[
 1074:     a=0^{J_{\mathrm r}},\quad k=1,\quad
 1075:     u_1=w_1=s_1=\varepsilon,\quad v_1=0,\quad u_2=1
 1076:   \]
 1077:   gives canonical words \(W(t)=0^{J_{\mathrm r}+t}1\) and
 1078:   \[
 1079:     \val_U(W(t))=U_{J_{\mathrm r}}B^t.
 1080:   \]
 1081:   This is a geometric synchronized scheme, proving
 1082:   \textup{(iii)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(ii)}.  The universal assertion
 1083:   for nonintegral \(\beta\) is the negation of \textup{(i)}.  Finally, a
 1084:   Pisot minimal polynomial has degree one exactly when its root is an
 1085:   integer, which gives the stated terminating decision procedure.
 1086: \end{proof}
 1087: 
 1088: \begin{remark}[Exact open interfaces]
 1089:   \label{rem:pisot-open-interfaces}
 1090:   The terminology for Pisot numeration systems is not uniform.

    <title>Progress on the unfair 0-1-polynomials conjecture using linear recurrences and numerical analysis</title>
    <updated>2022-09-20T16:41:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.09843v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.09843v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>If the product of two monic polynomials with real nonnegative coefficients has all coefficients equal to 0 or 1, does it follow that all the coefficients of the two factors are also equal to 0 or 1? Here is an equivalent formulation of this intriguing problem: is it possible to weigh unfairly a pair of dice so that the probabilities of every possible outcome (roll them and take the sum) were the same? If the two dice have six faces numbered 1 to 6, it is easy to show that the answer is no. But for general dice with finitely many faces, this is an open problem with no significant advancement since 1937. In this paper we examine, in some sense, the first infinite family of cases that cannot be treated with classical methods: the first die has three faces numbered with 0,2 and 5, while the second die is arbitrary. In other words, we examine factorizations of 0-1-polynomials with one factor equal to $x^5+a x^2 +1$ for some nonnegative $a$. We discover that this case may be solved (that is, necessarily $a=0$ or $a=1$) using the theory of linear recurrence sequences, computation of resultants, a fair amount of analytic and numerical approximations... and a little bit of luck.</summary>

    <title>Rotation-free Online Handwritten Character Recognition Using Linear Recurrent Units</title>
    <updated>2026-02-02T01:57:45Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.01533v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>

    <summary>Online handwritten character recognition leverages stroke order and dynamic features, which generally provide higher accuracy and robustness compared with offline recognition. However, in practical applications, rotational deformations can disrupt the spatial layout of strokes, substantially reducing recognition accuracy. Extracting rotation-invariant features therefore remains a challenging open problem. In this work, we employ the Sliding Window Path Signature (SW-PS) to capture local structural features of characters, and introduce the lightweight Linear Recurrent Units (LRU) as the classifier. The LRU combine the fast incremental processing capability of recurrent neural networks (RNN) with the efficient parallel training of state space models (SSM), while reliably modelling dynamic stroke characteristics. We conducted recognition experiments with random rotation angle up to $\pm 180^{\circ}$ on three subsets of the CASIA-OLHWDB1.1 dataset: digits, English upper letters, and Chinese radicals. The accuracies achieved after ensemble learning were $99.62\%$, $96.67\%$, and $94.33\%$, respectively. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed SW-PS+LRU framework consistently surpasses competing models in both convergence speed and test accuracy.</summary>

    <title>On the Counting Complexity of the Skolem Problem</title>
    <updated>2025-08-02T12:46:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.00098v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.00098v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Skolem Problem asks, given an integer linear recurrence sequence (LRS), to determine whether the sequence contains a zero term or not. Its decidability is a longstanding open problem in theoretical computer science and automata theory. Currently, decidability is only known for LRS of order at most 4. On the other hand, the sole known complexity result is NP-hardness, due to Blondel and Portier.
  A fundamental result in this area is the celebrated Skolem-Mahler-Lech theorem, which asserts that the zero set of any LRS is the union of a finite set and finitely many arithmetic progressions. This paper focuses on a computational perspective of the Skolem-Mahler-Lech theorem: we show that the problem of counting the zeros of a given LRS is #P-hard, and in fact #P-complete for the instances generated in our reduction.</summary>

    <summary>Dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs) are compact graphical representations used to model probabilistic systems where interdependent random variables and their distributions evolve over time. In this paper, we study the verification of the evolution of conditional-independence (CI) propositions against temporal logic specifications. To this end, we consider two specification formalisms over CI propositions: linear temporal logic (LTL), and non-deterministic Büchi automata (NBAs). This problem has two variants.     <title>On Petri Nets with Hierarchical Special Arcs</title>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2211.02365v6</id>
    <title>On Robustness for the Skolem, Positivity and Ultimate Positivity Problems</title>
    <updated>2024-06-04T09:29:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.02365v6" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.02365v6" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Skolem problem is a long-standing open problem in linear dynamical systems: can a linear recurrence sequence (LRS) ever reach 0 from a given initial configuration? Similarly, the positivity problem asks whether the LRS stays positive from an initial configuration. Deciding Skolem (or positivity) has been open for half a century: the best known decidability results are for LRS with special properties (e.g., low order recurrences). But these problems are easier for "uninitialized" variants, where the initial configuration is not fixed but can vary arbitrarily: checking if there is an initial configuration from which the LRS stays positive can be decided in polynomial time (Tiwari in 2004, Braverman in 2006). In this paper, we consider problems that lie between the initialized and uninitialized variants. More precisely, we ask if 0 (resp. negative numbers) can be avoided from every initial configuration in a neighborhood of a given initial configuration. This can be considered as a robust variant of the Skolem (resp. positivity) problem. We show that these problems lie at the frontier of decidability: if the neighbourhood is given as part of the input, then robust Skolem and robust positivity are Diophantine hard, i.e., solving either would entail major breakthroughs in Diophantine approximations, as happens for (non-robust) positivity. However, if one asks whether such a neighbourhood exists, then the problems turn out to be decidable with PSPACE complexity. Our techniques also allow us to tackle robustness for ultimate positivity, which asks whether there is a bound on the number of steps after which the LRS remains positive. There are two variants depending on whether we ask for a "uniform" bound on this number of steps. For the non-uniform variant, when the neighbourhood is open, the problem turns out to be tractable, even when the neighbourhood is given as input.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22344v1</id>
    <title>Matrices with cyclically monotone rows and Cantor numeration systems</title>
    <updated>2026-04-24T08:19:58Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2604.22344v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2604.22344v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study a class of square matrices with non-negative elements which have cyclically monotone rows in the sense that each row of a matrix from the class consists of a cyclically non-increasing sequence of numbers starting from a maximal element on the diagonal. We prove that if every diagonal element is strictly larger than all other elements in the respective row, then the matrix is regular. This property enables us to solve an open problem that comes from the theory of non-standard numeration systems, also called Cantor numeration systems. The problem concerns a one-to-one relationship between Cantor real bases, which are supposed to be alternate, that is, periodic with a period p, and lists of p sequences of non-negative integers satisfying the so-called Parry condition.</summary>

    <title>Numeration Systems: a Link between Number Theory and Formal Language Theory</title>
    <updated>2012-04-26T11:26:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1204.5887v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1204.5887v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We survey facts mostly emerging from the seminal results of Alan Cobham obtained in the late sixties and early seventies. We do not attempt to be exhaustive but try instead to give some personal interpretations and some research directions. We discuss the notion of numeration systems, recognizable sets of integers and automatic sequences. We briefly sketch some results about transcendence related to the representation of real numbers. We conclude with some applications to combinatorial game theory and verification of infinite-state systems and present a list of open problems.</summary>

    <title>Singular distributions of random variables with independent digits of representation in numeral system with natural base and redundant alphabet</title>
    <updated>2026-01-03T16:17:06Z</updated>

    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2601.01226v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Given natural parameters s and r, where $2\leq s\leq r$, we consider the distribution of a random variable $ξ=\sum\limits_{k=1}^{\infty}s^{-k}ξ_k\equivΔ^{r_s}_{ξ_1ξ_2...ξ_k...},$ where $(ξ_k)$ is a sequence of independent random variables taking values in $\{0,1,...,r\}$ with probabilities $p_0,p_1,...,p_r$, respectively, and all $ p_i&lt;1$. In the case s=3=r, necessary and sufficient conditions for the singularity and absolute continuity of the distribution of random variable are established. The work also discusses the connection between the distribution of random variable and infinite Bernoulli convolutions governed by the corresponding series as well as representations of numbers in the base-3 numeral system with one redundant digit. Several open problems are formulated.</summary>

    <title>Bit-Swap: Recursive Bits-Back Coding for Lossless Compression with Hierarchical Latent Variables</title>
    <updated>2019-10-02T09:57:24Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.06845v4" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.06845v4" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The bits-back argument suggests that latent variable models can be turned into lossless compression schemes. Translating the bits-back argument into efficient and practical lossless compression schemes for general latent variable models, however, is still an open problem. Bits-Back with Asymmetric Numeral Systems (BB-ANS), recently proposed by Townsend et al. (2019), makes bits-back coding practically feasible for latent variable models with one latent layer, but it is inefficient for hierarchical latent variable models. In this paper we propose Bit-Swap, a new compression scheme that generalizes BB-ANS and achieves strictly better compression rates for hierarchical latent variable models with Markov chain structure. Through experiments we verify that Bit-Swap results in lossless compression rates that are empirically superior to existing techniques. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/fhkingma/bitswap.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2104.10588v1</id>
    <title>IB-DRR: Incremental Learning with Information-Back Discrete Representation Replay</title>
    <updated>2021-04-21T15:32:11Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.10588v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2104.10588v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Incremental learning aims to enable machine learning models to continuously acquire new knowledge given new classes, while maintaining the knowledge already learned for old classes. Saving a subset of training samples of previously seen classes in the memory and replaying them during new training phases is proven to be an efficient and effective way to fulfil this aim. It is evident that the larger number of exemplars the model inherits the better performance it can achieve. However, finding a trade-off between the model performance and the number of samples to save for each class is still an open problem for replay-based incremental learning and is increasingly desirable for real-life applications. In this paper, we approach this open problem by tapping into a two-step compression approach. The first step is a lossy compression, we propose to encode input images and save their discrete latent representations in the form of codes that are learned using a hierarchical Vector Quantised Variational Autoencoder (VQ-VAE). In the second step, we further compress codes losslessly by learning a hierarchical latent variable model with bits-back asymmetric numeral systems (BB-ANS). To compensate for the information lost in the first step compression, we introduce an Information Back (IB) mechanism that utilizes real exemplars for a contrastive learning loss to regularize the training of a classifier. By maintaining all seen exemplars' representations in the format of `codes', Discrete Representation Replay (DRR) outperforms the state-of-art method on CIFAR-100 by a margin of 4% accuracy with a much less memory cost required for saving samples. Incorporated with IB and saving a small set of old raw exemplars as well, the accuracy of DRR can be further improved by 2% accuracy.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2208.02622v1</id>
    <title>The congruence speed formula</title>
    <updated>2022-07-30T03:14:28Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.02622v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2208.02622v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We solve a few open problems related to a peculiar property of the integer tetration ${^{b}a}$, which is the constancy of its congruence speed for any sufficiently large $b=b(a)$. Assuming radix-$10$ (the well-known decimal numeral system), we provide an explicit formula for the congruence speed $V(a) \in \mathbb{N}_0$ of any $a \in \mathbb{N}-\{0\}$ that is not a multiple of $10$. In particular, for any given $n \in \mathbb{N}$, we prove to be true Ripà's conjecture on the smallest $a$ such that $V(a)=n$. Moreover, for any $a \neq 1 : a \not\equiv 0 \pmod {10}$, we show the existence of infinitely many prime numbers $p_j:=p_j(V(a))$ such that $V(p_j)=V(a)$.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2209.09843v1</id>
    <title>Progress on the unfair 0-1-polynomials conjecture using linear recurrences and numerical analysis</title>
    <updated>2022-09-20T16:41:14Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.09843v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2209.09843v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>If the product of two monic polynomials with real nonnegative coefficients has all coefficients equal to 0 or 1, does it follow that all the coefficients of the two factors are also equal to 0 or 1? Here is an equivalent formulation of this intriguing problem: is it possible to weigh unfairly a pair of dice so that the probabilities of every possible outcome (roll them and take the sum) were the same? If the two dice have six faces numbered 1 to 6, it is easy to show that the answer is no. But for general dice with finitely many faces, this is an open problem with no significant advancement since 1937. In this paper we examine, in some sense, the first infinite family of cases that cannot be treated with classical methods: the first die has three faces numbered with 0,2 and 5, while the second die is arbitrary. In other words, we examine factorizations of 0-1-polynomials with one factor equal to $x^5+a x^2 +1$ for some nonnegative $a$. We discover that this case may be solved (that is, necessarily $a=0$ or $a=1$) using the theory of linear recurrence sequences, computation of resultants, a fair amount of analytic and numerical approximations... and a little bit of luck.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2602.01533v1</id>
    <title>Rotation-free Online Handwritten Character Recognition Using Linear Recurrent Units</title>
    <updated>2026-02-02T01:57:45Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2602.01533v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2602.01533v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Online handwritten character recognition leverages stroke order and dynamic features, which generally provide higher accuracy and robustness compared with offline recognition. However, in practical applications, rotational deformations can disrupt the spatial layout of strokes, substantially reducing recognition accuracy. Extracting rotation-invariant features therefore remains a challenging open problem. In this work, we employ the Sliding Window Path Signature (SW-PS) to capture local structural features of characters, and introduce the lightweight Linear Recurrent Units (LRU) as the classifier. The LRU combine the fast incremental processing capability of recurrent neural networks (RNN) with the efficient parallel training of state space models (SSM), while reliably modelling dynamic stroke characteristics. We conducted recognition experiments with random rotation angle up to $\pm 180^{\circ}$ on three subsets of the CASIA-OLHWDB1.1 dataset: digits, English upper letters, and Chinese radicals. The accuracies achieved after ensemble learning were $99.62\%$, $96.67\%$, and $94.33\%$, respectively. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed SW-PS+LRU framework consistently surpasses competing models in both convergence speed and test accuracy.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2403.00098v2</id>
    <title>On the Counting Complexity of the Skolem Problem</title>
    <updated>2025-08-02T12:46:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.00098v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2403.00098v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Skolem Problem asks, given an integer linear recurrence sequence (LRS), to determine whether the sequence contains a zero term or not. Its decidability is a longstanding open problem in theoretical computer science and automata theory. Currently, decidability is only known for LRS of order at most 4. On the other hand, the sole known complexity result is NP-hardness, due to Blondel and Portier.
  A fundamental result in this area is the celebrated Skolem-Mahler-Lech theorem, which asserts that the zero set of any LRS is the union of a finite set and finitely many arithmetic progressions. This paper focuses on a computational perspective of the Skolem-Mahler-Lech theorem: we show that the problem of counting the zeros of a given LRS is #P-hard, and in fact #P-complete for the instances generated in our reduction.</summary>

    <summary>Motivated by the famous Skolem-Mahler-Lech theorem we initiate in this paper the study of a natural class of determinantal varieties which we call {\em Vandermonde varieties}.     <title>Reachability in Injective Piecewise Affine Maps</title>
    <updated>2023-03-17T15:53:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.09752v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2301.09752v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>One of the most basic, longstanding open problems in the theory of dynamical systems is whether reachability is decidable for one-dimensional piecewise affine maps with two intervals. In this paper we prove that for injective maps, it is decidable. We also study various related problems, in each case either establishing decidability, or showing that they are closely connected to Diophantine properties of certain transcendental numbers, analogous to the positivity problem for linear recurrence sequences.   <entry>
    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10266v1</id>
    <title>Temporal Properties of Conditional Independence in Dynamic Bayesian Networks</title>
    <updated>2025-11-13T12:52:50Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.10266v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2511.10266v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Dynamic Bayesian networks (DBNs) are compact graphical representations used to model probabilistic systems where interdependent random variables and their distributions evolve over time. In this paper, we study the verification of the evolution of conditional-independence (CI) propositions against temporal logic specifications. To this end, we consider two specification formalisms over CI propositions: linear temporal logic (LTL), and non-deterministic Büchi automata (NBAs). This problem has two variants. Stochastic CI properties take the given concrete probability distributions into account, while structural CI properties are viewed purely in terms of the graphical structure of the DBN. We show that deciding if a stochastic CI proposition eventually holds is at least as hard as the Skolem problem for linear recurrence sequences, a long-standing open problem in number theory. On the other hand, we show that verifying the evolution of structural CI propositions against LTL and NBA specifications is in PSPACE, and is NP- and coNP-hard. We also identify natural restrictions on the graphical structure of DBNs that make the verification of structural CI properties tractable.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/1802.09263v2</id>
    <title>O-Minimal Invariants for Discrete-Time Dynamical Systems</title>
    <updated>2020-05-11T18:37:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.09263v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1802.09263v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Termination analysis of linear loops plays a key rôle in several areas of computer science, including program verification and abstract interpretation. Already for the simplest variants of linear loops the question of termination relates to deep open problems in number theory, such as the decidability of the Skolem and Positivity Problems for linear recurrence sequences, or equivalently reachability questions for discrete-time linear dynamical systems. In this paper, we introduce the class of \emph{o-minimal invariants}, which is broader than any previously considered, and study the decidability of the existence and algorithmic synthesis of such invariants as certificates of non-termination for linear loops equipped with a large class of halting conditions. We establish two main decidability results, one of them conditional on Schanuel's conjecture in transcendental number theory.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/1707.01157v1</id>
    <title>On Petri Nets with Hierarchical Special Arcs</title>
    <updated>2017-07-04T21:21:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.01157v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1707.01157v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We investigate the decidability of termination, reachability, coverability and deadlock-freeness of Petri nets endowed with a hierarchy on places, and with inhibitor arcs, reset arcs and transfer arcs that respect this hierarchy. We also investigate what happens when we have a mix of these special arcs, some of which respect the hierarchy, while others do not. We settle the decidability status of the above four problems for all combinations of hierarchy, inhibitor, reset and transfer arcs, except the termination problem for two combinations. For both these combinations, we show that the termination problem is as hard as deciding positivity for linear recurrent sequences -- a long-standing open problem.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2211.02365v6</id>
    <title>On Robustness for the Skolem, Positivity and Ultimate Positivity Problems</title>
    <updated>2024-06-04T09:29:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.02365v6" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.02365v6" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Skolem problem is a long-standing open problem in linear dynamical systems: can a linear recurrence sequence (LRS) ever reach 0 from a given initial configuration? Similarly, the positivity problem asks whether the LRS stays positive from an initial configuration. Deciding Skolem (or positivity) has been open for half a century: the best known decidability results are for LRS with special properties (e.g., low order recurrences). But these problems are easier for "uninitialized" variants, where the initial configuration is not fixed but can vary arbitrarily: checking if there is an initial configuration from which the LRS stays positive can be decided in polynomial time (Tiwari in 2004, Braverman in 2006). In this paper, we consider problems that lie between the initialized and uninitialized variants. More precisely, we ask if 0 (resp. negative numbers) can be avoided from every initial configuration in a neighborhood of a given initial configuration. This can be considered as a robust variant of the Skolem (resp. positivity) problem. We show that these problems lie at the frontier of decidability: if the neighbourhood is given as part of the input, then robust Skolem and robust positivity are Diophantine hard, i.e., solving either would entail major breakthroughs in Diophantine approximations, as happens for (non-robust) positivity. However, if one asks whether such a neighbourhood exists, then the problems turn out to be decidable with PSPACE complexity. Our techniques also allow us to tackle robustness for ultimate positivity, which asks whether there is a bound on the number of steps after which the LRS remains positive. There are two variants depending on whether we ask for a "uniform" bound on this number of steps. For the non-uniform variant, when the neighbourhood is open, the problem turns out to be tractable, even when the neighbourhood is given as input.</summary>

300-Definition 1. An infinite ordered set X = {x0 < x1 < x2 < · · · } such that
301-DX < + is said to be syndetic or with bounded gaps. Otherwise stated, X is
302-syndetic if there exists C > 0 such that, for all n  0, xn+1 - xn < C.
303-
304-    If X  N is ultimately periodic, then X is syndetic. Note that the converse
305-does not hold. For instance, consider the complement of the set {2n | n  0}
306:which is syndetic, 2-recognizable but not ultimately periodic.

310:ample, consider the set T = {n  N | s2(n)  0 mod 2}. This set is 2-recognizable
311-and syndetic but not ultimately periodic. It appears in several contexts [11] and
312-in particular, it provides a solution to Prouhet's problem (also known as the
313-Prouhet­Tarry­Escott problem which is a special case of a multi-grade equa-
314-tion).

441-Definition 5. Let k  2. A morphic word w  B is k-automatic if there exists
442-a morphism  : A  A and a coding  such that w =  ((a)) and, for
443-all c  A, |(c)| = k. A morphism satisfying this latter property is said to be
444-uniform.
445-
446:    The link between k-recognizable sets and k-automatic sequences is given by
447-the following result. In particular, in the proof of this result, it is interesting to
448-note that an automaton is canonically associated with a morphism.
449-
450-Theorem 4. [37] An infinite word w = w0w1w2 · · · over an alphabet A is k-
451-automatic if and only if, for all a  A, the set Xa = {i  N | wi = a} is
452:k-recognizable.
453-
454-    Otherwise stated, w = w0w1w2 · · ·  A is k-automatic if and only if there
455-exists a deterministic finite automaton with output (DFAO) M where Q is the
456-set of states of M,  : Q × Ak  Q (resp.  : Q  A) is the transition function
457-(resp. output function) of M, such that  ((q0, repk(n)) = wn for all n  0.

459:Remark 2. Using automata as a model of computation, U -recognizable sets nat-
460-urally raise some interest. On the same level, sets of integers having a morphic
461-characteristic sequence can be considered as another natural generalization of
462:the concept of k-recognizability. Iterations of a morphism may be used to get
463-inductively further elements of the set defined by the morphism and a coding.
464-As will be shown by Theorem 6, similarly to the case of uniform morphisms (as
465-given in Definition 5) described above, the computation of a given element can
466-also be done by using a DFAO and representations of integers in an abstract
467-numeration system.

539-and only if repU (x) is genealogically less than repU (y), we introduce the concept
540-of an abstract numeration system. To define the genealogical order (also called
541-radix or military order), first order words by increasing length and for words of

545-Definition 6. Let L be an infinite regular language over a totally ordered alpha-
546-bet (A, <). An abstract numeration system is the triple S = (L, A, <). Ordering
547-by increasing genealogical order the words in L provides a one-to-one correspon-
548-dence between L and N. The nth word in L (starting from 0) is denoted by
549-repS(n) and the inverse map valS : L  N is such that valS(repS(n)) = n.
550:Any numeration basis U such that N is U -recognizable is a particular case of an
551:abstract numeration system. In this respect, a set X  N is S-recognizable, if
552-repS(X) is a regular language.

664-on two player combinatorial games: no chance, no hidden information, same op-

666-games, we are looking for a winning strategy which allows a player to consum-
667-mate a win regardless of the moves chosen by the other player. If such a strategy
668-exists for given initial conditions, it is therefore natural to ask about the algo-
669:rithmic complexity of the computation of the winning strategy. A first question

673-egy exists for the player who starts. A P-position is a position for which all
674-options lead to a N -position, and is thus winning for the second player1. In the
