722-6 Applications for Verification of Infinite State Systems
723-
724:Sets of numbers recognized by finite automata arise when analyzing systems
725-with unbounded mixed variables taking integer or real values. Therefore are
726-considered systems such as timed or hybrid automata [21]. One needs to develop
727-data structures representing sets manipulated during the exploration of infinite
728-state systems. For instance, it is often needed to compute the set of reachable
729-configurations of such a system.
730-
731:    Let k  2 be an integer. Recall that A set X  R is k-recognizable if there
732-exists a Bu¨chi automaton accepting all the k-representations of the elements
733-in X. This notion extends to subsets of Rd and to Real Vector Automata or
734-RVA. Also Bu¨chi­Bruy`ere's Theorem giving a first order logical characterization
735:of k-recognizable sets of integers holds in this context of real numbers for a
736-suitable structure R, Z, +, 0, <, Vk , see [25]. Roughly speaking definability in
737- R, Z, +, 0, < of subsets of Rd is the natural extension of ultimately periodicity
738-of subsets in N.
739-14
740-
741-Theorem 9. [24] If a subset X  Rd is definable by a first-order formula in
742: R, Z, +, 0, < , then X written in base k  2 is recognizable by a weak determin-
743-istic RVA A.
744-
745-    Weakness means that each strongly connected component of A contains only
746-accepting states or non-accepting states.
747-
748-Theorem 10. [22] Let k,   2 be two multiplicatively independent integers. If
749:X  R is both k- and -recognizable by two weak deterministic RVA, then it is
750-definable in R, Z, +, 0, < .
751-
752-    The extension of Cobham­Semenov's theorem for subsets of Rd in this set-
753:ting is discussed in [23]. The case of two coprime bases was first considered in
754-[22]. Though written in a completely different language, a similar result was in-
755-dependently obtained in [1]. This latter paper is motivated by the study of some
756-fractal sets.
757-
758-Remark 4. Weak deterministic RVA have a particular interest from an algorith-
759:mic point of view. They recognize languages that are recognizable by determin-
760-istic Bu¨chi and deterministic co-Bu¨chi automata. For instance, minimization
761-algorithms in O(n log n) exist for this class [74].

793:8 Some Open Problems
794-
795:We conclude with some general (and probably quite hard) open problems.
796-
797- ­ As mentioned in Section 3, the most general version of Cobham's theorem
798-     still relies on some mild assumptions about the considered morphisms (de-
799-     tails are not given in this survey). F. Durand refers to these as "good sub-
800-     stitutions". One could hope to relax these hypotheses and still get the same
--
821-     S of N containing 0 and such that f (S)  S and g(S)  S. In our example,
822-     the first few elements in S are
823-
824-       0, 1, 2, 3, 5, 6, 7, 10, 11, 13, 14, 15, 21, 23, 26, 27, 29, 30, 31, 42, 43, 47, 53, . . ..
825-
826:     One can therefore study the k-recognizability of S. If one considers maps
827-     where the multiplicative constants are multiplicatively independent, then
828-     Allouche, Shallit and Skordev conjectured that the corresponding set cannot
829:     be k-recognizable [10]. With some technical hypothesis about the multiplica-
830-     tive coefficients when there are at least three affine maps, this conjecture has
831-     been proved to be true in [67]. One could hope to prove this conjecture in full
832-     generality. A possible connection with smooth numbers (having only small
833:     prime factors in their decomposition) has been pointed out by J. Shallit.
834- ­ In combinatorial game theory the Sprague-Grundy function g is of great
835-     interest. For instance, the positions for which g vanishes are exactly the P-
836-     position of the game and when considering sums of games (several games are
837-     played simultaneously and at each turn, the player chooses on which of those
838-     games he will made a move), it can be used to distinguish N -positions [16].
--
872-­ Theorem 10 is a Cobham-like theorem for sets of real numbers, definabil-
873-   ity in R, Z, +, 0, < being the counterpart to ultimate periodicity of a set
874-   of integers. Can a simpler proof of this result be achieved, for instance by
875-   considering the techniques developed in [1]? Also could this result be ex-
876-   tended to other kind of representations of real numbers. For instance, con-
877:   sidering -expansions of real numbers, we could define -recognizable sets
878-   of real numbers and consider two multiplicatively independent real numbers
879-   ,  > 1. As a first step (and to mimic what has chronologically been done
880-   for sets of integers), one could consider a set of real numbers X  R which
881:   is both k-recognizable and -recognizable by two weak deterministic RVA,
882:   with k  2 an integer and  a Pisot number like the Golden ratio, and ask
883-   is X definable in R, Z, +, 0, < ?
884:­ About abstract numeration systems, several questions about S-recognizable
885-   sets are open. For instance, is there some reasonable logical characterization
886:   of the S-recognizable sets of integers which could be compared to the char-
887-   acterization in the extended Presburger arithmetic N, +, Vk . But one can
888:   notice that in general, if X and Y are S-recognizable, there is no reason to
889:   have a S-recognizable set X + Y (even when considering multiplication by a
890:   constant). Another question is to relate the growth function n  #(L  An)
891-   of the regular language L on which the abstract numeration system S is
892:   based and the S-recognizable set. For instance, if P  N[X] is a polynomial
893:   such that P (N) is S-recognizable, what can be said about the growth func-
894-   tion of the language of numeration. Results like the one found in [14] could
895-   be of interest.
896-­ Recently numeration systems based on the powers of a rational number have
897:   been introduced [6] (motivated by a number theoretic question from Mahler).
898-                        17
899-
900-   These numerations reveal interesting and intriguing properties. For instance,
901-
902-   little is known about the properties of the language of numeration L3/2. For
--
923-j
924-
925-   exists and is independent of k, and the characteristic polynomial p(X) of
926-   U is such that p(X) = q(Xn) where q(X) is the minimal polynomial for a
927-   recurrence which gives a regular language [26].
928:­ Let p be a prime. Derksen proved that the zero set of a linear recurrence
929-   over a field of characteristic p is p-automatic [40,2]. Could such a result and
930-   Cobham's theorem be used to get back the classical Skolem­Mahler­Lech
931-   theorem (the zero set of a linear recurrence over a field of characteristic 0 is
932-   ultimately periodic)?
933:­ The reader fond of logic could also look back at the list of open problems
934-   given by Michaux and Villemaire [78]. This survey paper is devoted to prob-
935:   lems related to Bu¨chi's characterization of sets of natural numbers recogniz-
936-   able by finite automata in base k, as well as to Cobham's and Semenov's
937-   extensions of it.

    <summary>For every nonconstant monic polynomial $g \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$, let $\mathfrak{M}(g)$ be the set of positive integers $m$ for which there exist an integer linear recurrence $(s_n)_{n \geq 0}$ having characteristic polynomial $g$ and a positive integer $M$ such that $(s_n)_{n \geq 0}$ has exactly $m$ distinct residues modulo $M$. Dubickas and Novikas proved that $\mathfrak{M}(X^2 - X - 1) = \mathbb{N}$. We study $\mathfrak{M}(g)$ in the case in which $g$ is divisible by a monic quadratic polynomial $f \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ with roots $α,β$ such that $αβ= \pm 1$ and $α/ β$ is not a root of unity. We show that this problem is related to the existence of special primitive divisors of certain Lehmer sequences, and we deduce some consequences on $\mathfrak{M}(g)$. In particular, for $αβ= -1$, we prove that $m \in \mathfrak{M}(g)$ for every integer $m \geq 7$ with $m \neq 10$ and $4 \nmid m$.</summary>

    <title>On the number of residues of certain second-order linear recurrences</title>
    <updated>2024-01-15T13:04:06Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.07661v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2401.07661v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>For every monic polynomial $f \in \mathbb{Z}[X]$ with $\operatorname{deg}(f) \geq 1$, let $\mathcal{L}(f)$ be the set of all linear recurrences with values in $\mathbb{Z}$ and characteristic polynomial $f$, and let \begin{equation*}
  \mathcal{R}(f) := \big\{ρ(\mathbf{x}; m) : \mathbf{x} \in \mathcal{L}(f), \, m \in \mathbb{Z}^+ \big\} , \end{equation*} where $ρ(\mathbf{x}; m)$ is the number of distinct residues of $\mathbf{x}$ modulo $m$.
  Dubickas and Novikas proved that $\mathcal{R}(X^2 - X - 1) = \mathbb{Z}^+$. We generalize this result by showing that $\mathcal{R}(X^2 - a_1 X - 1) = \mathbb{Z}^+$ for every nonzero integer $a_1$. As a corollary, we deduce that for all integers $a_1 \geq 1$ and $k \geq 4$ there exists $ξ\in \mathbb{R}$ such that the sequence of fractional parts $\big(\!\operatorname{frac}(ξα^n)\big)_{n \geq 0}$, where $α:= \big(a_1 + \sqrt{a_1^2 + 4}\,\big) / 2$, has exactly $k$ limit points. Our proofs are constructive and employ some results on the existence of special primitive divisors of certain Lehmer sequences.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2008.00583v4</id>
    <title>Decision problems for linear recurrences involving arbitrary real numbers</title>
    <updated>2021-08-09T09:29:59Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2008.00583v4" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2008.00583v4" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We study the decidability of the Skolem Problem, the Positivity Problem, and the Ultimate Positivity Problem for linear recurrences with real number initial values and real number coefficients in the bit-model of real computation. We show that for each problem there exists a correct partial algorithm which halts for all problem instances for which the answer is locally constant, thus establishing that all three problems are as close to decidable as one can expect them to be in this setting. We further show that the algorithms for the Positivity Problem and the Ultimate Positivity Problem halt on almost every instance with respect to the usual Lebesgue measure on Euclidean space. In comparison, the analogous problems for exact rational or real algebraic coefficients are known to be decidable only for linear recurrences of fairly low order.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2308.06421v1</id>
    <title>Characterising Robust Instances of Ultimate Positivity for Linear Dynamical Systems</title>
    <updated>2023-08-12T00:00:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.06421v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2308.06421v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Linear Dynamical Systems, both discrete and continuous, are invaluable mathematical models in a plethora of applications such the verification of probabilistic systems, model checking, computational biology, cyber-physical systems, and economics. We consider discrete Linear Recurrence Sequences and continuous C-finite functions, i.e. solutions to homogeneous Linear Differential Equations. The Ultimate Positivity Problem gives the recurrence relation and the initialisation as input and asks whether there is a step $n_0$ (resp. a time $t_0$) such that the Linear Recurrence Sequence $u[n] \ge 0$ for $n &gt; n_0$ (resp. solution to homogeneous linear differential equation $u(t) \ge 0$ for $t &gt; t_0$). There are intrinsic number-theoretic challenges to surmount in order to decide these problems, which crucially arise in engineering and the practical sciences. In these settings, the difficult corner cases are seldom relevant: tolerance to the inherent imprecision is especially critical. We thus characterise \textit{robust} instances of the Ultimate Positivity Problem, i.e.\ inputs for which the decision is locally constant. We describe the sets of Robust YES and Robust NO instances using the First Order Theory of the Reals. We show, via the admission of quantifier elimination by the First Order Theory of the Reals, that these sets are semialgebraic.</summary>

  <entry>
    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2211.02365v6</id>
    <title>On Robustness for the Skolem, Positivity and Ultimate Positivity Problems</title>
    <updated>2024-06-04T09:29:53Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.02365v6" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2211.02365v6" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The Skolem problem is a long-standing open problem in linear dynamical systems: can a linear recurrence sequence (LRS) ever reach 0 from a given initial configuration? Similarly, the positivity problem asks whether the LRS stays positive from an initial configuration. Deciding Skolem (or positivity) has been open for half a century: the best known decidability results are for LRS with special properties (e.g., low order recurrences). But these problems are easier for "uninitialized" variants, where the initial configuration is not fixed but can vary arbitrarily: checking if there is an initial configuration from which the LRS stays positive can be decided in polynomial time (Tiwari in 2004, Braverman in 2006). In this paper, we consider problems that lie between the initialized and uninitialized variants. More precisely, we ask if 0 (resp. negative numbers) can be avoided from every initial configuration in a neighborhood of a given initial configuration. This can be considered as a robust variant of the Skolem (resp. positivity) problem. We show that these problems lie at the frontier of decidability: if the neighbourhood is given as part of the input, then robust Skolem and robust positivity are Diophantine hard, i.e., solving either would entail major breakthroughs in Diophantine approximations, as happens for (non-robust) positivity. However, if one asks whether such a neighbourhood exists, then the problems turn out to be decidable with PSPACE complexity. Our techniques also allow us to tackle robustness for ultimate positivity, which asks whether there is a bound on the number of steps after which the LRS remains positive. There are two variants depending on whether we ask for a "uniform" bound on this number of steps. For the non-uniform variant, when the neighbourhood is open, the problem turns out to be tractable, even when the neighbourhood is given as input.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2311.06241v1</id>
    <title>Nonnegativity Problems for Matrix Semigroups</title>
    <updated>2023-11-10T18:58:12Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.06241v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2311.06241v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The matrix semigroup membership problem asks, given square matrices $M,M_1,\ldots,M_k$ of the same dimension, whether $M$ lies in the semigroup generated by $M_1,\ldots,M_k$. It is classical that this problem is undecidable in general but decidable in case $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ commute. In this paper we consider the problem of whether, given $M_1,\ldots,M_k$, the semigroup generated by $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ contains a non-negative matrix. We show that in case $M_1,\ldots,M_k$ commute, this problem is decidable subject to Schanuel's Conjecture. We show also that the problem is undecidable if the commutativity assumption is dropped. A key lemma in our decidability result is a procedure to determine, given a matrix $M$, whether the sequence of matrices $(M^n)_{n\geq 0}$ is ultimately nonnegative. This answers a problem posed by S. Akshay (arXiv:2205.09190). The latter result is in stark contrast to the notorious fact that it is not known how to determine effectively whether for any specific matrix index $(i,j)$ the sequence $(M^n)_{i,j}$ is ultimately nonnegative (which is a formulation of the Ultimate Positivity Problem for linear recurrence sequences).</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04870v2</id>
    <title>Robust Positivity Problems for Linear Recurrence Sequences</title>
    <updated>2023-07-12T21:22:58Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04870v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.04870v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Linear Recurrence Sequences (LRS) are a fundamental mathematical primitive for a plethora of applications such as the verification of probabilistic systems, model checking, computational biology, and economics. Positivity (are all terms of the given LRS non-negative?) and Ultimate Positivity (are all but finitely many terms of the given LRS non-negative?) are important open number-theoretic decision problems. Recently, the robust versions of these problems, that ask whether the LRS is (Ultimately) Positive despite small perturbations to its initialisation, have gained attention as a means to model the imprecision that arises in practical settings. However, the state of the art is ill-equipped to reason about imprecision when its extent is explicitly specified. In this paper, we consider Robust Positivity and Ultimate Positivity problems where the neighbourhood of the initialisation, expressed in a natural and general format, is also part of the input. We contribute by proving sharp decidability results: decision procedures at orders our techniques are unable to handle for general LRS would entail significant number-theoretic breakthroughs.</summary>

  <entry>
    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04881v4</id>
    <title>Skolem and Positivity Completeness of Ergodic Markov Chains</title>
    <updated>2024-02-02T19:38:48Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.04881v4" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2305.04881v4" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We consider the following Markov Reachability decision problems that view Markov Chains as Linear Dynamical Systems: given a finite, rational Markov Chain, source and target states, and a rational threshold, does the probability of reaching the target from the source at the $n^{th}$ step: (i) equal the threshold for some $n$? (ii) cross the threshold for some $n$? (iii) cross the threshold for infinitely many $n$? These problems are respectively known to be equivalent to the Skolem, Positivity, and Ultimate Positivity problems for Linear Recurrence Sequences (LRS), number-theoretic problems whose decidability has been open for decades. We present an elementary reduction from LRS Problems to Markov Reachability Problems that improves the state of the art as follows. (a) We map LRS to ergodic (irreducible and aperiodic) Markov Chains that are ubiquitous, not least by virtue of their spectral structure, and (b) our reduction maps LRS of order $k$ to Markov Chains of order $k+1$: a substantial improvement over the previous reduction that mapped LRS of order $k$ to reducible and periodic Markov chains of order $4k+5$. This contribution is significant in view of the fact that the number-theoretic hardness of verifying Linear Dynamical Systems can often be mitigated by spectral assumptions and restrictions on order.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2007.08147v2</id>
    <title>Ultimate periodicity problem for linear numeration systems</title>
    <updated>2021-12-10T12:08:35Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.08147v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2007.08147v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We address the following decision problem. Given a numeration system $U$ and a $U$-recognizable set $X\subseteq\mathbb{N}$, i.e. the set of its greedy $U$-representations is recognized by a finite automaton, decide whether or not $X$ is ultimately periodic. We prove that this problem is decidable for a large class of numeration systems built on linearly recurrent sequences. Based on arithmetical considerations about the recurrence equation and on $p$-adic methods, the DFA given as input provides a bound on the admissible periods to test.</summary>

    <title>A Decision Problem for Ultimately Periodic Sets in Non-standard Numeration Systems</title>
    <updated>2009-07-03T12:43:20Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/0907.0620v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/0907.0620v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>  Consider a non-standard numeration system like the one built over the Fibonacci sequence where nonnegative integers are represented by words over $\{0,1\}$ without two consecutive 1. Given a set $X$ of integers such that the language of their greedy representations in this system is accepted by a finite automaton, we consider the problem of deciding whether or not $X$ is a finite union of arithmetic progressions.     <title>Numeration systems without a dominant root and regularity</title>
    <updated>2025-12-15T10:38:47Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13180v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2512.13180v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Positional numeration systems are a large family of numeration systems used to represent natural numbers. Whether the set of all representations forms a regular language or not is one of the most important questions that can be asked of such a system. This question was investigated in a 1998 article by Hollander. Central to his analysis is a property linking positional numeration systems and Rényi numeration systems, which use a real base to represent real numbers. However, this link only exists when the initial numeration system has a dominant root, which is not a necessary condition for regularity. In this article, we show a more general link between positional numeration systems and alternate base numeration systems, a family generalizing Rényi systems. We then take advantage of this link to provide a full characterization of those numeration systems that generate a regular language. We also discuss the effectiveness of our method, and comment Hollander's results and conjecture in the light of ours.</summary>

  <entry>
    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/1202.4205v2</id>
    <title>Variational description of Gibbs-non-Gibbs dynamical transitions for the Curie-Weiss model</title>
    <updated>2012-02-21T19:53:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1202.4205v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1202.4205v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>We perform a detailed study of Gibbs-non-Gibbs transitions for the Curie-Weiss model subject to independent spin-flip dynamics ("infinite-temperature" dynamics). We show that, in this setup, the program outlined in van Enter, Fernández, den Hollander and Redig can be fully completed, namely that Gibbs-non-Gibbs transitions are equivalent to bifurcations in the set of global minima of the large-deviation rate function for the trajectories of the magnetization conditioned on their endpoint. As a consequence, we show that the time-evolved model is non-Gibbs if and only if this set is not a singleton for some value of the final magnetization. A detailed description of the possible scenarios of bifurcation is given, leading to a full characterization of passages from Gibbs to non-Gibbs -and vice versa- with sharp transition times (under the dynamics Gibbsianness can be lost and can be recovered).
  Our analysis expands the work of Ermolaev and Kulske who considered zero magnetic field and finite-temperature spin-flip dynamics. We consider both zero and non-zero magnetic field but restricted to infinite-temperature spin-flip dynamics. Our results reveal an interesting dependence on the interaction parameters, including the presence of forbidden regions for the optimal trajectories and the possible occurrence of overshoots and undershoots in the optimal trajectories. The numerical plots provided are obtained with the help of MATHEMATICA.</summary>
    <category term="math.PR" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

    <title>How T-cells use large deviations to recognize foreign antigens</title>
    <updated>2008-05-15T08:47:37Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/q-bio/0605016v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/q-bio/0605016v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>  A stochastic model for the activation of T-cells is analysed. T-cells are part of the immune system and recognize foreign antigens against a background of the body's own molecules. The model under consideration is a slight generalization of a model introduced by Van den Berg, Rand and Burroughs in 2001, and is capable of explaining how this recognition works on the basis of rare stochastic events.     <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/math-ph/0303044v1</id>
    <title>Two-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian for the time-symmetric two-body problem of the relativistic action-at-a-distance electrodynamics</title>
    <updated>2003-03-18T21:48:07Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/math-ph/0303044v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/math-ph/0303044v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>  We find a two-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian for the time-symmetric problem of straight line motion of two electrons in direct relativistic interaction. This time-symmetric dynamical system appeared 100 years ago and it was popularized in the 1940s by the work of Wheeler and Feynman in electrodynamics, which was left incomplete due to the lack of a Hamiltonian description. The form of our Hamiltonian is such that the action of a Lorentz transformation is explicitly described by a canonical transformation (with rescaling of the evolution parameter). The method is closed and defines the Hamiltonian in implicit form without power expansions. We outline the method with an emphasis on the physics of this complex conservative dynamical system. The Hamiltonian orbits are calculated numerically at low energies using a self-consistent steepest-descent method (a stable numerical method that chooses only the nonrunaway solution). The two-degree-of-freedom Hamiltonian suggests a simple prescription for the canonical quantization of the relativistic two-body problem.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21350v2</id>
    <title>Optimal Structure of Signal Networks for Efficient Information Aggregation</title>
    <updated>2025-10-13T11:03:22Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.21350v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2505.21350v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>This paper develops a mathematical framework to study signal networks, in which nodes can be active or inactive, and their activation or deactivation is driven by external signals and the states of the nodes to which they are connected via links. The focus is on determining the optimal number of key nodes (= highly connected and structurally important nodes) required to represent the global activation state of the network accurately. Motivated by neuroscience, medical science, and social science examples, we describe the node dynamics as a continuous-time inhomogeneous Markov process. Under mean-field and homogeneity assumptions, appropriate for large scale-free and disassortative signal networks, we derive differential equations characterising the global activation behaviour and compute the expected hitting time to network triggering. Analytical and numerical results show that two or three key nodes are typically sufficient to approximate the overall network state well, balancing sensitivity and robustness. Our findings provide insight into how natural systems can efficiently aggregate information by exploiting minimal structural components.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17381v1</id>
    <title>Large deviation principle for friendship-biases in Galton--Watson trees</title>
    <updated>2026-06-16T00:37:43Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.17381v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2606.17381v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In this paper we consider the friendship-bias of the vertices in an infinite rooted Galton--Watson tree. The friendship-bias of a vertex is the difference between the average degree of the neighbours of the vertex and the degree of the vertex itself. A vertex is said to be of type $χ\in S$, with $S = \{-,0,+\}$, when its friendship-bias is, respectively, strictly negative, zero or strictly positive. We consider the fractions $f_l^χ$ of vertices of type $χ\in S$ along a random downward path up to branching depth $l \in \mathbb{N}$ and derive a large deviation principle (LDP) for the triple $(f_l^χ)_{χ\in S}$ as $l\to\infty$. The branching depth of a vertex counts the number of branchings that occur along the path that connects the vertex to the root of the tree. The rate in the LDP is $l$, while the rate function in the LDP is identified in terms of a variational formula minimising a relative entropy under a linear constraint.
  We focus on the case of binary branching, for which the rate function is already quite involved. We identify the qualitative properties of the rate function and show how it can be computed numerically. We briefly indicate how to proceed for more general branching and for vertex types along a tree consisting of a finite number of random downward paths. Our paper is the first to consider large deviations of vertex types.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/1701.07520v2</id>
    <title>Reaching for the quantum limits in the simultaneous estimation of phase and phase diffusion</title>
    <updated>2017-09-23T16:51:26Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.07520v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1701.07520v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Phase diffusion invariably accompanies all phase estimation strategies -- quantum or classical. A precise estimation of the former can often provide valuable understanding of the physics of the phase generating phenomena itself. We theoretically examine the performance of fixed-particle number probe states in the simultaneous estimation of phase and collective phase diffusion. We derive analytical quantum limits associated with the simultaneous local estimation of phase and phase diffusion within the quantum Cramer-Rao bound framework in the regimes of large and small phase diffusive noise. The former is for a general fixed-particle number state and the latter for Holland Burnett states, for which we show quantum-enhanced estimation of phase as well as phase diffusion. We next investigate the simultaneous attainability of these quantum limits using projective measurements acting on a single copy of the state in terms of a trade-off relation. In particular, we are interested how this trade-off varies as a function of the dimension of the state. We derive an analytical bound for this trade-off in the large phase diffusion regime for a particular form of the measurement, and show that the maximum of 2, set by the quantum Cramer-Rao bound, is attainable. Further, we show numerical evidence that as diffusion approaches zero, the optimal trade-off relation approaches 1 for Holland-Burnett states. These numerical results are valid in the small particle number regime and suggest that the trade-off for estimating one parameter with quantum-limited precision leads to a complete lack of precision for the other parameter as the diffusion strength approaches zero. Finally, we provide numerical results showing behaviour of the trade-off for a general value of phase diffusion when using Holland-Burnett probe states.</summary>

    <summary>Twisted $\operatorname{SL}_2 \mathbb{C}$ local systems on surfaces of finite type appear often in geometry and physics.     <title>Renormalization of quantum field theory on curved space-times, a causal approach</title>
    <updated>2013-12-22T16:02:57Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.5674v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1312.5674v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The subject of the thesis is the construction of a perturbative quantum theory of interacting fields on a curved space-time, following a point of view pioneered by Stueckelberg and Bogoliubov and developed by Epstein-Glaser on the flat Minkowski space-time. In 2000, a breakthrough was done by Brunetti and Fredenhagen who were able to extend the Epstein-Glaser theory by exploiting the point of view developed by Radzikowski to define quantum states on a curved space-time in terms of wave-front sets. These results were further extended by Fredenhagen, Brunetti, Hollands, Wald, Rejzner, etc. to Yang-Mills fields and the gravitation. However, even for theories without gauge invariance, many mathematical details were left unexplored and unquestioned. Our task was precisely to derive fully rigorously this theory in the case there is no gauge invariance. We propose in our work a complete review of the result, solving numerous questions, adding many new results around this program and, eventually, giving more precise details on the counterterms and ambiguities in the renormalization process, and a deeper understanding of the geometry of the wave front set of the n-point functions.</summary>

    <title>Modeling near ground-state cooling of two-dimensional ion crystals in a Penning trap using electromagnetically induced transparency</title>
    <updated>2018-09-18T16:41:38Z</updated>

    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1809.05492v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Penning traps, with their ability to control planar crystals of tens to hundreds of ions, are versatile quantum simulators. Thermal occupations of the motional drumhead modes, transverse to the plane of the ion crystal, degrade the quality of quantum simulations. Laser cooling using electromagnetically induced transparency (EIT cooling) is attractive as an efficient way to quickly initialize the drumhead modes to near ground-state occupations. We numerically investigate the efficiency of EIT cooling of planar ion crystals in a Penning trap, accounting for complications arising from the nature of the trap and from the simultaneous cooling of multiple ions.     <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/1408.0801v2</id>
    <title>Instabilities of extremal rotating black holes in higher dimensions</title>
    <updated>2015-04-30T11:06:02Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1408.0801v2" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1408.0801v2" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Recently, Durkee and Reall have conjectured a criterion for linear instability of rotating, extremal, asymptotically Minkowskian black holes in $d\ge 4$ dimensions, such as the Myers-Perry black holes. They considered a certain elliptic operator, $\cA$, acting on symmetric trace-free tensors intrinsic to the horizon. Based in part on numerical evidence, they suggested that if the lowest eigenvalue of this operator is less than the critical value $-1/4$ ( called "effective BF-bound"), then the black hole is linearly unstable. In this paper, we prove an extended version of their conjecture. Our proof uses a combination of methods such as (i) the "canonical energy method" of Hollands-Wald, (ii) algebraically special properties of the near horizon geometries associated with the black hole, (iii) the Corvino-Schoen technique, and (iv) semiclassical analysis. Our method of proof is also applicable to rotating, extremal asymptotically Anti-deSitter black holes. In that case, we find additional instabilities for ultra-spinning black holes. Although we explicitly discuss in this paper only extremal black holes, we argue that our results can be generalized to {\em near} extremal black holes.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09556v1</id>
    <title>A Hybrid Analytical Framework for Asymmetric Pressure and Boundary Layer Wind Simulation in Nor'easters</title>
    <updated>2025-09-11T15:45:44Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.09556v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2509.09556v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Nor'easters frequently impact the North American East Coast, bringing hazardous precipitation, winds, and coastal flooding. Accurate simulation of their pressure and wind fields is essential for forecasting, risk assessment, and infrastructure planning, yet remains challenging due to their complex, asymmetric structure. This study introduces a novel hybrid analytical-data-driven model designed to efficiently simulate Nor'easter pressure and boundary layer wind fields. The pressure field is modeled using an adapted Holland-type formulation, with azimuthally varying parameters estimated through Kriging surrogate models informed by sensitivity analysis of reanalysis data. The wind field is then derived analytically from the momentum equations by decomposing the wind flow into gradient and frictional components. Model performance is assessed against ERA-Interim reanalysis data and surface wind observations from a historical event. Results show that the proposed pressure model accurately reproduces elliptical isobars and key asymmetrical patterns, while the wind model captures the fundamental structure and intensity of the boundary layer flow, including the presence of supergradient winds. Owing to its physical basis, computational efficiency, and ability to represent critical storm asymmetries, the model offers a valuable alternative to computationally expensive numerical simulations for hazard assessment and scenario analysis of extreme Nor'easters.</summary>

    <updated>2019-05-13T19:04:03Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1905.05244v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1905.05244v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The interaction between aphids, ants and ladybirds has been investigated from an ecological point of view since many decades, while there are no attempts to describe it from a mathematical point of view. This paper introduces a new mathematical model to describe the within-season population dynamics in an ecological patch of a system composed by aphids, ants and ladybirds, through a set of four differential equations. The proposed model is based on the Kindlmann and Dixon set of differential equations, focused on the prediction of the aphids-ladybirds population densities, that share a prey-predator relationship. The population of ants, in mutualistic relationship with aphids and in interspecific competition with ladybirds, is described according to the Holland and De Angelis mathematical model, in which the authors faced the problem of mutualistic interactions in general terms. The set of differential equations proposed here is discretized by means the Nonstandard Finite Difference scheme, successfully applied by Gabbriellini to the mutualistic model. The constructed finite-difference scheme is positivity-preserving and characterized by four nonhyperbolic steady-states, as highlighted by the phase-space and time-series analyses. Particular attention is dedicated to the steady-state most interesting from an ecological point of view, whose asymptotic stability is demonstrated via the Centre Manifold Theory. The model allows to numerically confirm that mutualistic relationship effectively influences the population dynamic, by increasing the peaks of the aphids and ants population densities. Nonetheless, it is showed that the asymptotical populations of aphids and ladybirds collapse for any initial condition, unlike that of ants that, after the peak, settle on a constant asymptotic value.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21450v3</id>
    <title>Composite B-Spline Current Deposition and Interpolation Operators for Thin-Wire Finite-Difference Time-Domain Simulations</title>
    <updated>2026-06-01T11:46:05Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.21450v3" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2605.21450v3" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>Holland-Simpson thin-wire finite-difference time-domain (FDTD) simulations of obliquely oriented closed-loop antennas exhibit persistent low-frequency parasitic currents because the current-deposition operator fails to conserve charge. This deposition operator, together with an interpolation operator that samples the tangential electric field along the wire, can be realized as regularizations of distributions: the wire current is deposited as a source term by integrating it against a regularized delta function along the wire, and the electric field is sampled back to the wire by integrating it against the same regularized delta function. We show that charge conservation requires the deposited current to be discretely divergence-free when the wire carries a constant current, and we introduce a family of composite B-spline regularizations that satisfy this condition to machine precision. Exact evaluation of the coupling line integrals is possible because the B-spline kernels are piecewise polynomial with a priori-known breakpoints, allowing composite Gauss-Legendre quadrature with subinterval breakpoints at every grid-plane crossing. Taking the interpolation operator as the discrete adjoint of the deposition operator preserves skew-symmetry and ensures that a discretely irrotational electric field drives no net electromotive force around a closed loop. Numerical experiments on a center-fed dipole and on circular and square loop antennas show that the proposed regularizations yield orientation-independent impedance values consistent with known characteristics, whereas a simple trilinear regularization produces unphysical parasitic low-frequency currents in closed loops.</summary>

    <title>Parallel Hyperedge Replacement Grammars</title>

    <summary>In 2018, it was shown that all finitely generated virtually Abelian groups have multiple context-free word problems, and it is still an open problem as to where to precisely place the word problems of hyperbolic groups in the formal language hierarchy.   <entry>
    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09813v1</id>
    <title>Orders of algebraic numbers in finite fields</title>
    <updated>2021-06-17T20:53:45Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09813v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2106.09813v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>For an algebraic number $α$ we consider the orders of the reductions of $α$ in finite fields. In the case where $α$ is an integer, it is known by the work on Artin's primitive root conjecture that the order is "almost always almost maximal" assuming the generalized Riemann hypothesis, but unconditional results remain modest. We consider higher degree variants under GRH. First, we modify an argument of Roskam to settle the case where $α$ and the reduction have degree two. Second, we give a positive lower density result when $α$ is of degree three and the reduction is of degree two. Third, we give higher rank results in situations where the reductions are of degree two, three, four or six. As an application we give an almost equidistribution result for linear recurrences modulo primes. Finally, we present a general result conditional to GRH and a hypothesis on smooth values of polynomials at prime arguments.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26214v1</id>
    <title>Minimal Counterexamples of the MacWilliams Extension Theorem for Stabilizer Codes</title>
    <updated>2026-07-28T19:31:39Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/2607.26214v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.26214v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>The MacWilliams extension theorem fails for module alphabets with non-cyclic socle, and the label alphabet of qudit stabilizer codes, $\F_{q^2}$ over $\F_q$, is such an alphabet. Quantum error correction, however, only ever sees \emph{self-orthogonal} additive codes, and whether that rigidity rescues the theorem---equivalently, whether every weight-preserving isomorphism of stabilizer groups is implemented by local Cliffords and a qudit permutation---was asked by Gluesing-Luerssen and Pllaha and answered negatively by Pllaha for particular qubit codes. We develop the negative answer systematically and at the smallest possible scales. For every prime power $q$ we construct a pair of $[[q+1,q-1]]_q$ stabilizer codes and a weight-preserving isomorphism between them extending to no monomial transformation; the codespaces are inequivalent even under arbitrary local unitaries combined with permutations, though they share Shor--Laflamme enumerators. Self-orthogonality is automatic here, by two elementary lemmas which also show that Dyshko's threshold-length counterexamples were already self-orthogonal, unremarked. For qubits we prove by exhaustive search that length $3$ is minimal and the counterexample essentially unique. Dropping the ``idle qudit'' invariant that detects these, we find the minimal full-support lengths: $4$ for a non-extendable isometry, $5$ for a weight-isometric pair that is not monomially equivalent, realized by explicit $[[5,2]]$ codes; at length $6$ all nontrivial stabilizer elements can have weight $\ge 4$. Whether these codespaces are locally unitarily equivalent is posed as an open problem, connecting the extension problem to the LU--LC circle of questions.</summary>

    <category term="math-ph" scheme="http://arxiv.org/schemas/atom"/>

  <entry>
    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/1807.11899v1</id>
    <title>The Formal Inverse of the Period-Doubling Sequence</title>
    <updated>2018-07-31T16:22:08Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1807.11899v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1807.11899v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>If $p$ is a prime number, consider a $p$-automatic sequence $(u_n)_{n\ge 0}$, and let $U(X) = \sum_{n\ge 0} u_n X^n \in \mathbb{F}_p[[X]]$ be its generating function. Assume that there exists a formal power series $V(X) = \sum_{n\ge 0} v_n X^n \in \mathbb{F}_p[[X]]$ which is the compositional inverse of $U$, i.e., $U(V(X))=X=V(U(X))$. The problem investigated in this paper is to study the properties of the sequence $(v_n)_{n\ge 0}$. The work was first initiated for the Thue-Morse sequence, and more recently the case of two variations of the Baum-Sweet sequence has been treated. In this paper, we deal with the case of the period-doubling sequence. We first show that the sequence of indices at which the period-doubling sequence takes value $0$ (resp., $1$) is not $k$-regular for any $k\ge 2$. Secondly, we give recurrence relations for its formal inverse, then we easily show that it is $2$-automatic, and we also provide an automaton that generates it. Thirdly, we study the sequence of indices at which this formal inverse takes value $1$, and we show that it is not $k$-regular for any $k\ge 2$ by connecting it to the characteristic sequence of Fibonacci numbers. We leave as an open problem the case of the sequence of indices at which this formal inverse takes value $0$. We end the paper with a remark on the case of generalized Thue-Morse sequences.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/1711.06410v1</id>
    <title>A lower bound for the two-variable Artin conjecture and prime divisors of recurrence sequences</title>
    <updated>2017-11-17T05:09:09Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.06410v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/1711.06410v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>In 1927, Artin conjectured that any integer other than -1 or a perfect square generates the multiplicative group $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}^\times$ for infinitely many $p$. In \cite{MoSt}, Moree and Stevenhagen considered a two-variable version of this problem, and proved a positive density result conditionally to the generalized Riemann Hypothesis by adapting a proof by Hooley for the original conjecture (\cite{Ho}). In this article, we prove an unconditional lower bound for this two-variable problem. In particular, we prove an estimate for the number of distinct primes which divide one of the first $N$ terms of a non-degenerate binary recurrence sequence. We also prove a weaker version of the same theorem, and give three proofs that we consider to be of independent interest. The first proof uses a transcendence result of Stewart \cite{Stew}, the second uses a theorem of Bombieri and Schmidt on Thue equations \cite{BoSc} and the third uses Mumford's gap principle for counting points on curves by their height \cite{Mum}. We finally prove a disjunction theorem, where we consider the set of primes satisfying either our two-variable condition or the original condition of Artin's conjecture. We give an unconditional lower bound for the number of such primes.</summary>

    <id>http://arxiv.org/abs/math/9912250v1</id>
    <title>A two variable Artin conjecture</title>
    <updated>1999-12-06T00:00:00Z</updated>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/abs/math/9912250v1" rel="alternate" type="text/html"/>
    <link href="https://arxiv.org/pdf/math/9912250v1" rel="related" type="application/pdf" title="pdf"/>
    <summary>  Let a and b be non-zero rational numbers that are multiplicatively independent. We study the natural density of the set of primes p for which the subgroup of the multiplicative group of the finite field with p elements generated by (a\mod p) contains (b\mod p). It is shown that, under assumption of the generalized Riemann hypothesis (GRH), this density exists and equals a positive rational multiple of the universal constant S=\prod_{p prime}(1-p/(p^3-1)). An explicit value of the density is given under mild conditions on a and b. This extends and corrects earlier work of P.J. Stephens (1976). Our result, in combination with earlier work of the second author, allows us to deduce that any second order linear recurrence with reducible characteristic polynomial having integer elements, has a positive density of prime divisors (under GRH).</summary>

22-                                       Let Pb be the language of primes expressed in base b  2, using the most significant digit first,
23-                                       and disallowing leading zeroes. Minsky and Papert [2] proved in 1966 that Pb is not regular.
24-                                       Furthermore, Shallit [4] proved in 1996 that any finite automaton that correctly recognizes
25-                                       primes up to N must have (N 1/43) states. Hartmanis and Shank [1], and, independently,
26:                                       Schu¨tzenberger [3] proved in 1968 that the primes are not context-free.
27-
28-                                           We show a new result that Pb is not regular. Firstly, assume Pb is regular. Using number
29-                                       theory, we find a prime of the form K × bn + 1 where K is sufficiently large, and k × bn + 1
30-                                       is composite for all k < K. Using the classical pumping lemma for regular languages, Pb
31-                                       contains k × bn + 1 for some k < K. This leads to a contradiction.

20-                                            If A = {0, 1, . . . , q-1}, then we can identify words over A with integers by means
21-                                         of the q-adic representation. Studying number theoretic properties of automatic sets
22-                                         of integers is a topic with quite some history. Hartmanis and Shanks [4] showed
23:                                         that the set of primes is not automatic. This leads to the question how far the set
24-                                         of primes deviates from an automatic set. One way to measure this is automaticity:
25-                                         We define the automaticity of a set X as the function A(x) that associates to an
26-                                         integer x the size of the smallest automaton accepting an integer n  x if and only
27-                                         if n  X . Clearly, the automaticity of any set satisfies A(x)  x, and a set is
28-                                         automatic if and only if A(x) = O(1). Here we show that the set of primes is close
29-                                         to the maximal automaticity.

       <p>Given a deterministic finite automaton (DFA) A, we present a simple algorithm for constructing deterministic finite automata that accept the shortest forbidden factors, the shortest forbidden prefixes, the shortest forbidden suffixes, the shortest forbidden words, the shortest allowed suffixes, and the shortest allowed words of the automaton A. We refer to these sets as the shortest characteristic factors of the automaton A. If the given automaton is local, and therefore the language it accepts is strictly locally testable, the sets of its shortest characteristic factors are finite, and these automata are acyclic. Otherwise, they accept infinite languages. This approach simplifies existing methods for the extraction of forbidden factors, allows the extraction of more types of characteristic factors, and also generalizes the extraction for all classes of DFAs. Furthermore, we demonstrate that this type of extraction can be used for a sublinear run of an automaton for certain inputs. We define a positive position run of a deterministic finite automaton, representing all positions in an input string where the automaton reaches a final state. Finally, we present an algorithm for computing the positive position run of the automaton, which utilizes pattern set matching of its shortest forbidden factors and its shortest forbidden or allowed suffixes, provided that the sets are finite. 13:       Abstract. We study the decidability of the Skolem Problem, the Positivity Problem,
14:       and the Ultimate Positivity Problem for linear recurrences with real number initial values
15-       and real number coefficients in the bit-model of real computation. We show that for each
16-       problem there exists a correct partial algorithm which halts for all problem instances
17-       for which the answer is locally constant, thus establishing that all three problems are as
18:       close to decidable as one can expect them to be in this setting. We further show that
19:       the algorithms for the Positivity Problem and the Ultimate Positivity Problem halt on
20-       almost every instance with respect to the usual Lebesgue measure on Euclidean space. In
21-       comparison, the analogous problems for exact rational or real algebraic coefficients are
22:       known to be decidable only for linear recurrences of fairly low order.
23-
24-                                               1. Introduction
25-
26-A real linear recurrence sequence is a sequence (uk)k of real numbers satisfying a linear
27-recurrence relation of the form uk+n = c1uk+n-1 + · · · + cnuk. The Skolem-Mahler-Lech
--
29-simple form: it is the union of a finite set F and an empty or infinite set I which is the
30-union of a finite number of arithmetic progressions. For given rational or integer coefficients
31-c1, . . . , cn and initial values u1, . . . , un the set I can be effectively computed [BM76]. The
32-same is not known of the set F . It is well known [EvdPSW03] that the problem of computing
33-the set F is equivalent to the problem of deciding whether a given linear recurrence has a zero.
34:The latter problem, often referred to as the Skolem Problem in the literature, has proven to
35:be infamously difficult. It is generally believed to be decidable for linear recurrences of any
36:order, but known to be decidable only up to order four [TMS84, Ver85]. Two closely related
37:decision problems of note are the Positivity Problem, which asks for given a linear recurrence
38:to decide whether all of its terms are non-negative, and the Ultimate Positivity Problem,
39-which asks for given a linear recurrence to decide whether all but finitely many of its terms
40-are non-negative. In [OW14b] it was shown that both Positivity and Ultimate Positivity are
41:decidable up to order five. At the same time it was shown that a feasible algorithm for solving
42-
43:    Key words and phrases: Skolem Problem, Linear Recurrences, Computable Analysis.
44-    This work was conducted while the author was affiliated with the Department of Computer Science,
45-Oxford University, UK.

50-
51-either Positivity or Ultimate Positivity at order six would entail major breakthroughs in
52-the field of Diophantine approximation, making it highly unlikely for existing mathematical
53-methods to allow for further progress to be made on these problems. For linear recurrences
54:with simple characteristic roots the Positivity Problem is known to be decidable up to order
55:nine [OW14a] and the Ultimate Positivity Problem is known to be decidable for all orders
56-[OW14c]. These and related decision problems have numerous applications in theoretical
57-computer science and beyond, see [OW14b] and references therein. See the survey [OW15]
58-for a more detailed historical overview and further related results.
59-
60:     In this paper we study the Skolem Problem, the Positivity Problem, and the Ultimate
61:Positivity Problem for linear recurrences whose coefficients and initial values are arbitrary
62-real numbers which are given as fast converging Cauchy sequences of rational numbers. For
63:topological reasons no non-trivial problem is decidable in this setting. Instead one should
64-ask if there exists a maximal partial algorithm for deciding a given problem. When such an
65-algorithm is given a problem instance as input it either diverges or halts and outputs the
66-correct answer for the decision problem. It is required to halt on every problem instance
67-for which the answer for the decision problem is locally constant. We will call such problem
68-instances robust instances. This ensures that its halting set contains the halting set of any
69-correct partial algorithm for deciding the problem.
70-
71-     Besides being mathematically interesting in their own right, the real number versions of
72:the Skolem Problem and its variants can be motivated by practical applications. In most
73-applications to engineering and the natural sciences the assumption that the input be given
74-as an exact integer, rational number, or real algebraic number is quite unrealistic. There
75-it is usually more appropriate to assume that the inputs be known only approximately to
76-finite accuracy, but with a known error bound. This can be modelled by assuming that one
77-is given a rational box which contains the problem instance of interest. A maximal partial
78-algorithm for deciding the real number version of a decision problem can be automatically
79-translated to an algorithm which takes as input such a box, halts and outputs 1 if the box is
80-contained in the set of robust "yes"-instances, halts and outputs 0 if the box is contained in
81-the set of robust "no"-instances, halts and outputs -1 if the box contains both robust "no"-
82-and robust "yes"-instances, and diverges in all other cases. Such an algorithm need not exist
83:when the problem is decidable on rational inputs: There exist sets A  R such that A  Q is
84:decidable but A is not maximally partially decidable. One can for instance take the union
85:of any decidable subset of Q with a singleton {x} that is not co-c.e. closed. It is of course
86:conversely true that there exist sets A  R that are maximally partially decidable such that
87:A  Q is not decidable. One can take for instance any undecidable co-c.e. set of integers.
88-
89:     We will show that the real number versions of the Skolem Problem, the Positivity
90:Problem, and the Ultimate Positivity Problem are maximally partially decidable for linear
91-recurrences of any order. Thus, the real number versions of all three problems are, in a
92:sense, as close to decidable as one can expect them to be. That this is achievable for real
93-linear recurrences despite the hardness results for rational ones is perhaps not too surprising.
94:The existing decidability proofs for low orders only fail to generalise to higher orders due
95-to the presence of "critical" problem instances where the dominant part of the exponential
96-polynomial solution does not admit an exponential lower bound. Since this situation is
97-unstable under small perturbations one will not be obliged to decide the problems in these
98-critical instances for real number inputs, thus avoiding the aforementioned hardness results.
99-
100-     Indeed, our proof consists almost entirely of translating the known decision methods
101-for low-orders to the real number setting and noting that these already suffice to establish
102-Vol. 17:3   DECISION PROBLEMS FOR LINEAR RECURRENCES  16:3
103-
104:maximal partial decidability for all orders. The proof is considerably more elementary than
105-its counterparts for integer coefficients. The use of Baker's theorem and similar deep results
106-from analytic number theory can be entirely avoided. On the other hand new problems
107-appear in the real number setting that are absent from the discrete setting. The study of the
108-asymptotic behaviour of a linear recurrence relies heavily on the study of its exponential
109-polynomial solution. It is easy to see that in the real number setting the exponential
110-polynomial solution is not in general computable from the linear recurrence. This is where
111-new ideas are required. It is relatively easy to see that one can still compute those coefficients
112-of the exponential polynomial solution which belong to simple characteristic roots. This
113:will suffice to computably recognise all robust instances of the Skolem Problem and the
114:Positivity Problem, and all robust "yes"-instances of the Ultimate Positivity Problem. For the
115:Ultimate Positivity Problem there exist robust "no"-instances whose dominant characteristic
116-roots are not simple, which implies that the corresponding coefficients in the exponential
117-polynomial solution do not depend continuously on the input. These instances are by far
118-the most difficult ones to handle. They will be treated by reduction to the first-order theory
119-of the reals. Recall that the first-order theory of the reals is the first-order theory of the
120-structure R, 0, 1, +, ×, -, >, = . By the Tarski-Seidenberg theorem [BPR06, Theorem 2.77]
121:this theory is decidable. The main ideas in this case are best illustrated with the help of a
122-simple example:
123-

126-its exponential polynomial solution is uk =  + k - k(k - 1). It is hence a "no"-instance
127:of the Ultimate Positivity Problem. Let us show how we can verify this computationally
128-when the coefficients and initial values are given as sequences of approximations. This is not
129-completely straightforward since, as mentioned earlier, the exponential polynomial solution
130-does not depend continuously on the input.

256-     Let us now discuss decision problems in this context. With any subset A  Rn one can
257-associate a decision problem: given x  Rn as input halt in finite time and output 1 if and
258-only if x  A or output 0 if x / A. It is easy to see that for continuity reasons the only
259:subsets of Rn that are decidable in this sense are the empty set and Rn itself.
260-
261-     The next best thing one can hope for is to find an algorithm which decides the problem
262-in as many points as possible. This is somewhat of a folklore idea in computable analysis,
263-but there does not appear to be an established standard terminology in the literature. Let
264-X be a represented space. A partial2 algorithm for deciding a set A  X is an algorithm
--
277-and output on termination depend only on the point x but not on the choice of name3. We
278-further require that it be correct, i.e., that it halt and return 1 only when x  A and that
279-it halt and return 0 only when x / A. Its halting set is the set of points for which it halts.
280-This set is well-defined by the extensionality assumption. A partial algorithm for deciding A
281-is called maximal if its halting set contains the halting set of all other partial algorithms
282:for deciding A. We call A maximally partially decidable if there exists a maximal partial
283-algorithm for deciding A.
284-
285-Proposition 2.1. Let X be an admissibly represented countably based T0 space. A partial
286-algorithm for deciding A is maximal if and only if its halting set is equal to the set of points
287-of continuity of the characteristic function A : X  {0, 1}, where {0, 1} carries the discrete
--
295-halting set.
296-
297-     In other words, a maximal partial algorithm for deciding A is an algorithm that takes as
298-input x  X, halts and outputs 1 if x is contained in the interior of A, halts and outputs
299-0 if x is contained in the interior of the complement of A, and diverges if x is contained
300:in the boundary of A. In particular, every set is maximally partially decidable relative to
301:some oracle, and if X is a discrete space then A  X is maximally partially decidable if and
302:only if it is decidable. Therefore maximal partial decidability seems to be, in some sense, a
303:more appropriate generalisation of decidability over N than "naive" decidability. One should
304-however bear in mind that this is a relative notion: The set of rational numbers Q, say, is a
305:maximally partially decidable subset of R. A maximal partial correct algorithm is given by
306:the algorithm that never halts. Once maximal partial decidability of a problem is established
307-one is hence naturally lead to the study of the "absolute size" of the halting set.

22:Abstract. The Skolem problem is a long-standing open problem in linear dynamical
23-systems: can a linear recurrence sequence (LRS) ever reach 0 from a given initial config-
24:uration? Similarly, the positivity problem asks whether the LRS stays positive from an
25:initial configuration. Deciding Skolem (or positivity) has been open for half a century:
26-the best known decidability results are for LRS with special properties (e.g., low order
27-recurrences). On the other hand, these problems are much easier for "uninitialised" variants,
28-where the initial configuration is not fixed but can vary arbitrarily: checking if there is an
29-initial configuration from which the LRS stays positive can be decided by polynomial time
30-algorithms (Tiwari in 2004, Braverman in 2006).
--
35-considered as a robust variant of the Skolem (resp. positivity) problem. We show that these
36-problems lie at the frontier of decidability: if the neighbourhood is given as part of the input,
37-then robust Skolem and robust positivity are Diophantine hard, i.e., solving either would
38-entail major breakthroughs in Diophantine approximations, as happens for (non-robust)
39-positivity. Interestingly, this is the first Diophantine hardness result on a variant of the
40:Skolem problem. On the other hand, if one asks whether such a neighbourhood exists, then
41-the problems turn out to be decidable in their full generality, with PSPACE complexity. Our
42-analysis is based on the set of initial configurations such that positivity holds, which leads
43-to new insights into these difficult problems, and interesting geometrical interpretations.
44-
45:    Key words and phrases: Skolem problem, verification, dynamical systems, robustness.

190:Related work. As mentioned earlier, the Skolem problem and its variants have received
191-a lot of attention. Given the hardness of these problems, -approximate solutions have
192-been considered, e.g., in [BHM14, AAGT15] with different definitions of approximations. In
193-comparison with our work, these are designed towards allowing approximate model checking.
194-More recently, the notion of imprecision in Skolem and related problems was considered
195-in [BFJ+20, DKM+21]. In [BFJ+20], the authors consider rounding functions at every step
196:of the trajectory. In [DKM+21], the so called Pseudo-Skolem problem is defined, where
197-imprecisions up to  are allowed at every step of the trajectory, which is shown to be
198-decidable in PTIME. These are quite different from our notion of robustness, which faithfully
199-considers the trajectories generated from a ball representing -perturbations around the
200-initial configuration. In a very recent extension [DKM+22] of [DKM+21], it is shown that
201:the existential robust Skolem question and a special case of the Pseudo-Skolem problem
202-can be solved using o-minimality of the theory of reals with exponentiation. Lastly, [Neu21]
203-considers the problem when specified in a model of computation that takes real numbers,
204-as opposed to rational numbers, as input. In this setting, perturbations are permitted in
205-both the initialisation and the recurrence itself. This approach sidesteps several of the
206-number-theoretic challenges, and decides problems on Linear Recurrence Sequences on all
--

210-robustness focussed with respect to the initial configuration, covering several possible cases

212-underlying number theory to prove our results; third, we show hardness results, in particular
213:Diophantine hardness for a variant of the Skolem problem. This paper is an extended version
214-of the work [ABGV22] that featured in the proceedings of STACS 2022. The additional

226-Structure of the paper. The structure of this paper is as follows: In Section 2 we define
227:preliminaries, in particular the Skolem and (ultimate) positivity problem as well as known
228-number-theoretic hardness results. In Section 3 we define the problem of our interest, namely
229-robustness with respect to the initial configuration of Skolem as well as (ultimate) positivity
230-and state all our main results. In Section 4 we provide a geometric interpretation of the
231-behaviour of linear recurrences, which allows us to better understand and characterise the
232-number-theoretic hardness results. In Section 5, we build upon the geometric insights to
233-prove the hardness results claimed for robustness. In Section 6, we again use and generalise
234-the geometric interpretation in Section 4 to prove our positive results stated in Section 3
235-both in terms of decidability and complexity upper bounds. Finally we end with a conclusion
236-in Section 7.

365:2.2. Skolem and (ultimate) positivity problems.

367:Definition 2.4. Let (un)nN be a rational LRR and c  Q. The Skolem problem is to
368-determine if there exists n  N such that un(c) = 0. The positivity (resp. strict positivity)
369-problem is to determine if for all n  N, un(c)  0 (resp. un(c) > 0). The ultimate positivity
370-(resp. ultimate strict positivity) problem is to determine if there exists N  N such that for
371-all n  N , un(c)  0 (resp. un(c) > 0).

377-     The famous Skolem-Mahler-Lech theorem states that when c is algebraic, the set
378-{i | ui(c) = 0} is the union of a finite set F and finitely many arithmetic progressions
379-[Sko34, Mah35, BM76]. These arithmetic progressions can be computed but the hard part
380-lies in deciding if the set F is empty: although we know that there is N such that for all
381:n > N , n / F , we do not have an effective bound on this N in general. The Skolem problem
382:has been shown to be decidable for LRS of order up to 4 [MST84, Ver85] and is still open for
383-LRS of higher order. Also, only an NP hardness bound is known if the order is unrestricted
384-[BP02, ABV17].

388-In [OW14c], it is proved that positivity for simple LRS is hard for coR, the class of
389-problems whose complements are solvable in the existential theory of the reals. A last result,
390-from [OW14b], shows the difficulty of positivity, linking it to Diophantine approximations:

437-
438:The Skolem and (Ultimate) Positivity problems, as defined in the previous section, consider
439-a single initial configuration c. In this article, we investigate the notion of robustness, that
440-is, whether the property is true in a neighbourhood of c, which is important for real systems,
441-where setting c with an arbitrary precision is not possible. We will consider two variants.
442-The first one fixes the neighbourhood as a ball B, while the second asks for the existence of a
443-ball B centred around a given initial configuration c, such that for every initial configuration
--

459-  exists Nc  N such that for all n > Nc, we have un(c)  0.

487-

489:      (a) the robust positivity problem is T -Diophantine hard,

500-
501-     Our theorem above implies that for uninitialised positivity, one really needs the initial
502-configuration to take a value possibly anywhere in the space rather than in a fixed neigh-
503-bourhood to obtain decidability via [Tiw04, Bra06]. We remark that Diophantine hardness
504-is known for the non-robust variant of positivity [OW14b], but to the best of our knowledge,
505:it was not known for any variant of the Skolem problem. In fact, in light of the latest results
506-in [BLN+22], Diophantine hardness for (exact) Skolem seems unlikely, unless either of Skolem
507-conjecture or p-adic Schanuel conjecture is falsified. We note that the p-adic techniques used
508-therein rely on the input being integral, or rational, or algebraic. Our Diophantine hardness
509:result, on the other hand, has connections to the positivity problem, and is intrinsically
510-related to the common underlying geometry. In a nutshell, the distinction is that the robust
511-variants of the problem implicitly reason about a continuum of initialisations, including those
512-with transcendental coordinates, for which standard results like the Skolem-Mahler-Lech
513-Theorem do not hold.

The audit found a clean, non-speculative hypothesis removal: the linear-Pisot classification proof never uses that the other conjugates lie inside the unit circle. It only uses that the dominant root strictly exceeds their moduli. That is the standard Perron condition. I’m checking the precise numeration convention and literature now; if it holds, the paper can replace its Pisot-only standard-object corollary by a Perron one with the same iff, while being explicit that this does not solve Skolem/Positivity.

   90: def matmul(left: Matrix, right: Matrix, modulus: int | None = None) -> Matrix:
   91:     rows = len(left)
   92:     inner = len(right)
   93:     columns = len(right[0])
   94:     entries = []

   96:         out_row = []

   98:             value = sum(left[row][k] * right[k][column] for k in range(inner))
   99:             out_row.append(value if modulus is None else value % modulus)

  111: def determinant(matrix: Matrix) -> int:
  112:     size = len(matrix)
  113:     if size == 1:
  114:         return matrix[0][0]
  115:     total = 0
  116:     for column, entry in enumerate(matrix[0]):
  117:         minor = tuple(
  118:             tuple(row[j] for j in range(size) if j != column)
  119:             for row in matrix[1:]
  120:         )
  121:         total += (-1) ** column * entry * determinant(minor)
  122:     return total
