  961: \begin{corollary}[Linear Perron \(U\)-systems]
  962:   \label{cor:linear-perron-prime-cf-immunity}
  963:   Let \(U=(U_n)_{n\ge0}\) be a linear Perron \(U\)-system in the
  964:   following precise sense: \(U_0=1\), the \(U_n\) are strictly increasing
  965:   integers with bounded quotients, \(\mathcal R_U\) is the LSD-first
  966:   reversal of the usual greedy representation language, and \(U\)
  967:   eventually satisfies an integral recurrence whose characteristic
  968:   polynomial is the minimal polynomial of a Perron number \(\beta\). Thus
  969:   \(\beta>1\) is a real algebraic integer and every other conjugate
  970:   \(\beta'\) satisfies \(\abs{\beta'}<\beta\); compare
  971:   \cite{LindMarcus1995,Rigo2014Vol2}. Then its prime
  972:   representation language is MCF-immune, hence CF-immune, REG-immune and
  973:   nonrecognizable. The same statements hold in the usual MSD-first
  974:   convention.
  975: 
  976:   If the dominant Perron number is a unit and the chosen recurrence has
  977:   trailing coefficient \(a_0=\pm1\), then the full coprime-quotient and
  978:   bounded-prime-support MCF-immunity conclusions of
  979:   \Cref{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity} hold.
  980: \end{corollary}
  981: 
  982: \begin{proof}
  983:   Greedy expansion gives a unique representation of every positive
  984:   integer, and its length-\(m\) words represent values between successive
  985:   place-value thresholds; thus \textup{(U1)--(U3)} hold. The defining
  986:   Pisot recurrence gives \textup{(U4)}. Apply
  987:   \Cref{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity}. The immunity proof
  988:   uses only \textup{(U1)--(U4)} and does not assume that the full greedy
  989:   language is regular. In the Pisot subclass, Frougny's finite
  990:   normalization theorem supplies a finite transducer, and the associated
  991:   canonical syntax and Bertrand/substitution descriptions are standard
  992:   \cite{Frougny1992,BruyereHansel1997,Fabre1995,FrougnySolomyak1992}.
  993:   Finally, multiple context-free, context-free, and
  994:   regular languages are closed under reversal, so changing between the LSD-first proof
  995:   convention and the usual MSD-first convention preserves every
  996:   conclusion.
  997: \end{proof}
  998: 
  999: \begin{example}[Pisot and non-Pisot Perron systems]
 1000:   \label{ex:pisot-unit-nonunit}
 1001:   The Fibonacci recurrence has characteristic polynomial
 1002:   \(X^2-X-1\), the Pell recurrence has \(X^2-2X-1\), and the
 1003:   Tribonacci recurrence has \(X^3-X^2-X-1\). Their trailing recurrence
 1004:   coefficient is \(a_0=1\), so the iterated conclusion applies. In
 1005:   ordinary base \(b\), \(U_n=b^n\) and \(a_0=b\); prime MCF-immunity
 1006:   follows, recovering the classical conclusion, but the unit iteration
 1007:   is not being asserted. A genuinely nonintegral, nonunit Pisot example
 1008:   is the dominant root \(1+\sqrt3\) of \(X^2-2X-2\): the recurrence
 1009:   \(U_{n+2}=2U_{n+1}+2U_n\) has \(a_0=2\), and the action is singular
 1010:   modulo \(2\).  Nevertheless,
 1011:   \Cref{cor:linear-perron-bounded-support-classification} shows that every
 1012:   infinite MCFL in this nonintegral system acquires unbounded prime support
 1013:   away from \(2\); singularity of the ambient action does not produce a
 1014:   valuation-only escape language.
 1015: 
 1016:   The polynomial \(X^2-5X+5\) gives a genuinely non-Pisot instance. Its
 1017:   dominant root \(\beta=(5+\sqrt5)/2\) is Perron, while its other conjugate
 1018:   \((5-\sqrt5)/2\) is greater than one. The integer sequence
 1019:   \[
 1020:     U_0=1,\qquad U_1=4,\qquad
 1021:     U_{n+2}=5U_{n+1}-5U_n
 1022:   \]
 1023:   begins \(1,4,15,55,200,\ldots\) and is strictly increasing. Indeed, the
 1024:   simultaneous inequalities
 1025:   \[
 1026:     U_{n+1}>U_n>0,\qquad 4U_{n+1}>5U_n
 1027:   \]
 1028:   hold at \(n=0\); if they hold at \(n\), then
 1029:   \[
 1030:     U_{n+2}=5(U_{n+1}-U_n)>U_{n+1},
 1031:     \qquad
 1032:     4U_{n+2}-5U_{n+1}=15U_{n+1}-20U_n>0.
 1033:   \]
 1034:   Its quotients are bounded (in fact \(1<U_{n+1}/U_n\le4\)), so its greedy
 1035:   language is a linear Perron \(U\)-system in the stated sense. The
 1036:   classification below implies that every infinite MCFL in this standard
 1037:   greedy language has unbounded prime support away from \(5\).
 1038: \end{example}
 1039: 
 1040: \begin{corollary}[Bounded-support classification for linear Perron systems]
 1041:   \label{cor:linear-perron-bounded-support-classification}
 1042:   Let \(U\) be a linear Perron \(U\)-system in the precise sense of
 1043:   \Cref{cor:linear-perron-prime-cf-immunity}, let \(\beta\) be its dominant
 1044:   Perron number, and let \(S_{\mathrm r}\) be the prime divisors of the
 1045:   constant coefficient of its minimal tail recurrence.  The following are
 1046:   equivalent:
 1047:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 1048:     \item there is an infinite MCFL \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) such that
 1049:     \[
 1050:       \sup_{w\in L}\omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(\val_U(w))<\infty;
 1051:     \]
 1052:     \item \(U\) admits a geometric synchronized scheme;
 1053:     \item \(\beta\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\).
 1054:   \end{enumerate}
 1055:   Consequently, if \(\beta\) is nonintegral, every infinite MCFL
 1056:   \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) has unbounded prime support outside
 1057:   \(S_{\mathrm r}\).  For effective input as in
 1058:   \Cref{cor:bounded-outside-support-semidecidable}, the three equivalent
 1059:   properties are decidable in this linear Perron class: the answer is positive
 1060:   exactly when the supplied minimal polynomial has degree one.
 1061: \end{corollary}
 1062: 
 1063: \begin{proof}
 1064:   The equivalence of \textup{(i)} and \textup{(ii)} is
 1065:   \Cref{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}.  Suppose that
 1066:   \textup{(ii)} holds, write
 1067:   \[
 1068:     \val_U(W(t))=cb^t,
 1069:     \qquad \abs{W(t)}=L+Dt,
 1070:   \]
 1071:   where \(D>0\) is the total pumped length.  In a greedy \(U\)-system, a
 1072:   canonical word of length \(m\) represents a value in the half-open interval
 1073:   \([U_{m-1},U_m)\).  Hence
 1074:   \[
 1075:     U_{L+Dt-1}\le cb^t<U_{L+Dt}.
 1076:   \]
 1077:   The standard solution of the recurrence defined by the minimal polynomial
 1078:   of the Perron number gives
 1079:   \[
 1080:     \lim_{n\to\infty}U_n^{1/n}=\beta.
 1081:   \]
 1082:   Indeed, the coefficient of the dominant root is nonzero because the
 1083:   displayed polynomial is the minimal tail recurrence, while every other
 1084:   conjugate has modulus strictly less than \(\beta\). Taking
 1085:   \(t\)-th roots in the preceding inequalities therefore yields
 1086:   \(b=\beta^D\).
 1087: 
 1088:   If \(\beta\) had degree greater than one, any other conjugate
 1089:   \(\beta'\) would satisfy \((\beta')^D=b\), and hence
 1090:   \(\abs{\beta'}=b^{1/D}=\beta\), contrary to the defining Perron
 1091:   inequality.  Thus \(\beta\) has degree one; being an algebraic integer
 1092:   greater than one, it belongs to \(\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\).  This proves
 1093:   \textup{(ii)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(iii)}.
 1094: 
 1095:   Conversely, suppose \(\beta=B\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\).  Its minimal
 1096:   polynomial is \(X-B\), so, after the minimal recurrence threshold
 1097:   \(J_{\mathrm r}\), one has \(U_{n+1}=BU_n\).  The greedy representation
 1098:   of \(U_n\), in the LSD-first convention, is \(0^n1\).  Taking
 1099:   \[
 1100:     a=0^{J_{\mathrm r}},\quad k=1,\quad
 1101:     u_1=w_1=s_1=\varepsilon,\quad v_1=0,\quad u_2=1
 1102:   \]
 1103:   gives canonical words \(W(t)=0^{J_{\mathrm r}+t}1\) and
 1104:   \[
 1105:     \val_U(W(t))=U_{J_{\mathrm r}}B^t.
 1106:   \]
 1107:   This is a geometric synchronized scheme, proving
 1108:   \textup{(iii)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(ii)}.  The universal assertion
 1109:   for nonintegral \(\beta\) is the negation of \textup{(i)}.  Finally, a
 1110:   Perron minimal polynomial has degree one exactly when its root is an
 1111:   integer, which gives the stated terminating decision procedure.
 1112: \end{proof}
 1113: 
 1114: \begin{remark}[Exact open interfaces]
 1115:   \label{rem:pisot-open-interfaces}
 1116:   The terminology for Pisot numeration systems is not uniform.
 1117:   \Cref{cor:linear-perron-prime-cf-immunity} covers the standard
 1118:   positional linear \(U\)-systems just specified, including integer
 1119:   bases, Zeckendorf/Fibonacci, Pell, higher-order Pisot recurrences, and
 1120:   non-Pisot Perron examples such as \(X^2-5X+5\).
 1121:   It does not assert the theorem for arbitrary real-base
 1122:   \(\beta\)-shift representations, non-positional abstract numeration
 1123:   systems, redundant noninjective digit systems, or systems lacking an
 1124:   eventual integral recurrence and strict length ordering. Extending
 1125:   the argument to any of those classes requires a stationary finite
 1126:   block action that is invertible modulo represented primes.
 1127: 
 1128:   For a fixed nonunit recurrence witness, the ambient action can be
 1129:   singular modulo primes dividing \(a_0\), so the unrestricted unit-system
 1130:   divisibility tree need not follow. The witness-relative surviving
 1131:   statement is \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}: every infinite
 1132:   MCFL must acquire unbounded prime support outside that finite set or
 1133:   unbounded valuation at one of its primes. The invariant restricted
 1134:   action and the failure of arbitrary recurrence witnesses to classify
 1135:   escape behavior are distinguished in
 1136:   \Cref{prop:recurrence-witness-separation}.
 1137:   Within linear Perron \(U\)-systems, the residual alternative is classified
 1138:   by \Cref{cor:linear-perron-bounded-support-classification}: it occurs exactly
 1139:   for an integral dominant root.  The ordinary-base example preceding
 1140:   \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain} shows that the valuation
 1141:   alternative cannot be removed.
 1142: \end{remark}

+  \((5-\sqrt5)/2\) is greater than one. The integer sequence
+  \[
+    U_0=1,\qquad U_1=4,\qquad
+    U_{n+2}=5U_{n+1}-5U_n
+  \]
+  begins \(1,4,15,55,200,\ldots\) and is strictly increasing. Indeed,
+  \[
+    U_{n+1}>3U_n>0
+  \]
+  holds at \(n=0\), and if it holds at \(n\), then
+  \[
+    U_{n+2}=5(U_{n+1}-U_n)
+      >\frac{10}{3}U_{n+1}>3U_{n+1}.
+  \]
+  Its quotients are bounded (in fact \(3<U_{n+1}/U_n\le4\)), so its greedy
+  language is the greedy language of a linear numeration basis with Perron
+  recurrence in the stated sense. The
+  classification below implies that every infinite MCFL in this standard
+  greedy language has unbounded prime support away from \(5\).
 \end{example}

 130: \subsection{Relation to prior work}\label{subsec:prior-work}
 131: 
 132: The fixed-base context-free prime obstruction is classical, due to
  14: prime-ideal norm bound to reduce a fixed-support recurrence to one
  15: characteristic root; Schur's theorem removes its polynomial factor. The
  16: ratio \(b\) uses only primes dividing the minimal tail constant. In a
  17: standard greedy linear numeration basis with Perron recurrence, length
  18: thresholds then show that such
  19: a ray exists exactly for an integral dominant root.
  20: 
  21: For an effectively presented regular canonical system, positive instances
  22: can be enumerated and certified. The unresolved general step is not
  23: candidate verification but witness compression: no computable bound is
  24: known for the fan-out and word lengths of a smallest geometric synchronized
  25: scheme. DFA path compression does not preserve the associated affine
  26: recurrence matrices. Conversely, no reduction proving undecidability is
  27: known that also preserves unique canonical representation, strict length
  28: ordering, the minimal tail recurrence, and the special digit-matrix form.
  29: Accordingly the general decision problem remains open, while the
  30: Perron-recurrence subclass of greedy linear numeration bases is decidable.
  31: This removes the Pisot hypothesis: strict
  32: dominance of the Perron root over its conjugates is exactly what the greedy
  33: length argument uses.

+    U_0=1,\qquad U_1=4,\qquad
+    U_{n+2}=5U_{n+1}-5U_n
+  \]
+  begins \(1,4,15,55,200,\ldots\) and is strictly increasing. Indeed,
+  \[
+    U_{n+1}>3U_n>0
+  \]
+  holds at \(n=0\), and if it holds at \(n\), then
+  \[
+    U_{n+2}=5(U_{n+1}-U_n)
+      >\frac{10}{3}U_{n+1}>3U_{n+1}.
+  \]
+  Its quotients are bounded (in fact \(3<U_{n+1}/U_n\le4\)), so its greedy
+  language is the greedy language of a linear numeration basis with Perron
+  recurrence in the stated sense. The
+  classification below implies that every infinite MCFL in this standard
+  greedy language has unbounded prime support away from \(5\).
 \end{example}

## Instruction Priority

Superpowers skills override default system prompt behavior, but **user instructions always take precedence**:

1. **User's explicit instructions** (CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, AGENTS.md, direct requests) â€” highest priority
2. **Superpowers skills** â€” override default system behavior where they conflict
3. **Default system prompt** â€” lowest priority

If CLAUDE.md, GEMINI.md, or AGENTS.md says "don't use TDD" and a skill says "always use TDD," follow the user's instructions. The user is in control.

## How to Access Skills

**In Claude Code:** Use the `Skill` tool. When you invoke a skill, its content is loaded and presented to youâ€”follow it directly. Never use the Read tool on skill files.

**In Copilot CLI:** Use the `skill` tool. Skills are auto-discovered from installed plugins. The `skill` tool works the same as Claude Code's `Skill` tool.

**In Gemini CLI:** Skills activate via the `activate_skill` tool. Gemini loads skill metadata at session start and activates the full content on demand.

**In other environments:** Check your platform's documentation for how skills are loaded.

## Platform Adaptation

Skills use Claude Code tool names. Non-CC platforms: see `references/copilot-tools.md` (Copilot CLI), `references/codex-tools.md` (Codex) for tool equivalents. Gemini CLI users get the tool mapping loaded automatically via GEMINI.md.

# Using Skills

## The Rule

**Invoke relevant or requested skills BEFORE any response or action.** Even a 1% chance a skill might apply means that you should invoke the skill to check. If an invoked skill turns out to be wrong for the situation, you don't need to use it.

## Skill Priority

When multiple skills could apply, use this order:

1. **Process skills first** (brainstorming, debugging) - these determine HOW to approach the task
2. **Implementation skills second** (frontend-design, mcp-builder) - these guide execution

"Let's build X" â†’ brainstorming first, then implementation skills.
"Fix this bug" â†’ debugging first, then domain-specific skills.

## Skill Types

**Rigid** (TDD, debugging): Follow exactly. Don't adapt away discipline.

**Flexible** (patterns): Adapt principles to context.

The skill itself tells you which.

Instructions say WHAT, not HOW. "Add X" or "Fix Y" doesn't mean skip workflows.

---
name: verification-before-completion
description: Use when about to claim work is complete, fixed, or passing, before committing or creating PRs - requires running verification commands and confirming output before making any success claims; evidence before assertions always
---

# Verification Before Completion

## Overview

Claiming work is complete without verification is dishonesty, not efficiency.

**Core principle:** Evidence before claims, always.

**Violating the letter of this rule is violating the spirit of this rule.**

## The Iron Law

```
NO COMPLETION CLAIMS WITHOUT FRESH VERIFICATION EVIDENCE
```

If you haven't run the verification command in this message, you cannot claim it passes.

## The Gate Function

```
BEFORE claiming any status or expressing satisfaction:

1. IDENTIFY: What command proves this claim?
2. RUN: Execute the FULL command (fresh, complete)
3. READ: Full output, check exit code, count failures
4. VERIFY: Does output confirm the claim?
   - If NO: State actual status with evidence
   - If YES: State claim WITH evidence
5. ONLY THEN: Make the claim

Skip any step = lying, not verifying
```

## Common Failures

| Claim | Requires | Not Sufficient |
|-------|----------|----------------|
| Tests pass | Test command output: 0 failures | Previous run, "should pass" |
| Linter clean | Linter output: 0 errors | Partial check, extrapolation |
| Build succeeds | Build command: exit 0 | Linter passing, logs look good |
| Bug fixed | Test original symptom: passes | Code changed, assumed fixed |
| Regression test works | Red-green cycle verified | Test passes once |
| Agent completed | VCS diff shows changes | Agent reports "success" |
| Requirements met | Line-by-line checklist | Tests passing |

## Red Flags - STOP

- Using "should", "probably", "seems to"
- Expressing satisfaction before verification ("Great!", "Perfect!", "Done!", etc.)
- About to commit/push/PR without verification
- Trusting agent success reports
- Relying on partial verification
- Thinking "just this once"
- Tired and wanting work over
- **ANY wording implying success without having run verification**

## Rationalization Prevention

| Excuse | Reality |
|--------|---------|
| "Should work now" | RUN the verification |
| "I'm confident" | Confidence â‰  evidence |
| "Just this once" | No exceptions |
| "Linter passed" | Linter â‰  compiler |
| "Agent said success" | Verify independently |
| "I'm tired" | Exhaustion â‰  excuse |
| "Partial check is enough" | Partial proves nothing |
| "Different words so rule doesn't apply" | Spirit over letter |

## Key Patterns

**Tests:**
```
âœ… [Run test command] [See: 34/34 pass] "All tests pass"
âŒ "Should pass now" / "Looks correct"
```

**Regression tests (TDD Red-Green):**
```
âœ… Write â†’ Run (pass) â†’ Revert fix â†’ Run (MUST FAIL) â†’ Restore â†’ Run (pass)
âŒ "I've written a regression test" (without red-green verification)
```

**Build:**
```
âœ… [Run build] [See: exit 0] "Build passes"
âŒ "Linter passed" (linter doesn't check compilation)
```

**Requirements:**
```
âœ… Re-read plan â†’ Create checklist â†’ Verify each â†’ Report gaps or completion
âŒ "Tests pass, phase complete"
```

**Agent delegation:**
```
âœ… Agent reports success â†’ Check VCS diff â†’ Verify changes â†’ Report actual state
âŒ Trust agent report
```

## Why This Matters

From 24 failure memories:
- your human partner said "I don't believe you" - trust broken
- Undefined functions shipped - would crash
- Missing requirements shipped - incomplete features
- Time wasted on false completion â†’ redirect â†’ rework
- Violates: "Honesty is a core value. If you lie, you'll be replaced."

## When To Apply

**ALWAYS before:**
- ANY variation of success/completion claims
- ANY expression of satisfaction
- ANY positive statement about work state
- Committing, PR creation, task completion
- Moving to next task
- Delegating to agents

**Rule applies to:**
- Exact phrases
- Paraphrases and synonyms
- Implications of success
- ANY communication suggesting completion/correctness

## The Bottom Line

**No shortcuts for verification.**

Run the command. Read the output. THEN claim the result.

This is non-negotiable.

 146: rigidity step; it does not state the synchronized-language characterization.
 147: Broughan's adic-topology classification \cite{Broughan2003} supplies
 148: classical context for the deleted-congruence topology. Frougny's
 149: normalization theorem and the Bertrand and substitution literature provide
 150: the regular canonical interfaces for Pisot numeration
 151: \cite{Frougny1992,BruyereHansel1997,Fabre1995,FrougnySolomyak1992}.
 152: 
 153: The nearest algorithmic boundary is the decision theory of linear
 154: recurrences. The Skolem problem remains open in general; see
 155: Ouaknine--Worrell \cite{OuaknineWorrell2012}. Tarasov--Vyalyi relate orbit
 156: hitting to a regular-language intersection problem
 157: \cite{TarasovVyalyi2011}. At the other extreme, unrestricted multiplicative
 158: matrix equations contain undecidable families
 159: \cite{BellEtAl2008MatrixEquations}. These works explain why a finite witness
 160: bound cannot be inferred from general matrix-semigroup theory, but none
 161: settles the constrained decision problem formulated here.
 162: 
 163: More precisely, the three named neighboring questions are Skolem
 164: (does a given linear recurrence ever vanish?), Positivity (are all its terms
 165: nonnegative?), and Ultimate Positivity (are all sufficiently late terms
 166: nonnegative?); all remain open in unrestricted order
 167: \cite{AkshayBazilleGenestVahanwala2024}. Our value recurrence does not resolve
 168: any of them. The orbit extracted in
 169: \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit} is positive and strictly
 170: increasing by construction, while
 171: \Cref{cor:bounded-outside-support-semidecidable} decides whether the entire
 172: recurrence \(N(t+1)-bN(t)\) is identically zero. This is different from
 173: deciding whether one term of an arbitrary recurrence is zero or has a
 174: prescribed sign, and no reduction in either direction is claimed.
 175: 
 176: The compiled supplement retains the separate finite-state results: the
 177: density dichotomy and effective fixed-DFA prime-slice bounds in ordinary
 178: bases, the corresponding Zeckendorf growth and regular-language results,
 179: and the classical analytic comparisons. They are not used in the proof of
 180: the recurrent MCFL theorem chain.

  32: For the intrinsic minimal tail recurrence we prove an inverse theorem:
  33: bounded prime support away from its constant term occurs on an infinite
  34: MCFL if and only if the canonical language contains a synchronized ray
  35: whose values are \(cb^t\) with integers \(c\ge1\), \(b\ge2\). The
  36: arithmetic rigidity step is deduced explicitly from Evertse's theorem on
  37: prime ideals in quotients of nondegenerate recurrences. With a DFA for the
  38: canonical language, positive instances are semidecidable; the missing
  39: uniform witness bound for a general decision procedure is isolated. For
  40: standard greedy linear numeration bases with Perron recurrence the problem
  41: is decidable and is positive exactly when the dominant Perron number is an
  42: integer. Thus the Pisot hypothesis can be replaced by the weaker
  43: strict-dominance hypothesis.

 941:   \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) has unbounded
 942:   \(\omega(\val_U(w))\). More precisely, \(L\) contains a
 943:   coprime-quotient chain \(N_{i+1}=N_iQ_i\) with
 944:   \(Q_i>1\) and \(Q_i\equiv1\pmod {N_i}\). Thus the bounded-\(\omega\),
 945:   bounded-\(\Omega\), and finite-prime-support languages of a unit
 946:   system are MCF-immune whenever they are infinite. Without the unit
 947:   hypothesis, every bounded-\(\Omega\) language is still MCF-immune.
 948: \end{theorem}
 949: 
 950: \begin{proof}
 951:   The MCF-immunity assertions follow from
 952:   \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}, including its
 953:   bounded-\(\Omega\) conclusion. In a unit system \(S\) is empty, so
 954:   that theorem gives unbounded \(\omega\). Taking
 955:   \(M_i=r_i=1\) in
 956:   \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain} gives the stated chain.
 957:   Regular languages are context-free and context-free languages are
 958:   MCFLs. Finally, \textup{(U2)} and Euclid's theorem make
 959:   \(\mathcal P_U\) infinite.
 960: \end{proof}

 962: \begin{corollary}[Linear numeration bases with Perron recurrence]
 963:   \label{cor:linear-perron-prime-cf-immunity}
 964:   Let \(U=(U_n)_{n\ge0}\) be a standard greedy linear numeration basis in
 965:   the following precise sense: \(U_0=1\), the \(U_n\) are strictly
 966:   increasing integers with bounded quotients, \(\mathcal R_U\) is the LSD-first
 967:   reversal of the usual greedy representation language, and \(U\)
 968:   has minimal tail recurrence polynomial equal to the minimal polynomial
 969:   of a Perron number \(\beta\). Thus
 970:   \(\beta>1\) is a real algebraic integer and every other conjugate
 971:   \(\beta'\) satisfies \(\abs{\beta'}<\beta\); compare
 972:   \cite{LindMarcus1995,Rigo2014Vol2}. Then its prime
 973:   representation language is MCF-immune, hence CF-immune, REG-immune and
 974:   nonrecognizable. The same statements hold in the usual MSD-first
 975:   convention.
 976: 
 977:   If the dominant Perron number is a unit and the chosen recurrence has
 978:   trailing coefficient \(a_0=\pm1\), then the full coprime-quotient and
 979:   bounded-prime-support MCF-immunity conclusions of
 980:   \Cref{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity} hold.
 981: \end{corollary}
 982: 
 983: \begin{proof}
 984:   Greedy expansion gives a unique representation of every positive
 985:   integer, and its length-\(m\) words represent values between successive
 986:   place-value thresholds; thus \textup{(U1)--(U3)} hold. The defining
 987:   Perron recurrence gives \textup{(U4)}. Apply
 988:   \Cref{thm:recurrent-numeration-prime-cf-immunity}. The immunity proof
 989:   uses only \textup{(U1)--(U4)} and does not assume that the full greedy
 990:   language is regular. In the Pisot subclass, Frougny's finite
 991:   normalization theorem supplies a finite transducer, and the associated
 992:   canonical syntax and Bertrand/substitution descriptions are standard
 993:   \cite{Frougny1992,BruyereHansel1997,Fabre1995,FrougnySolomyak1992}.
 994:   Finally, multiple context-free, context-free, and
 995:   regular languages are closed under reversal, so changing between the LSD-first proof
 996:   convention and the usual MSD-first convention preserves every
 997:   conclusion.
 998: \end{proof}

1000: \begin{example}[Pisot and non-Pisot Perron systems]
1001:   \label{ex:pisot-unit-nonunit}
1002:   The Fibonacci recurrence has characteristic polynomial
1003:   \(X^2-X-1\), the Pell recurrence has \(X^2-2X-1\), and the
1004:   Tribonacci recurrence has \(X^3-X^2-X-1\). Their trailing recurrence
1005:   coefficient is \(a_0=1\), so the iterated conclusion applies. In
1006:   ordinary base \(b\), \(U_n=b^n\) and \(a_0=b\); prime MCF-immunity
1007:   follows, recovering the classical conclusion, but the unit iteration
1008:   is not being asserted. A genuinely nonintegral, nonunit Pisot example
1009:   is the dominant root \(1+\sqrt3\) of \(X^2-2X-2\): the recurrence
1010:   \(U_{n+2}=2U_{n+1}+2U_n\) has \(a_0=2\), and the action is singular
1011:   modulo \(2\).  Nevertheless,
1012:   \Cref{cor:linear-perron-bounded-support-classification} shows that every
1013:   infinite MCFL in this nonintegral system acquires unbounded prime support
1014:   away from \(2\); singularity of the ambient action does not produce a
1015:   valuation-only escape language.
1016: 
1017:   The polynomial \(X^2-5X+5\) gives a genuinely non-Pisot instance. Its
1018:   dominant root \(\beta=(5+\sqrt5)/2\) is Perron, while its other conjugate
1019:   \((5-\sqrt5)/2\) is greater than one. The integer sequence
1020:   \[
1021:     U_0=1,\qquad U_1=4,\qquad
1022:     U_{n+2}=5U_{n+1}-5U_n
1023:   \]
1024:   begins \(1,4,15,55,200,\ldots\) and is strictly increasing. Indeed,
1025:   \[
1026:     U_{n+1}>3U_n>0
1027:   \]
1028:   holds at \(n=0\), and if it holds at \(n\), then
1029:   \[
1030:     U_{n+2}=5(U_{n+1}-U_n)
1031:       >\frac{10}{3}U_{n+1}>3U_{n+1}.
1032:   \]
1033:   Its quotients are bounded (in fact \(3<U_{n+1}/U_n\le4\)), so its greedy
1034:   language is the greedy language of a linear numeration basis with Perron
1035:   recurrence in the stated sense. The
1036:   classification below implies that every infinite MCFL in this standard
1037:   greedy language has unbounded prime support away from \(5\).
1038: \end{example}
1039: 
1040: \begin{corollary}[Bounded support for Perron-recurrence numeration]
1041:   \label{cor:linear-perron-bounded-support-classification}
1042:   Let \(U\) be a greedy linear numeration basis in the precise sense of
1043:   \Cref{cor:linear-perron-prime-cf-immunity}, let \(\beta\) be its dominant
1044:   Perron number, and let \(S_{\mathrm r}\) be the prime divisors of the
1045:   constant coefficient of its minimal tail recurrence.  The following are
1046:   equivalent:
1047:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
1048:     \item there is an infinite MCFL \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) such that
1049:     \[
1050:       \sup_{w\in L}\omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(\val_U(w))<\infty;
1051:     \]
1052:     \item \(U\) admits a geometric synchronized scheme;
1053:     \item \(\beta\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\).
1054:   \end{enumerate}
1055:   Consequently, if \(\beta\) is nonintegral, every infinite MCFL
1056:   \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) has unbounded prime support outside
1057:   \(S_{\mathrm r}\).  For effective input as in
1058:   \Cref{cor:bounded-outside-support-semidecidable}, the three equivalent
1059:   properties are decidable in this Perron-recurrence class: the answer is positive
1060:   exactly when the supplied minimal polynomial has degree one.
1061: \end{corollary}
1062: 
1063: \begin{proof}
1064:   The equivalence of \textup{(i)} and \textup{(ii)} is
1065:   \Cref{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}.  Suppose that
1066:   \textup{(ii)} holds, write
1067:   \[
1068:     \val_U(W(t))=cb^t,
1069:     \qquad \abs{W(t)}=L+Dt,
1070:   \]
1071:   where \(D>0\) is the total pumped length.  In a greedy \(U\)-system, a
1072:   canonical word of length \(m\) represents a value in the half-open interval
1073:   \([U_{m-1},U_m)\).  Hence
1074:   \[
1075:     U_{L+Dt-1}\le cb^t<U_{L+Dt}.
1076:   \]
1077:   The standard solution of the recurrence defined by the minimal polynomial
1078:   of the Perron number gives
1079:   \[
1080:     \lim_{n\to\infty}U_n^{1/n}=\beta.
1081:   \]
1082:   Indeed, the coefficient of the dominant root is nonzero because the
1083:   displayed polynomial is the minimal tail recurrence, while every other
1084:   conjugate has modulus strictly less than \(\beta\). Taking
1085:   \(t\)-th roots in the preceding inequalities therefore yields
1086:   \(b=\beta^D\).
1087: 
1088:   If \(\beta\) had degree greater than one, any other conjugate
1089:   \(\beta'\) would satisfy \((\beta')^D=b\), and hence
1090:   \(\abs{\beta'}=b^{1/D}=\beta\), contrary to the defining Perron
1091:   inequality.  Thus \(\beta\) has degree one; being an algebraic integer
1092:   greater than one, it belongs to \(\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\).  This proves
1093:   \textup{(ii)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(iii)}.
1094: 
1095:   Conversely, suppose \(\beta=B\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\).  Its minimal
1096:   polynomial is \(X-B\), so, after the minimal recurrence threshold
1097:   \(J_{\mathrm r}\), one has \(U_{n+1}=BU_n\).  The greedy representation
1098:   of \(U_n\), in the LSD-first convention, is \(0^n1\).  Taking
1099:   \[
1100:     a=0^{J_{\mathrm r}},\quad k=1,\quad
1101:     u_1=w_1=s_1=\varepsilon,\quad v_1=0,\quad u_2=1
1102:   \]
1103:   gives canonical words \(W(t)=0^{J_{\mathrm r}+t}1\) and
1104:   \[
1105:     \val_U(W(t))=U_{J_{\mathrm r}}B^t.
1106:   \]
1107:   This is a geometric synchronized scheme, proving
1108:   \textup{(iii)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(ii)}.  The universal assertion
1109:   for nonintegral \(\beta\) is the negation of \textup{(i)}.  Finally, a
1110:   Perron minimal polynomial has degree one exactly when its root is an
1111:   integer, which gives the stated terminating decision procedure.
1112: \end{proof}
1113: 
1114: \begin{remark}[Exact open interfaces]
1115:   \label{rem:pisot-open-interfaces}
1116:   The terminology for linear numeration systems with Perron or Pisot
1117:   recurrence is not uniform.
1118:   \Cref{cor:linear-perron-prime-cf-immunity} covers the standard
1119:   positional linear \(U\)-systems just specified, including integer
1120:   bases, Zeckendorf/Fibonacci, Pell, higher-order Pisot recurrences, and
1121:   non-Pisot Perron examples such as \(X^2-5X+5\).
1122:   It does not assert the theorem for arbitrary real-base
1123:   \(\beta\)-shift representations, non-positional abstract numeration
1124:   systems, redundant noninjective digit systems, or systems lacking an
1125:   eventual integral recurrence and strict length ordering. Extending
1126:   the argument to any of those classes requires a stationary finite
1127:   block action that is invertible modulo represented primes.
1128: 
1129:   For a fixed nonunit recurrence witness, the ambient action can be
1130:   singular modulo primes dividing \(a_0\), so the unrestricted unit-system
1131:   divisibility tree need not follow. The witness-relative surviving
1132:   statement is \Cref{thm:nonunit-mcfl-escape-dichotomy}: every infinite
1133:   MCFL must acquire unbounded prime support outside that finite set or
1134:   unbounded valuation at one of its primes. The invariant restricted
1135:   action and the failure of arbitrary recurrence witnesses to classify
1136:   escape behavior are distinguished in
1137:   \Cref{prop:recurrence-witness-separation}.
1138:   Within greedy linear numeration bases with Perron recurrence, the residual
1139:   alternative is classified
1140:   by \Cref{cor:linear-perron-bounded-support-classification}: it occurs exactly
1141:   for an integral dominant root.  The ordinary-base example preceding
1142:   \Cref{thm:unit-mcfl-deep-congruence-chain} shows that the valuation
1143:   alternative cannot be removed.
1144: \end{remark}

  26: multiplicity; put \(\omega(1)=\Omega(1)=0\). The required Zeckendorf
  27: block action is recorded in \suppref{Lemma~2.5}.
  28: 
  29: \begin{lemma}[Paired Zeckendorf pumping congruence]
  30:   \label{lem:zeckendorf-paired-pumping-congruence}
  31:   Let \(u,v,x,y,z\in\{0,1\}^\ast\), and put
  32:   \[
  33:     N(k):=\val(uv^kxy^kz)\qquad(k\ge0).
  34:   \]
  35:   Suppose that \(\abs v+\abs y>0\). If \(q\ge2\), and \(h\) is a
  36:   common multiple of the orders modulo \(q\) of the nonempty-block
  37:   matrices among \(M_v,M_y\) (with \(M_\varepsilon=I\)), then
  38:   \[
  39:     N(k+h)\equiv N(k)\pmod q
  40:     \qquad(k\ge0).
  41:   \]
  42: \end{lemma}
  43: 
  44: \begin{proof}
  45:   With \(v_0=(0,1,1)^t\), concatenation and
  46:   \suppref{Lemma~2.5} gives
  47:   \[
  48:     N(k)=e_1^tM_zM_y^kM_xM_v^kM_uv_0.
  49:   \]
  50:   Every nonempty block matrix is invertible modulo \(q\). By the
  51:   definition of \(h\), both \(M_v^h\equiv I\pmod q\) and
  52:   \(M_y^h\equiv I\pmod q\), where the same identities are automatic for
  53:   an empty block. Substitution in the displayed product proves the
  54:   congruence.
  55: \end{proof}
  56: 
  57: \begin{theorem}[Context-free coprime-quotient Zeckendorf pumping]
  58:   \label{thm:context-free-coprime-quotient-zeckendorf-pumping}
  59:   Let \(L\subseteq\mathcal Z\) be context-free. There is an integer
  60:   \(P_L\ge1\) such that every \(w\in L\) with
  61:   \(\abs w\ge P_L\) and \(\val(w)\ge2\) begins a sequence
  62:   \(w_0=w,w_1,w_2,\ldots\) in \(L\) whose lengths are strictly
  63:   increasing and whose values \(N_i=\val(w_i)\) satisfy
  64:   \[
  65:     N_{i+1}=N_iQ_i,\qquad Q_i>1,\qquad
  66:     Q_i\equiv1\pmod {N_i},\qquad \gcd(Q_i,N_i)=1.
  67:   \]
  68: \end{theorem}
  69: 
  70: \begin{proof}
  71:   Apply Ogden's lemma with every position distinguished. It supplies a
  72:   constant \(P_L\) such that each \(w\in L\) of length at least \(P_L\)
  73:   has a factorisation
  74:   \[
  75:     w=uvxyz,\qquad \abs v+\abs y>0,\qquad
  76:     uv^kxy^kz\in L\quad(k\ge0).
  77:   \]
  78:   The additional marked-position bound in Ogden's lemma is not needed
  79:   here. Starting with \(w_i\in L\), choose such a factorisation and
  80:   let \(h_i\) be a common multiple of the orders of \(M_v\) and \(M_y\)
  81:   in
  82:   \(\operatorname{GL}_3(\ZZ/N_i^2\ZZ)\), omitting an empty block. These
  83:   orders exist by
  84:   \suppref{Lemma~2.5}. Define
  85:   \[
  86:     w_{i+1}:=uv^{\,1+h_i}xy^{\,1+h_i}z.
  87:   \]
  88:   By \Cref{lem:zeckendorf-paired-pumping-congruence},
  89:   \(N_{i+1}\equiv N_i\pmod {N_i^2}\). Hence
  90:   \(N_{i+1}=N_i(1+t_iN_i)\) for an integer \(t_i\).
  91: 
  92:   Since \(h_i\ge1\) and \(\abs v+\abs y>0\), the new word is longer.
  93:   Both words belong to \(L\subseteq\mathcal Z\), and canonical
  94:   Zeckendorf intervals are strictly ordered by length; consequently
  95:   \(N_{i+1}>N_i\), so \(t_i\ge1\). Taking
  96:   \(Q_i=1+t_iN_i\) gives all four assertions. The new word still has
  97:   length at least \(P_L\) and value at least \(2\), so the construction
  98:   iterates.
  99: \end{proof}
 100: 
 101: \begin{corollary}[Zeckendorf CF-immunity package]
 102:   \label{cor:zeckendorf-context-free-immunity-package}
 103:   Every infinite context-free \(L\subseteq\mathcal Z\) satisfies
 104:   \[
 105:     \sup_{w\in L}\omega(\val(w))=\infty.
 106:   \]
 107:   Consequently, for each \(K\ge1\), the bounded-distinct-prime language
 108:   \(\mathcal B_K\), the bounded-almost-prime language \(\mathcal A_K\),
 109:   and every infinite finite-prime-support language \(\mathcal Z_S\)
 110:   are CF-immune. In particular, the Zeckendorf prime language
 111:   \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal Z}\) is CF-immune.
 112: \end{corollary}
 113: 
 114: \begin{proof}
 115:   Choose a sufficiently long word in \(L\) and apply
 116:   \Cref{thm:context-free-coprime-quotient-zeckendorf-pumping}. Since
 117:   \(N_j\mid N_i\) for \(j\le i\), while every \(Q_i>1\) is coprime to
 118:   \(N_i\), a prime divisor of \(Q_i\) divides no earlier value. Thus
 119:   \(\omega(N_i)\ge\omega(N_0)+i\). The immunity conclusions follow
 120:   exactly as in the regular cases: \(\omega\le K\) on \(\mathcal B_K\),
 121:   \(\mathcal A_K\subseteq\mathcal B_K\), and
 122:   \(\omega\le\abs S\) on \(\mathcal Z_S\). Finally prime values have
 123:   \(\omega=1\), while Euclid's theorem makes
 124:   \(\mathcal P_{\mathcal Z}\) infinite.
 125: \end{proof}
 126: 
 127: We next isolate the precise base-independent interface. This is
 128: deliberately narrower than every object called a Pisot or abstract
 129: numeration system in the literature.
 130: 
 131: \begin{definition}[Canonical eventually recurrent numeration]
 132:   \label{def:canonical-eventually-recurrent-numeration}
 133:   A canonical eventually recurrent numeration system consists of:
 134:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(U\arabic*)}]
 135:     \item a strictly increasing sequence of positive integers
 136:     \(U=(U_n)_{n\ge0}\) and a finite digit alphabet
 137:     \(A\subseteq\NN\) containing \(0\);
 138:     \item an LSD-first language \(\mathcal R_U\subseteq A^\ast\), with
 139:     \[
 140:       \val_U(x_0\cdots x_{m-1})
 141:         :=\sum_{j=0}^{m-1}x_jU_j,
 142:     \]
 143:     for which \(\val_U:\mathcal R_U\to\NN_{\ge1}\) is a bijection;
 144:     \item strict length ordering: if \(r,s\in\mathcal R_U\) and
 145:     \(\abs r<\abs s\), then \(\val_U(r)<\val_U(s)\);
 146:     \item integers \(J\ge0,d\ge1,a_0,\ldots,a_{d-1}\), with
 147:     \(a_0\ne0\), such that
 148:     \[
 149:       U_{n+d}=a_0U_n+a_1U_{n+1}+\cdots+a_{d-1}U_{n+d-1}
 150:       \qquad(n\ge J).
 151:     \]

 succeeded in 177ms:
 631:   \(n=j+h_0t\) and collection within the equivalence classes gives
 632:   \[
 633:     Y(j+h_0t)=\sum_C g_{C,j}(t)\beta_C^t,
 634:     \qquad \beta_C=\alpha_i^{h_0}\quad(i\in C).
 635:   \]
 636:   Delete the identically zero summands. Distinct remaining \(\beta_C\)
 637:   have quotient that is not a root of unity. Thus every residue
 638:   subsequence is a nonzero nondegenerate recurrence; it is nonzero
 639:   because all of its terms are positive.
 640: 
 641:   Every term of every residue subsequence is a nonzero rational integer
 642:   supported on the prescribed finite set. If a residue subsequence had
 643:   at least two characteristic roots, the consequence in
 644:   \Cref{lem:evertse-quotient-support-input} would contradict the fixed
 645:   support of all its term quotients. Hence every residue subsequence has
 646:   exactly one characteristic root and therefore has the form
 647:   \[
 648:     Z(n)=f(n)\lambda^n
 649:   \]
 650:   with one characteristic root.
 651: 
 652:   Choose one residue subsequence and shift its index if necessary so
 653:   that the displayed expansion holds from \(n=0\). The Hankel matrix of
 654:   \(Z\) has rational entries and finite rank, so a minimal linear
 655:   dependence among its shift columns has coefficients in
 656:   \(\mathbb Q\). Thus the minimal annihilating polynomial of \(Z\) lies
 657:   in \(\mathbb Q[X]\). Over \(\overline{\mathbb Q}\) it is a power of
 658:   \(X-\lambda\). Galois invariance therefore gives
 659:   \(\lambda\in\mathbb Q\). Now \(f(n)=Z(n)/\lambda^n\in\mathbb Q\)
 660:   for every \(n\), and interpolation from \(\deg(f)+1\) integer
 661:   arguments gives \(f\in\mathbb Q[X]\). If \(f\) were nonconstant, clear its
 662:   denominators to obtain a nonconstant \(g\in\mathbb Z[X]\). The
 663:   identity \(Z(n)=f(n)\lambda^n\) would confine every prime divisor of
 664:   every nonzero \(g(n)\) to a fixed finite set. Indeed, if
 665:   \(\lambda=a/b\) is in lowest terms and \(g=Df\), then
 666:   \[
 667:     g(n)a^n=Db^nZ(n).
 668:   \]
 669:   Thus that fixed set is the union of the prescribed prime set and the
 670:   prime divisors of \(Dab\). This contradicts Schur's theorem that a
 671:   nonconstant integer polynomial has values divisible by infinitely
 672:   many primes; see, for example, \cite{HardyWright2008}. Hence \(f\) is
 673:   constant.
 674: 
 675:   We have therefore \(Z(n)=c\lambda^n\), where
 676:   \(c=Z(0)\) is a positive integer. If \(\lambda=a/b\) in lowest terms,
 677:   integrality for every \(n\) forces \(b^n\mid c\) for every \(n\), so
 678:   \(b=1\). Positivity and strict increase then force
 679:   \(\lambda\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\). Translating the chosen residue and
 680:   index shift back to \(Y\) supplies the asserted \(r\) and \(h\).
 681: \end{proof}
 682: 
 683: \begin{theorem}[Geometric-ray characterization]
 684:   \label{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}
 685:   For a canonical eventually recurrent numeration system satisfying
 686:   \textup{(U1)--(U4)}, the following are equivalent.
 687:   \begin{enumerate}[label=\textup{(\roman*)}]
 688:     \item There are a finite \(k\) and an infinite \(k\)-MCFL
 689:     \(L\subseteq\mathcal R_U\) such that
 690:     \[
 691:       \sup_{w\in L}\omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(\val_U(w))<\infty.
 692:     \]
 693:     \item The system admits a geometric synchronized scheme in the
 694:     sense of \Cref{def:geometric-synchronized-scheme}.
 695:     \item The language \(\mathcal R_U\) contains an infinite linear MCFL
 696:     \(L_0=\{W(t):t\ge0\}\) of finite fan-out for which there are
 697:     \(c\ge1,b\ge2\) satisfying
 698:     \[
 699:       \val_U(W(t))=cb^t\qquad(t\ge0).
 700:     \]
 701:   \end{enumerate}
 702: \end{theorem}
 703: 
 704: \begin{proof}
 705:   Suppose first that \textup{(i)} holds. Use the minimal tail recurrence
 706:   as the witness in
 707:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}, and write its resulting
 708:   ray and strictly increasing value sequence as \(W(t)\) and \(N(t)\).
 709:   Let
 710:   \[
 711:     K_0=\max_{t\ge0}\omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(N(t)),
 712:   \]
 713:   and choose \(t_0\) attaining the maximum. Let \(T\) be the set of
 714:   primes outside \(S_{\mathrm r}\) that divide \(N(t_0)\), and put
 715:   \(q=\prod_{\ell\in T}\ell\). If \(T\ne\varnothing\), take the return
 716:   time \(H=H(q)\) from
 717:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit}; if \(T=\varnothing\),
 718:   put \(H=1\). Every prime in \(T\) divides every \(N(t_0+nH)\). A prime
 719:   divisor outside \(S_{\mathrm r}\cup T\) would therefore give at least
 720:   \(K_0+1\) distinct prime divisors outside \(S_{\mathrm r}\), contrary
 721:   to the definition of \(K_0\). Thus all terms of
 722:   \[
 723:     Y(n)=N(t_0+nH)
 724:   \]
 725:   are supported on the fixed finite set \(S_{\mathrm r}\cup T\).
 726: 
 727:   The entries of every matrix power \(M^n\) satisfy a linear recurrence
 728:   by Cayley--Hamilton. The expression for \(N(t)\) is a finite sum of
 729:   finite products of such entries, and linear recurrence sequences are
 730:   closed under sums and termwise products. Hence \(Y\) is a strictly
 731:   increasing positive integer recurrence. By
 732:   \Cref{lem:s-unit-increasing-recurrence-rigidity}, there are
 733:   \(r\ge0,h\ge1,c\ge1,b\ge2\) such that
 734:   \(N(t_\ast+h_\ast n)=cb^n\), where
 735:   \(t_\ast=t_0+Hr\) and \(h_\ast=Hh\).
 736: 
 737:   In the synchronized factorization, replace
 738:   \[
 739:     u_j\ \text{by}\ u_jv_j^{t_\ast},\qquad
 740:     v_j\ \text{by}\ v_j^{h_\ast},\qquad
 741:     w_j\ \text{by}\ w_js_j^{t_\ast},\qquad
 742:     s_j\ \text{by}\ s_j^{h_\ast}.
 743:   \]
 744:   This absorbs the fixed powers and parametrizes exactly the subray
 745:   \(W(t_\ast+h_\ast n)\). Its total pumped length remains positive, so
 746:   it is a geometric synchronized scheme. This proves
 747:   \textup{(i)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(ii)}.
 748: 
 749:   The implication \textup{(ii)}\(\Rightarrow\)\textup{(iii)} is
 750:   \Cref{lem:synchronized-ray-linear-mcfg}. Finally, under
 751:   \textup{(iii)}, the language \(L_0\) is an infinite MCFL and
 752:   \[
 753:     \omega_{S_{\mathrm r}^c}(cb^t)\le\omega(cb)
 754:     \qquad(t\ge0),
 755:   \]
 756:   proving \textup{(i)}.
 757: \end{proof}
 758: 
 759: \begin{lemma}[Prime support of the geometric ratio]
 760:   \label{lem:geometric-ratio-tail-support}
 761:   In every geometric synchronized scheme
 762:   \(\val_U(W(t))=cb^t\), each prime divisor of \(b\) divides the
 763:   constant coefficient \(c_0\) of the minimal tail recurrence.  Equivalently,
 764:   \[
 765:     \operatorname{rad}(b)\mid\operatorname{rad}(\abs{c_0}).
 766:   \]
 767: \end{lemma}
 768: 
 769: \begin{proof}
 770:   Suppose that a prime \(p\mid b\) does not divide \(c_0\), put
 771:   \(e=v_p(c)\), and take the allowed modulus \(q=p^{e+1}\).  Every
 772:   nonempty block matrix among the \(M_{v_j}\) and \(M_{s_j}\) is invertible
 773:   modulo \(q\) by \Cref{lem:affine-recurrence-block-action}.  A common
 774:   multiple \(H\ge1\) of their orders gives, by the matrix product defining
 775:   the scheme exactly as in the proof of
 776:   \Cref{thm:mcfl-synchronized-congruence-orbit},
 777:   \[
 778:     \val_U(W(t+H))\equiv\val_U(W(t))\pmod q
 779:     \qquad(t\ge0).
 780:   \]
 781:   At \(t=0\) this says
 782:   \[
 783:     cb^H\equiv c\pmod {p^{e+1}}.
 784:   \]
 785:   But \(p\mid b\) implies \(p\nmid b^H-1\), so
 786:   \(v_p(c(b^H-1))=e\), contradicting the displayed congruence.
 787: \end{proof}
 788: 
 789: \begin{corollary}[Positive semidecidability]
 790:   \label{cor:bounded-outside-support-semidecidable}
 791:   Suppose the numeration system is given effectively by its finite
 792:   digit alphabet, recurrence and initial data, and a DFA recognizing
 793:   \(\mathcal R_U\), with the minimal tail recurrence and a valid
 794:   threshold \(J_{\mathrm r}\) effectively computable from these data.
 795:   Then the property in
 796:   \Cref{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}\textup{(i)} is
 797:   recursively enumerable, equivalently it has a \(\Sigma^0_1\) upper
 798:   bound.
 799: \end{corollary}
 800: 
 801: \begin{proof}
 802:   Enumerate \(k\ge1\), \(a\in A^{J_{\mathrm r}}\), and all finite tuples
 803:   of words occurring in
 804:   \Cref{def:geometric-synchronized-scheme}, rejecting tuples of zero
 805:   total pumped length. For a fixed tuple, whether the DFA accepts
 806:   \(W(t)\) for every \(t\ge0\) is decidable: the tuple of powers of the
 807:   finitely many pumped-block transformations is eventually periodic in
 808:   the finite transition monoid, and its preperiod and period are found
 809:   by exhaustive iteration.
 810: 
 811:   The affine matrices construct an exact linear recurrence for
 812:   \[
 813:     N(t)=\val_U(W(t)).
 814:   \]
 815:   Kronecker products implement the termwise
 816:   products arising from the several synchronized block powers. For a
 817:   tuple accepted at every parameter, compute \(c=N(0)\). The only
 818:   possible integer ratio is \(b=N(1)/N(0)\). Check that
 819:   \(b\in\mathbb Z_{\ge2}\), and then decide whether the recurrence
 820:   \(N(t+1)-bN(t)\) is identically zero by checking an initial segment of
 821:   length equal to an explicitly constructed recurrence order. Thus each
 822:   candidate scheme is decidable, and the enumeration halts exactly on
 823:   positive instances by
 824:   \Cref{thm:bounded-outside-support-geometric-ray}. No claim of a
 825:   decision procedure for negative instances is made.
 826: \end{proof}
 827: 
 828: \begin{remark}[Exact algorithmic boundary]
 829:   \label{rem:general-decision-interface}
 830:   The preceding corollary does not yield a decision procedure. To turn
 831:   its enumeration into one, it would suffice to compute from the input
 832:   DFA and minimal tail recurrence a bound \(B\) such that every positive
 833:   instance has a geometric synchronized scheme with fan-out and total
 834:   constant and pumped-block length at most \(B\). No such compression
 835:   follows from DFA pumping: replacing a long loop by a shorter word with
 836:   the same DFA endpoints need not preserve its affine recurrence matrix,
 837:   and can therefore destroy the identity
 838:   \(\val_U(W(t+1))=b\val_U(W(t))\).
 839: 
 840:   The neighboring decision theory does not close this step. Orbit and
 841:   zero problems for linear recurrences already contain the open Skolem
 842:   problem \cite{OuaknineWorrell2012,TarasovVyalyi2011}, while unrestricted
 843:   multiplicative matrix equations include undecidable families
 844:   \cite{BellEtAl2008MatrixEquations}. Neither observation is a reduction
 845:   for the companion-form digit matrices here, and conditions
 846:   \textup{(U1)--(U3)} must also be preserved. Thus general decidability,
 847:   undecidability, and any hardness classification remain open; the proved
 848:   effective statement is exactly the positive semidecision above. The
 849:   Perron-recurrence subclass of greedy linear numeration bases is resolved
 850:   separately below.
 851: \end{remark}

# Literature and Novelty Check

Checked on 2026-08-02.  The arXiv searches below used the public Atom API
endpoint `https://export.arxiv.org/api/query`; DOI metadata was checked against
the Crossref REST API.  The purpose of the search was to delimit the theorem
claims, not to infer novelty from a null keyword search.

## arXiv API queries

The following literal `search_query` values were sent to the API (20 results
maximum per query):

- `all:"context-free" AND all:prime AND all:language`: four returned records,
  none on prime numeration languages.  The only mathematically related record
  was Borchert--Rampersad, *Inverse Star, Borders, and Palstars*,
  arXiv:1008.2440; it does not concern prime recognizability.
- `all:Pisot AND all:numeration AND all:automata`: eight returned records,
  including Carton--Couvreur--Delacourt--Ollinger,
  *Linear Recurrence Sequence Automata and the Addition of Abstract Numeration
  Systems*, arXiv:2406.09868 (conference DOI
  10.1007/978-3-031-97548-6_7); Charlier--Cisternino--Stipulanti,
  *Robustness of Pisot-regular sequences*, arXiv:2006.11126,
  DOI 10.1016/j.aam.2020.102151; Massuir--Peltomaki--Rigo,
  *Automatic sequences based on Parry or Bertrand numeration systems*,
  arXiv:1810.11081, DOI 10.1016/j.aam.2019.03.003; and
  Frougny--Steiner, *Minimal weight expansions in Pisot bases*,
  arXiv:0803.2874, DOI 10.1515/JMC.2008.017.  None of the returned records
  states prime-language REG- or CF-immunity.
- `all:"prime language" AND all:automata`: no returned records.
- `all:"abstract numeration systems" AND all:prime`: no returned records.
- `all:Ogden AND all:"interchange lemma"`: no returned records.  These are
  pre-arXiv classical papers and are cited by DOI below.
- Exact-title queries confirmed Dubbe, *The automaticity of the set of
  primes*, arXiv:2409.04314, DOI 10.1016/j.tcs.2025.115480, and Yuen,
  *Kleene Star of the Primes is not Regular in Any Base*, arXiv:2203.16088.

The arXiv API search is negative evidence only.  In particular, the older
JACM papers settle a stronger fixed-base question than their titles alone
suggest, so the paper does not advertise fixed-base CF-immunity as new.

## Exact classical citations

- William Ogden, "A helpful result for proving inherent ambiguity,"
  *Mathematical Systems Theory* 2 (1968), 191--194,
  DOI 10.1007/BF01694004.  This is the marked-position pumping lemma now
  called Ogden's lemma.
- William Ogden, Rockford J. Ross, and Karl Winklmann, "An 'Interchange
  Lemma' for Context-Free Languages," *SIAM Journal on Computing* 14 (1985),
  410--415, DOI 10.1137/0214031.  The present proof does not claim or reproduce
  their interchange lemma; ordinary context-free pumping suffices after a
  fixed-prefix quotient, while Ogden's lemma gives an alternative way to
  localize pumping beyond an eventual-recurrence transient.
- J. Hartmanis and H. Shank, "On the Recognition of Primes by Automata,"
  *Journal of the ACM* 15 (1968), 382--389,
  DOI 10.1145/321466.321470.
- M. P. Schutzenberger, "A Remark on Acceptable Sets of Numbers,"
  *Journal of the ACM* 15 (1968), 300--303,
  DOI 10.1145/321450.321461.  Contemporary citation records describe the
  Hartmanis--Shank and Schutzenberger conclusion as: no infinite set of
  base-`b` primes is recognized by a finite automaton or a pushdown automaton.
  Thus fixed-base prime CF-immunity is prior art.
- M. Minsky and S. Papert, "Unrecognizable Sets of Numbers,"
  *Journal of the ACM* 13 (1966), 281--286,
  DOI 10.1145/321328.321337.
- D. P. Allen, Jr., "On a characterization of the nonregular set of primes,"
  *Journal of Computer and System Sciences* 2 (1968), 464--467,
  DOI 10.1016/S0022-0000(68)80038-8.

## Pisot and numeration references

- Christiane Frougny, "Representations of numbers and finite automata,"
  *Mathematical Systems Theory* 25 (1992), 37--60,
  DOI 10.1007/BF01368783.  This is the normalization/finite-transducer source
  used for linear numeration systems whose characteristic polynomial has the
  Pisot property.
- Veronique Bruyere and Georges Hansel, "Bertrand numeration systems and
  recognizability," *Theoretical Computer Science* 181 (1997), 17--43,
  DOI 10.1016/S0304-3975(96)00260-5.
- Christiane Frougny and Boris Solomyak, "Finite beta-expansions,"
  *Ergodic Theory and Dynamical Systems* 12 (1992), 713--723,
  DOI 10.1017/S0143385700007057.
- Stephane Fabre, "Substitutions et beta-systemes de numeration,"
  *Theoretical Computer Science* 137 (1995), 219--236,
  DOI 10.1016/0304-3975(95)91132-A.
- P. B. A. Lecomte and M. Rigo, "Numeration Systems on a Regular Language,"
  *Theory of Computing Systems* 34 (2001), 27--44,
  DOI 10.1007/S002240010014.  This is cited to distinguish abstract
  numeration systems from the narrower linear Pisot `U`-systems proved here.

## Novelty boundary used in the manuscript

The following assertions are treated as new only relative to the literature
located above and are stated with their full hypotheses:

1. The two-pump block-action congruence modulo the square of the represented
   value and the resulting coprime-quotient chain for an arbitrary
   context-free sublanguage of canonical Zeckendorf representations.
2. CF-immunity of the Zeckendorf prime language, and the stronger unbounded
   distinct-prime-divisor consequences for context-free Zeckendorf
   sublanguages.
3. Prime REG- and CF-immunity for the explicitly defined class of positional
   linear Pisot `U`-systems: integer weights, finite digit alphabet, injective
   canonical representations ordered by length, and an eventual integral
   recurrence with nonzero trailing coefficient.  The proof uses only the
   recurrence block action; Frougny normalization supplies the standard
   finite-state canonical syntax/normalization interface for Pisot
   `U`-systems.

No claim is made for every object sometimes called a "Pisot numeration
system."  In particular, arbitrary real-base beta-shifts, non-positional
abstract numeration systems, systems without an eventual integral recurrence,
and non-injective redundant representations are explicit open interfaces.
The Pisot-unit hypothesis is needed for the unrestricted deep-quotient and
induced-tree conclusions and for unconditional bounded-omega immunity. For a
nonunit recurrence, primes dividing the trailing coefficient make the
companion action singular modulo some composite values. The local-adic
dichotomy nevertheless gives prime and bounded-Omega MCF-immunity; bounded
distinct-prime support can escape only through unbounded valuation at a prime
dividing the trailing coefficient.

## Multiple-context-free and adic extension (2026-08-03)

The public arXiv Atom endpoint at https://export.arxiv.org/api/query was queried
with the following literal searches (and with a single-record
search_query=id:2509.02117 control):

- all:"multiple context-free" AND all:pumping;
- all:"multiple context-free" AND all:prime;
- all:"adic topology" AND all:integers;
- all:"Cantor-Bendixson" AND all:"prime factors";
- all:"divisibility tree" AND all:language.

Every API request returned HTTP 429 after retries with an identifying user
agent and four-second spacing. These failures are not treated as null search
results. The corresponding arXiv web searches, Crossref bibliographic
searches, DBLP metadata, and exact-source checks located no paper asserting an
MCFL prime-immunity theorem for recurrence numeration, an MCFL-induced local
congruence orbit, or the induced divisibility-tree conclusion.

The following published inputs delimit what is not new:

- H. Seki, T. Matsumura, M. Fujii, and T. Kasami, "On multiple
  context-free grammars," *Theoretical Computer Science* 88 (1991),
  191--229, DOI 10.1016/0304-3975(91)90374-B. Its Lemma 3.2 is the weak
  pumping lemma supplying one synchronized family with 2k pumped factors.
- M. Kanazawa, G. M. Kobele, J. Michaelis, S. Salvati, and R. Yoshinaka,
  "The Failure of the Strong Pumping Lemma for Multiple Context-Free
  Languages," *Theory of Computing Systems* 55 (2014), 250--278,
  DOI 10.1007/S00224-014-9534-Z.
- A. Duncan, M. Elder, L. Frenkel, and M. Liu, "A substitution lemma for
  multiple context-free languages," *International Journal of Algebra and
  Computation* (2026), DOI 10.1142/S0218196726500463,
  arXiv:2509.02117. The direct arXiv PDF was checked; its Lemma 5.3 quotes
  the exact Seki weak-pumping factorization used in the manuscript.
- K. A. Broughan, "Adic Topologies for the Rational Integers," *Canadian
  Journal of Mathematics* 55 (2003), 711--723,
  DOI 10.4153/CJM-2003-030-3. The Cambridge primary PDF was checked.
  Theorem 2.4 gives the rational-space classification, Corollary 3.1 gives
  the Cantor completion, and Theorem 4.3 treats full-adic prime-factor
  strata counted with multiplicity.

Accordingly, the manuscript cites the Seki pumping family and Broughan's
topological classifications as inputs. The claims retained as new are the
combination with a fixed recurrence block orbit, the deleted-prime intrinsic
Cantor--Bendixson rank for distinct prime support with bounded local
valuations, the nonunit escape dichotomy and MCF-immunity consequences, and
the unit-system arbitrary-depth quotient and induced-tree constructions.

- `all:"multiple context-free" AND all:prime`.

The broader query `all:"Pisot numeration" AND all:prime` returned only
Adrian-Maria Scheerer, "Normality in Pisot Numeration Systems,"
arXiv:1503.08047, published in *Ergodic Theory and Dynamical Systems* 37

studies Condition F, topological
groups, and torus factors; it does not state the minimal-reachable determinant
lemma or the base-\(p\)/inflated-Fibonacci escape separation.

The cyclic-subspace identities used in the oracle response---equality of the
minimal and characteristic polynomials on a cyclic restriction, and recovery
of the minimal polynomial from the first Krylov dependence---are standard
rational-canonical-form facts; see F. R. Gantmacher, *The Theory of Matrices*,
vol. I, Chelsea, 1959, Chapter VI. They are not retained as new theorem
content.

Crossref bibliographic searches for `multiple context-free Pisot numeration

Fibonacci recurrence nonunit Pisot`, and `affine semigroup p-adic numeration`

## Geometric-ray characterization (2026-08-07)

The public arXiv Atom API returned zero records for each of the following
literal queries:

- \`all:"multiple context-free" AND all:"geometric progression"\`;
- \`all:"multiple context-free" AND all:"bounded prime support"\`;
- \`all:"multiple context-free" AND all:"linear recurrence"\`;
- \`all:"multiple context-free" AND all:"S-unit"\`;
- \`all:"Pisot numeration" AND all:"geometric progression"\`;
- \`all:"numeration system" AND all:"bounded prime support"\`;
- \`all:"linear MCFG" AND all:"geometric progression"\`;
- \`all:"semidecidable" AND all:"multiple context-free" AND all:"numeration"\`.

Crossref and OpenAlex searches for the corresponding unquoted combinations
returned general references on MCFGs, geometric-progression-free sets, and
Pisot numeration, but no work combining an MCFL sublanguage, bounded prime
support, and an exact geometric numerical ray. This is negative novelty
evidence only.

Two published inputs delimit the claim. Seki--Matsumura--Fujii--Kasami,
*Theoretical Computer Science* 88 (1991), 191--229, supply the weak
synchronized pumping family. J.-H. Evertse, "On sums of \(S\)-units and
linear recurrences," *Compositio Mathematica* 53 (1984), 225--244,
Theorem 3, proves unbounded prime-ideal support in ratios of terms of a
nondegenerate recurrence with at least two characteristic roots. The latter
excludes a fixed-\(S\)-unit nondegenerate subsequence; Schur's polynomial
prime-divisor theorem handles the remaining one-root polynomial factor.
Neither published input states the manuscript's equivalence with the
existence of a finite-fan-out synchronized MCFG ray, nor the resulting
positive-semidecidability statement.

## Refreshed prior-art and decision-target audit (2026-08-08)

The two referee-critical classical records were rechecked against their
publisher metadata and indexed abstracts, rather than inferred from their
titles. Crossref gives DOI 10.1145/321466.321470 for Hartmanis--Shank and DOI
10.1145/321450.321461 for Schutzenberger. The Hartmanis--Shank abstract states
that neither the primes nor any infinite subset of the primes, in fixed-base
notation, is accepted by a pushdown or finite automaton. The Schutzenberger
abstract states that the two negative results on acceptable sets are extended
to arbitrary context-free languages. CORE's Cornell record reproduces the
Hartmanis--Shank abstract; Semantic Scholar and Unpaywall confirm the records
and publisher copies. The manuscript already cites both papers where it calls
fixed-base prime CF-immunity classical and explicitly says that their proofs
are not reproduced as new.

The reference lists supplied by Crossref were also inspected. They lead to
the already cited Minsky--Papert paper on unrecognizable sets, the classical
context-free-language sources, and the contemporary finite-automata work.
No item in those lists concerns Zeckendorf or Pisot numeration, MCFLs, a
recurrence block action, or the geometric-ray criterion.

A live arXiv API query for `all:"multiple context-free" AND all:prime`
returned zero records. Google Scholar searches for `"primes" "multiple
context-free" language`, `"Pisot numeration" prime language automata`, and
`"S-unit" "linear recurrence" geometric progression` returned the standard
MCFG pumping literature, general numeration references, and recurrence/S-unit
sources, but no prime-language result in Pisot numeration. Crossref searches
confirmed the two 1968 JACM papers and their citation trails. A zbMATH API
keyword search for `multiple context-free prime numeration` returned no
record. OpenAlex exhausted its anonymous daily query budget during the audit,
and the first Semantic Scholar search was rate-limited; these failures are
recorded as failures, not as negative results.

The proposed decision target does not define a new problem for the class
proved in the manuscript. Theorem~3.18 proves that the prime representation
language of every system satisfying (U1)--(U4) is MCF-immune, and Euclid's
theorem plus canonical representation makes that language infinite.
Consequently it is never an MCFL. For effectively presented regular canonical
linear Pisot U-systems, the requested terminating algorithm is therefore the
constant algorithm returning `NO`; this is an immediate corollary, not a
tier-raising decision theorem.

The genuinely nontrivial nearby decision problem is whether the bounded-
outside-support condition in Theorem~3.14 holds, equivalently whether a
geometric synchronized scheme exists. Corollary~3.15 gives only positive
semidecidability. A full decision procedure would require an effective finite
bound on the number and lengths of synchronized pumped blocks, or an
equivalent negative certificate for the absence of exact geometric identities
among recurrence sequences generated by finite transition and affine-matrix
semigroups. No such bound follows from the cited pumping or recurrence
theorems; general zero/equality questions for linear recurrences already meet
Skolem-type barriers. The present tools therefore do not justify promoting
that semidecision procedure to a decision theorem.

## Deep exploration: bounded-support classification (2026-08-08)

Six theorem candidates were compared on a five-point scale (reach, novelty,
value).

1. General decidability of geometric synchronized schemes: (2, 5, 5).
   Corollary 3.15 checks any guessed scheme, but no finite bound on fan-out or
   block length is available. The nearest decision literature is the Skolem
   problem for linear recurrences, including Min Sha,
   "Effective results on the Skolem Problem for linear recurrence sequences,"
   J. Number Theory 201 (2019), DOI 10.1016/j.jnt.2018.08.012.
2. Classification for standard linear Pisot systems: (5, 4, 5). Greedy length
   thresholds and Pisot asymptotics force a geometric ratio to equal a power
   of the dominant root. The nearest numeration work is Frougny's finite
   normalization theory and Sadahiro's "Multiple points of tilings associated
   with Pisot numeration systems," DOI 10.1016/j.tcs.2006.02.017; neither
   concerns bounded prime support or MCFLs.
3. Prime support of every geometric ratio is contained in the minimal tail
   constant: (5, 4, 4). This follows from the manuscript's local return
   congruence. Evertse's 1984 S-unit recurrence theorem is the nearest
   arithmetic input, but it does not give this numeration-specific local
   restriction.
4. Remove the valuation-only escape alternative for nonintegral Pisot bases:
   (5, 4, 5). This is the universal negative half of candidate 2. The nearest
   prior work is again Pisot normalization/recognizability, not prime-support
   behavior of MCFL sublanguages.
5. Compute the local Cantor--Bendixson behavior with unbounded bad-prime
   valuations: (5, 3, 3). Broughan, "Adic Topologies for the Rational
   Integers," DOI 10.4153/CJM-2003-030-3, is nearest; the claim would mainly
   sharpen why the manuscript's bounded local valuations are necessary.
6. Extend the quantitative density theorem to bounded-ambiguity automata:
   (2, 2, 3). The deterministic stochastic decomposition does not control
   multiplicities or cancellation. Nearby ambiguity work includes Christian
   Herzog, "Pushdown automata with bounded nondeterminism and bounded
   ambiguity," DOI 10.1016/S0304-3975(96)00267-8, but it supplies no required
   prime-slice asymptotics.

Live API checks used the arXiv Atom API, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, and
zbMATH. Exact arXiv queries combining "multiple context-free" or "Pisot
numeration" with "geometric progression" or "bounded prime support" returned
zero entries. Crossref returned separate Pisot numeration, recurrence
prime-divisor, adic-topology, and ambiguity papers, with no combined result.
Semantic Scholar's broad search endpoint returned HTTP 429, so DOI lookups
were used to confirm Sadahiro (2006), Broughan (2003), and the classical
second-order recurrence prime-divisor record. Exact combined zbMATH searches
returned no entries; broader searches found 120 Pisot-numeration records and
105 multiple-context-free-language records, but no overlap matching the new
classification. These are negative search results, not a priority proof.

Candidates 2--4 were proved together. In a geometric synchronized scheme,
the finite-group block return modulo \(p^{v_p(c)+1}\) excludes every
\(p\mid b\) with \(p\nmid c_0\). For a linear Pisot greedy system, a scheme
of word lengths \(L+Dt\) satisfies
\[
U_{L+Dt-1}\le cb^t<U_{L+Dt},
\]
so \(b=\beta^D\). A nonintegral Pisot number cannot have a positive integral
power: every conjugate would then have modulus \(\beta>1\). Conversely, an
integer root \(B\) supplies the canonical ray \(0^{J+t}1\) of values
\(U_JB^t\). Thus the bounded-outside-support property is decidable on the
standard linear Pisot class and is positive exactly in degree one.

## Tier-up decision audit and refreshed prior art (2026-08-10)

The arXiv Atom API, Crossref, Semantic Scholar, and zbMATH Open APIs were
searched before the new proof audit. Exact arXiv combinations of `multiple
context-free` with `geometric progression` returned no record; searches for
effective linear-recurrence decision problems returned Min Sha's arXiv
1505.07147 and the current Skolem literature. Crossref confirmed the metadata
for Sha (DOI 10.1016/j.jnt.2018.08.012), Tarasov--Vyalyi (DOI
10.1007/978-3-642-20712-9_24), Ouaknine--Worrell (DOI
10.1007/978-3-642-33512-9_3), and Bell--Halava--Harju--Karhumaki--Potapov
(DOI 10.1142/S0218196708004925). Semantic Scholar's DOI lookup for Sha
succeeded and exposed the surrounding orbit/Skolem citation graph; later
broad searches were rate-limited and are not treated as negative evidence.
zbMATH returned the Skolem decision survey and Tarasov--Vyalyi's regular-
language/orbit work, while the exact MCFL/numeration/geometric query returned
no record.

The nearest mechanism remains the pair of classical inputs already used:
Seki--Matsumura--Fujii--Kasami's weak synchronized pumping lemma and
Evertse's Theorem 3 on unbounded prime-ideal support in quotients of a
nondegenerate recurrence. The nearest algorithmic boundary is
Tarasov--Vyalyi's equivalence between an orbit-hitting problem and a regular-
language intersection problem, together with the still-open general Skolem
problem surveyed by Ouaknine--Worrell. Bell et al. prove undecidability for
unrestricted multiplicative matrix equations, but their matrices do not
preserve the companion-form digit action or canonical conditions (U1)--(U3),
so this is not an undecidability result for the manuscript's promise class.

The attempted full decision procedure stops at witness compression. For a
fixed synchronized scheme, DFA acceptance and the identity `N(t)=c b^t` are
decidable. To decide negative instances one needs a computable bound, from
the DFA and minimal tail recurrence, on fan-out and total block length of a
smallest positive witness. Ordinary DFA cycle deletion does not supply it:
two words with the same DFA endpoints can have different affine recurrence
matrices, and replacing one by the other can destroy `N(t+1)=b N(t)`. No
located result provides this bound, and no promise-preserving reduction was
obtained. General decidability, undecidability, and hardness therefore remain
open; only the existing positive semidecision and the linear Pisot decision
theorem are integrated.

The Perron argument is mathematically sound: minimality makes the dominant coefficient nonzero, the greedy length bounds force \(b=\beta^D\), and conjugating that rational identity rules out degree \(>1\). I found one small exposition gap in the non-Pisot example: the text asserted the quotient upper bound without showing its one-line induction, so I’m closing that before the final verification.

id               : http://arxiv.org/abs/2211.02365v6
title            : On Robustness for the Skolem, Positivity and Ultimate Positivity Problems
updated          : 2024-06-04T09:29:53Z
link             : {link, link, link}
summary          : The Skolem problem is a long-standing open problem in linear dynamical systems: can a linear 
                   recurrence sequence (LRS) ever reach 0 from a given initial configuration? Similarly, the 
                   positivity problem asks whether the LRS stays positive from an initial configuration. Deciding 
                   Skolem (or positivity) has been open for half a century: the best known decidability results are 
                   for LRS with special properties (e.g., low order recurrences). But these problems are easier for 
                   "uninitialized" variants, where the initial configuration is not fixed but can vary arbitrarily: 
                   checking if there is an initial configuration from which the LRS stays positive can be decided in 
                   polynomial time (Tiwari in 2004, Braverman in 2006). In this paper, we consider problems that lie 
                   between the initialized and uninitialized variants. More precisely, we ask if 0 (resp. negative 
                   numbers) can be avoided from every initial configuration in a neighborhood of a given initial 
                   configuration. This can be considered as a robust variant of the Skolem (resp. positivity) problem. 
                   We show that these problems lie at the frontier of decidability: if the neighbourhood is given as 
                   part of the input, then robust Skolem and robust positivity are Diophantine hard, i.e., solving 
                   either would entail major breakthroughs in Diophantine approximations, as happens for (non-robust) 
                   positivity. However, if one asks whether such a neighbourhood exists, then the problems turn out to 
                   be decidable with PSPACE complexity. Our techniques also allow us to tackle robustness for ultimate 
                   positivity, which asks whether there is a bound on the number of steps after which the LRS remains 
                   positive. There are two variants depending on whether we ask for a "uniform" bound on this number 
                   of steps. For the non-uniform variant, when the neighbourhood is open, the problem turns out to be 
                   tractable, even when the neighbourhood is given as input.
